# OIDC login: wiring Google, Microsoft Entra, GitHub, and Okta into your app

OpenID Connect lets your app sign people in with their Google, Microsoft Entra or Okta account; GitHub sign-in uses plain OAuth 2.0 without ID tokens. This guide helps your AI assistant wire them in securely, including the code flow with PKCE, validated ID tokens, and a per-provider allowlist check.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/oidc-integration.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against OpenID Connect Core 1.0, OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, and OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0; 4 further sources are pinned to a commit and 10 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-21; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 52 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

Adding "Sign in with Google" takes an afternoon; the recurring defects are in what happens after the redirect comes back: an unvalidated ID token, an account matched by email, or an app that admits every Google or Microsoft account in existence because nobody checked whose it was. This guide gives the one flow every recipe shares, the exact claim to check per provider, the registration steps, and library pointers. Choosing a provider is covered in [identity-providers.md](identity-providers.md); login placed in front of an app without code changes is covered in [cloud-identity-proxies.md](cloud-identity-proxies.md). Authorizing an MCP client to a remote server layers additional obligations on this flow and is covered in [mcp-clients.md](mcp-clients.md).

## 1. The flow every recipe uses

Authorization code flow with PKCE from a server-side (confidential) client. RFC 9700 requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for all others, web applications included; it requires exact string matching of redirect URIs at the authorization server; and it says clients should not use the implicit grant (`response_type=token`).

1. Register the exact callback URL at the provider (scheme, host, path, trailing slash). Prefix or wildcard matching is what makes redirect-based code theft work.
2. Send a random `state` bound to the browser session and a random `nonce` on every authorization request, plus `code_challenge` with `code_challenge_method=S256`. Scopes: `openid email profile`.
3. Exchange the code at the token endpoint from the server, with the client secret and the `code_verifier` that produced the `code_challenge`. Never from the browser.
4. Validate the ID token before trusting any claim (OpenID Connect Core section 3.1.3.7): the signature against the key set at the provider's `jwks_uri`, using an algorithm you pinned (Core says RS256 unless you registered another; the discovery document lists the provider's `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`) rather than whatever the token header names; `iss` exactly equals the issuer you configured; `aud` contains your client ID and lists no audience you do not trust (per OIDC Core, reject a token carrying an untrusted additional audience, and where an `azp` claim is present confirm it equals your client ID); `exp` is in the future; `nonce` equals the one you sent.
5. Start a server-side session and give the browser only a session cookie marked `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and `SameSite` per [authentication.md](authentication.md). Do not put ID or access tokens in `localStorage` or a script-readable cookie; nothing in the browser needs them. Keep authorization codes and tokens out of server logs, traces, and analytics, set `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on the callback, and redirect to a clean URL so the code does not linger in browser history or a `Referer` header. This login recipe does not request offline access, but refresh-token issuance is provider-specific, so treat any refresh token you receive as a server-side secret, send it only to the token endpoint, and revoke it on offboarding.
6. Link the identity to a local account by the pair (issuer, `sub`). OpenID Connect Core section 5.7 says `email`, `phone_number`, and `preferred_username` are not guaranteed unique and may change; Google and Microsoft document the same for their `email` claims. Matching by email alone lets a re-used or unverified address take over an account.
7. Logout: destroy the server-side session and expire the cookie; where the discovery document lists an `end_session_endpoint`, also redirect there with `id_token_hint` and a registered `post_logout_redirect_uri` (Entra: `/oauth2/v2.0/logout`).

The discovery document at `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` supplies the endpoints and `jwks_uri`; for tenant-specific discovery its `issuer` value must be identical to the prefix you fetched it from (Entra's tenant-independent `common`/`organizations` metadata instead returns a templated issuer, handled below). Every library in section 4 reads it for you.

## 2. Login is not authorization

The provider proves who the person is. Whether they may use your app is your check, run after token validation and before the session exists, against an allowlist. The claim differs per provider:

- **Google**: the `hd` claim in the ID token must equal your Workspace domain (`example.com`). The `hd` request parameter only optimizes the account picker; Google's documentation says not to rely on it for access control and to validate the returned `hd` claim. Treat a missing `hd` claim as a rejection.
- **Microsoft Entra**: the `tid` claim must be your tenant ID and `iss` must be `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant-id>/v2.0`. Register the app as **Single tenant only** when only your organization signs in. The `organizations` authority accepts any Entra tenant and `common` also accepts personal accounts; the issuer then varies per tenant, so an app on those authorities that does not check `tid` (or the GUID in `iss`) admits every Microsoft account. Microsoft documents `email` and `preferred_username` as mutable and unfit for authorization; key the local account on `oid` or `sub` plus `tid`.
- **GitHub**: GitHub OAuth apps speak OAuth 2.0, not OpenID Connect; there is no discovery document and no ID token. After the token exchange call `GET https://api.github.com/user` for the identity, then check `GET /user/memberships/orgs/<org>` (200 with `"state": "active"` means a member; 404 means not affiliated) or a team with `GET /orgs/<org>/teams/<team_slug>/memberships/<username>` (200 with `"state": "active"`; the REST reference documents `pending` for an unaccepted invitation, and 404 means no membership). Both need the `read:org` scope. Key the local account on the numeric `id` from `/user`, not the `login`.
- **Okta**: add a `groups` claim to the ID token (org authorization server: **Applications > Applications >** your app **> Sign On**, edit the OpenID Connect ID Token section, filter **Matches regex** `.*`; the client must also request the `groups` scope) and require membership of a named group. The claim holds at most 100 groups and the request fails beyond that; use a narrower filter in large orgs.

The default for an identity that passes none of these is to reject and log it, never to create a pending account an admin later forgets to review.

## 3. Register the app at each provider

Keep the web app client secret confidential, as [RFC 6749 section 10.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6749.html#section-10.1) requires. Prefer a secret manager (this guide's advice; OWASP lists [secret managers](https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/blob/668ba7db3d0da5868b8a0305c259f7f6914a6ecd/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md#L313) as an option). In containers, use an orchestrator-mounted secret or secret-store fetch where possible; use a runtime environment variable only if those are unavailable, per [OWASP container guidance](https://github.com/OWASP/CheatSheetSeries/blob/668ba7db3d0da5868b8a0305c259f7f6914a6ecd/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.md#L462-L464). Never commit the secret to a repository or bake it into an image (this guide's advice; [Docker documents](https://github.com/docker/docs/blob/4e9a5751518ed8223a8dcde53693badddd72604f/content/manuals/build/building/secrets.md#L13-L15) that build `ARG` and `ENV` persist in the final image). See [secrets.md](secrets.md). Substitute the callback path your library expects for `https://app.example.com/auth/callback`.

- **Google**: Google Cloud console **Clients** page (`https://console.developers.google.com/auth/clients`); create an OAuth client and add the redirect URI. The match is exact, including scheme, case, and trailing slash. Discovery: `https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`; `iss` is `https://accounts.google.com` or `accounts.google.com`.
- **Microsoft Entra**: Microsoft Entra admin center, **Entra ID > App registrations > New registration**; under **Supported account types** choose **Single tenant only** unless you are building for other organizations. Then **Authentication > Add a platform > Web** and add the redirect URI. Record the Application (client) ID and create a client secret. Discovery: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration` with `<tenant>` your directory (tenant) ID; prefer this tenant-specific form for a single-tenant app. `common` and `organizations` return a templated issuer `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenantid}/v2.0`, so validate by substituting the token's `tid` into the template, confirming `tid` is a GUID and the result equals `iss` exactly, restricting the signing key by its published `issuer` scope, and enforcing your tenant allowlist; never relax issuer validation to make `common` work.
- **GitHub**: profile picture **> Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App**; set the Authorization callback URL. Authorize at `https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize` with `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope=read:user read:org`, `state`, and PKCE (`code_challenge` with `code_challenge_method=S256`; GitHub does not accept `plain`); exchange at `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` with `client_id`, `client_secret`, `code`, the `code_verifier` that produced the challenge, and the same `redirect_uri`. Always send `redirect_uri`; when it is absent GitHub uses the first registered callback. Apps that had a single callback URL before August 3, 2026 keep wildcard matching for it, which accepts any subdomain or subdirectory of the registered host; disable wildcard matching in the app settings so the callback must match exactly.
- **Okta**: Admin Console, **Applications and Resources > Applications > Create App Integration**, sign-in method **OIDC - OpenID Connect**, type **Web Application**; set the sign-in and sign-out redirect URIs and the assignment (Okta's guide allows everyone in the org; narrow it to a group). Client ID and secret are on the **General** tab under Client Credentials. Discovery: `https://<org>.okta.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` for the org authorization server, `https://<org>.okta.com/oauth2/<authorizationServerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration` for a custom one; `iss` equals that prefix.

## 4. Libraries

Use a maintained library; do not hand-parse JWTs. The snippets are from each library's documentation; the section 2 check is yours to add.

- **Node, [openid-client](https://github.com/panva/openid-client)** (`npm install openid-client`):
  ```javascript
  let config = await client.discovery(server, clientId, clientSecret)
  client.enableNonRepudiationChecks(config)   // enforce rule 4's ID-token signature check; by default openid-client trusts the token-endpoint TLS channel for the code flow
  let code_verifier = client.randomPKCECodeVerifier()
  let code_challenge = await client.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(code_verifier)
  let state = client.randomState()
  let nonce = client.randomNonce()
  let redirectTo = client.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, { redirect_uri, scope, code_challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256', state, nonce })
  // callback (store code_verifier, state, and nonce in the initiating browser's server-side session, not local variables):
  let tokens = await client.authorizationCodeGrant(config, currentUrl, { pkceCodeVerifier: code_verifier, expectedState: state, expectedNonce: nonce })
  ```
- **Node, [Auth.js](https://authjs.dev/)** (`npm install next-auth@beta` for Next.js; SvelteKit and Express integrations exist): providers `next-auth/providers/google`, `github`, `okta`, and `microsoft-entra-id`, configured through `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_ID`, `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_SECRET`, and for Okta and Entra `AUTH_<PROVIDER>_ISSUER`; callbacks land on `/api/auth/callback/<provider>`. Sessions are an encrypted JWT, or a database session ID, in an `HttpOnly` cookie. With the JWT strategy, sign-out destroys the cookie but the token itself stays valid until `exp` unless your server keeps a blocklist (Auth.js documents this limitation); use database sessions, or the blocklist just mentioned, so logout invalidates a copied cookie rather than leaving it valid until `exp` ([authentication.md](authentication.md) requires logout to invalidate the session server-side). Set `AUTH_MICROSOFT_ENTRA_ID_ISSUER` to your tenant's `/v2.0` issuer: the documented default is `common`. Put the section 2 check in the `signIn` callback.
- **Python, [Authlib](https://docs.authlib.org/)** (`pip install Authlib`; Flask, Django, Starlette, FastAPI):
  ```python
  oauth.register('google', client_id='YOUR_CLIENT_ID', client_secret='YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET',
      server_metadata_url='https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration',
      client_kwargs={'scope': 'openid profile email', 'code_challenge_method': 'S256'})
  # login:    return oauth.google.authorize_redirect(redirect_uri)
  # callback: token = oauth.google.authorize_access_token(); claims = token['userinfo']
  ```
- **Go, [go-oidc](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/coreos/go-oidc/v3/oidc)** (`github.com/coreos/go-oidc/v3/oidc`):
  ```go
  provider, err := oidc.NewProvider(ctx, "https://accounts.google.com")
  verifier := provider.Verifier(&oidc.Config{ClientID: clientID})
  idToken, err := verifier.Verify(ctx, rawIDToken)   // signature, issuer, audience, expiry
  ```
  The package documents that it does not check the nonce value: compare `idToken.Nonce` to the one you stored. Leave `SkipIssuerCheck` off.

## 5. Where MFA comes from

Your app does not run the second factor; the provider does, under its policy: Conditional Access in Entra (**Entra ID > Conditional Access > Policies**, grant **Require authentication strength**; a P1 feature per [identity-providers.md](identity-providers.md)), 2-Step Verification in the Google Admin console (**Security > Authentication > 2-step verification**, Enforcement **On** for every user who signs in to the app, as this guide advises), and authentication policies plus the global session policy in Okta. Ordering and options in [mfa.md](mfa.md).

An app can additionally refuse a session whose ID token shows no second factor, where the provider documents the claim. Okta's `amr` array carries values such as `pwd`, `mfa`, `otp`, and `hwk`. For Entra, check the ID token claims reference and the optional claims reference for the `amr` claim and its `mfa` value before relying on it. For Google Workspace, super administrators can enforce 2-Step Verification in the Admin console for all users, or for a selected organizational unit or configuration group. Guide advice: set Enforcement **On** for every user who signs in to the app; no ID token MFA claim was verified for this guide.

GitHub OAuth has no ID token. The pinned [organization policy](https://github.com/github/docs/blob/cb051611377a0d2904411e6157154e9b4953d870/content/organizations/keeping-your-organization-secure/managing-two-factor-authentication-for-your-organization/requiring-two-factor-authentication-in-your-organization.md#L22-L35) says that when an organization requires 2FA, members without 2FA retain membership but cannot access organization resources until they enable it; outside collaborators without 2FA are removed and lose repository access, including their forks of private repositories, and outside collaborators who later disable 2FA are automatically removed.

The [enterprise administration page](https://github.com/github/docs/blob/cb051611377a0d2904411e6157154e9b4953d870/content/admin/managing-accounts-and-repositories/managing-organizations-in-your-enterprise/requiring-two-factor-authentication-for-an-organization.md#L15), which is versioned for GitHub Enterprise Server only (page front matter), describes 2FA support with LDAP or built-in authentication. Its [warning](https://github.com/github/docs/blob/cb051611377a0d2904411e6157154e9b4953d870/content/admin/managing-accounts-and-repositories/managing-organizations-in-your-enterprise/requiring-two-factor-authentication-for-an-organization.md#L30-L32) says that when 2FA is required, members without it retain membership but cannot access enterprise resources until they enable it, while outside collaborators (including bot accounts) without it are removed from the enterprise and its organization and lose repository access, including their forks of private repositories. It also says that outside collaborators who disable 2FA while it is required are automatically removed from the enterprise and its organizations, while members who disable it lose enterprise and organization resource access until they re-enable it. The same page documents [audit-log searches for people automatically removed for non-compliance when 2FA was required](https://github.com/github/docs/blob/cb051611377a0d2904411e6157154e9b4953d870/content/admin/managing-accounts-and-repositories/managing-organizations-in-your-enterprise/requiring-two-factor-authentication-for-an-organization.md#L45).

An active organization membership check establishes membership only; inference from the cited organization and GitHub Enterprise Server policies: membership alone does not prove MFA, because both pages say members without 2FA retain membership; neither establishes the membership API response for such a member. Guide assessment: MFA depends on the organization's effective 2FA requirement and whether it is enabled. Guide advice: verify that requirement before relying on it for MFA. This guide has not established that a member without 2FA fails the app's membership check; test with such an account before relying on it.

GitHub's pinned REST API description says the [list-members endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L39346-L39376) (`GET /orgs/{org}/members`) takes a `2fa_disabled` filter, available only to organization owners, that returns only members without two-factor authentication enabled, so the description treats such accounts as members. Its [membership-check endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L39435-L39473) (`GET /orgs/{org}/members/{username}`) documents 204 when the requester is an organization member and the user is a member, with no 2FA condition stated. Its [authenticated-user membership endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L94998-L95037) (`GET /user/memberships/orgs/{org}`, the check in section 2) returns the authenticated user's membership if they are an active or pending member of the organization, 404 if they are not affiliated with it, and 403 if the request is made by a GitHub App that the organization has blocked, with no 2FA condition stated. This is an API description, not observed API behaviour. Guide assessment: an application that treats organization membership as proof of MFA would accept such a member; whether a given application's check fails for them is unestablished.

Source reading of the same pinned description, which is an API description, not observed API behaviour: the [`org-membership` schema](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L143753-L143830) that the authenticated-user membership endpoint returns, the [`organization-simple`](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L137588-L137660) and [`nullable-simple-user`](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L130511-L130635) schemas it references, and the [`team-membership` schema](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L151708-L151741) that the [team-membership endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L48557-L48606) (`GET /orgs/{org}/teams/{team_slug}/memberships/{username}`, the team check in section 2) returns list no two-factor authentication property, and neither endpoint's description states a 2FA condition. Guide assessment: as described, neither membership response tells an application whether the member has 2FA.

The same pinned description documents an organization-level 2FA field; this is an API description, not observed API behaviour, and this guide has not observed its value. Its [get-an-organization endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L20918-L20942) (`GET /orgs/{org}`) says that when `two_factor_requirement_enabled` is `true`, the organization requires all members, billing managers, outside collaborators, guest collaborators, repository collaborators, or everyone with access to any repository within the organization to enable two-factor authentication; that the authenticated user must be an organization owner to see the full details about an organization; and that OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the `admin:org` scope to see them. The [`organization-full` schema](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L138768-L138772) types the field as a nullable boolean; the description does not say whether the field is among the full details or what a `null` value means. Guide advice: an organization owner can read this field as one way to verify the organization's requirement that this section's advice depends on; it reports the organization's setting, never proof of any one member's MFA, and it is an owner's check, not part of the sign-in app's `read:user read:org` request.

The description also documents an account-level field. Its [get-the-authenticated-user endpoint](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L91436-L91470) (`GET /user`, the identity call in section 2) says that OAuth app tokens and personal access tokens (classic) need the `read:user` scope, or the broader `user` scope, to return the private user response, which includes `two_factor_authentication`, and that tokens without these scopes receive the public user response; the [`private-user` schema](https://github.com/github/rest-api-description/blob/755ee33b4a81d51f6f07a902cce26cbec3b822f2/descriptions/api.github.com/api.github.com.json#L169648-L169719) types `two_factor_authentication` as a boolean and lists it as required. This is an API description, not observed API behaviour; the description gives the field no meaning beyond its name and type, and this guide has not observed its value for any account. Guide assessment: as described, the `read:user` scope that section 3 requests returns the field, but it is at most an account-level flag: it is not proof that a sign-in used a second factor or of any one member's MFA, and whether a given application's check of it rejects an account without 2FA is unestablished.

REASONED: discovery and anonymous-admin probes follow the Google OIDC and OpenID Connect sources below; the protected-endpoint check needs an application deployment, which was not supplied for this metadata review. ```

REASONED: preceding block; the discovery and anonymous-admin probes in the block above, per the guide's cited Google OpenID Connect entry and OpenID Connect Core 1.0 and Discovery 1.0 entry, with the expected outcomes in the block's comment, and this paragraph's framing of the negative tests below, which carry their own declarations; the authoring environment has no network access and no application deployment, so neither probe was sent. At marking time both lines passed bash -n and ShellCheck 0.11.0, and the jq filter printed issuer and jwks_uri from a fixture discovery document and printed nothing, with exit 0, for empty input, so empty output means a failed fetch, not a pass. Negative tests matter more than the happy path:

- REASONED: allowlist refusal per the guide's cited Google OpenID Connect, Microsoft identity platform ID token claims reference, GitHub REST organization and team members, and Okta groups claim entries, with the expected outcome stated in this item; no application deployment and no provider accounts outside an allowlist are available in the authoring environment, and this item names no command, so no part of it ran locally. Sign in with a valid account outside the allowlist (a personal Gmail, another Entra tenant, a GitHub user outside the org, an Okta user outside the group): the provider authenticates, your app refuses and logs the identity.
- REASONED: exact redirect-URI matching per the guide's cited RFC 9700 and the cited Microsoft identity platform OpenID Connect and GitHub OAuth apps authorizing entries; no client registered at any provider is available in the authoring environment, so no authorization request was sent, and this item names no command. A redirect to the edited URI is the exposed state and the provider error the fixed one. Edit `redirect_uri` in the authorization URL (add a path segment or change the host): the provider shows an error and never redirects.
- REASONED: callback state checking per the guide's cited RFC 9700 and openid-client entries; no application deployment is available in the authoring environment and no OIDC client library is installed there, so no callback was replayed, and this item names no command. An accepted callback with a changed state is the exposed state and its rejection the fixed one. Change `state` on the callback URL: your app rejects the callback.
- REASONED: ID-token validation per the guide's cited OpenID Connect Core 1.0 entry (ID token validation 3.1.3.7); no application validation path is available in the authoring environment, so the reader's code was not exercised. At marking time RS256 fixtures signed with an OpenSSL 3.5.5 key ran through PyJWT 2.10.1 with the algorithm, issuer and audience pinned and 60 seconds of leeway: it accepted the control and rejected a token expired 600 seconds earlier, a wrong-aud token and a broken-signature token, while the same library with signature verification off accepted all four, and openssl dgst verified the control's signature and failed the broken one. Two further validly signed fixtures, each with aud listing the client ID and a second audience, ran through the same configuration: it accepted both the one whose azp equals the client ID and the one whose azp names another client, so the shown configuration alone rejects neither a wrong azp nor the untrusted second audience. An explicit comparison of the decoded azp with the client ID accepted the first and rejected the second; whether the reader's validation path makes that comparison was not exercised. Feed your rule-4 ID-token validation path (not the callback, which receives a code and never an ID token) a valid token as a positive control, then fixtures each differing in one property: expired beyond the allowed clock skew, a validly signed token with a wrong `aud`/`azp`, and an otherwise-valid token with a broken signature. It must accept the control and reject every fixture.
- REASONED: logout invalidation per the guide's cited Auth.js session strategies and OWASP Cheat Sheet Series server-side session invalidation entries, with the expected outcomes stated in this item; no application deployment is available in the authoring environment, and this item names no command, so no part of it ran locally. Log out, then reload a protected page: it redirects to login. With database sessions the old session cookie no longer works; with JWT sessions it works until `exp`, so use database sessions or a revocation check; a copied pre-logout cookie must stop authorizing requests after logout, per [authentication.md](authentication.md).

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- code-flow (REASONED; oauth): Use server-side authorization code flow with PKCE; RFC 9700 requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for others, and discourages implicit grant.
- redirect-match (REASONED; oauth): Register an exact callback URI including scheme, host, path and trailing slash; avoid prefix and wildcard matching.
- transaction-binding (REASONED; oauth, core): Generate state bound to the browser session, nonce and S256 code_challenge for each authorization; request openid email profile.
- code-exchange (REASONED; oauth, core): Exchange the code server-side with client secret and the code_verifier that produced the challenge.
- token-signature (REASONED; core, discovery): Validate the ID-token signature against provider JWKS using a pinned algorithm; Core defaults to RS256 unless another was registered.
- token-issuer (REASONED; core): Require iss to equal the configured issuer before trusting claims.
- token-audience (REASONED; core): aud must include the client ID and no untrusted additional audience; confirm azp equals the client ID where present.
- token-expiry-nonce (REASONED; core): Require unexpired exp and nonce equal to the value sent.
- token-leaks (REASONED; oauth): Keep codes and tokens out of logs, traces and analytics; set callback Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and redirect to a clean URL.
- refresh-tokens (REASONED; oauth): No offline access is requested, but provider-specific refresh tokens must remain server-side secrets, go only to the token endpoint and be revoked on offboarding.
- account-linking (REASONED; core, google, entra): Link by issuer and sub, not mutable or non-unique email, phone_number or preferred_username.
- logout (REASONED; logout, entra, owasp-docs): Destroy the server session and cookie; where advertised, redirect to end_session_endpoint with id_token_hint and registered post_logout_redirect_uri; Entra uses /oauth2/v2.0/logout.
- discovery (REASONED; discovery, entra): Fetch issuer/.well-known/openid-configuration for endpoints and jwks_uri; tenant-specific issuer must match, with Entra common/organizations handled separately.
- google-allowlist (REASONED; google): Require verified ID-token hd to equal the Workspace domain; absent hd is rejection and the request parameter is not access control.
- entra-allowlist (REASONED; entra): Require allowed tid and tenant-specific iss; prefer Single tenant only. organizations accepts any Entra tenant, common also personal accounts; key identity by oid or sub plus tid.
- github-identity (REASONED; github): GitHub OAuth has no discovery or ID token; fetch GET https://api.github.com/user and key identity by numeric id, not login.
- github-org (REASONED; github): With read:org, GET /user/memberships/orgs/&lt;org&gt; must return 200 and state active; 404 is unaffiliated.
- github-team (REASONED; github): With read:org, GET /orgs/&lt;org&gt;/teams/&lt;team_slug&gt;/memberships/&lt;username&gt; must return 200 and state active; pending is an unaccepted invitation and 404 is no membership.
- okta-groups (REASONED; okta): Add an ID-token groups claim on the org authorization server and request groups scope; require a named group. More than 100 groups fails, so narrow the filter.
- default-deny (REASONED; google, entra, okta): Reject and log identities outside the allowlist before creating a session; do not create pending accounts by default.
- google-registration (REASONED; google): Register a Google OAuth client and exact callback; discovery is https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration and iss is https://accounts.google.com or accounts.google.com.
- entra-registration (REASONED; entra): Register a Web application, callback and client secret; prefer tenant-specific /v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration discovery for single-tenant apps.
- entra-template (REASONED; entra): For common/organizations, substitute GUID tid into the issuer template, match iss exactly, restrict signing keys by issuer scope and enforce the tenant allowlist.
- github-registration (REASONED; github): Register an OAuth app callback; authorize at /login/oauth/authorize with read:user read:org, state and S256 PKCE; exchange at /login/oauth/access_token with secret, code, verifier and redirect_uri.
- github-callback-default (REASONED; github): Always send redirect_uri: omission selects the first callback. Apps with one callback before August 3, 2026 retain wildcard matching; disable it for exact matching.
- okta-registration (REASONED; okta): Create an OIDC Web Application with sign-in/out URIs and narrowed assignment; use org discovery or /oauth2/&lt;authorizationServerId&gt; discovery, with iss matching the prefix.
- openid-client-signature (REASONED; openid-client): Call enableNonRepudiationChecks: openid-client otherwise trusts token-endpoint TLS in code flow; retain verifier, state and nonce in the initiating browser's server session.
- authjs-config (REASONED; authjs): Auth.js uses AUTH_&lt;PROVIDER&gt;_ID/SECRET and Okta/Entra ISSUER, with /api/auth/callback/&lt;provider&gt;; add the allowlist in signIn and override Entra common with the tenant issuer.
- authjs-revocation (REASONED; authjs): Auth.js JWT-cookie logout leaves a copied token valid until exp unless blocked; use database sessions or a blocklist for server-side revocation.
- authlib-config (REASONED; authlib): Authlib registration uses Google discovery, openid profile email and S256; authorize_redirect and authorize_access_token implement the callback flow.
- go-oidc-verifier (REASONED; go-oidc): go-oidc verifies signature, issuer, audience and expiry; compare idToken.Nonce separately and leave SkipIssuerCheck off.
- entra-mfa (REASONED; entra): Require authentication strength through Entra Conditional Access; check ID-token and optional-claims documentation before relying on amr=mfa.
- google-mfa (REASONED; google): Google Workspace super administrators can enforce 2-Step Verification in the Admin console for all users, or for a selected organizational unit or configuration group. Guide advice: set Enforcement On for every user who signs in to the app; no Google ID-token MFA claim was verified for this guide.
- okta-mfa (REASONED; okta): Use Okta authentication and global-session policies; its amr includes pwd, mfa, otp and hwk.
- verify-discovery (REASONED; google, discovery): The discovery probe reads Google issuer and jwks_uri; this does not demonstrate application authorization.
- verify-anonymous (REASONED; core): Unauthenticated /admin must return 401 or a 302 to provider/login, never 200 or protected content; an unrelated redirect is not success.
- verify-allowlist (REASONED; google, entra, github, okta): A valid account outside the Google domain, Entra tenant, GitHub organization or Okta group authenticates at the provider but is rejected and logged by the app.
- verify-redirect (REASONED; oauth): Changing redirect_uri host or adding a path segment must cause a provider error without redirection.
- verify-state (REASONED; oauth): A changed callback state must be rejected.
- verify-token (REASONED; core): Accept a valid ID-token control and reject one-property fixtures for expiry beyond skew, wrong aud/azp and broken signature in the token-validation path, not the code callback.
- verify-logout (REASONED; authjs, logout, owasp-docs): After logout a protected page returns to login and a copied old cookie stops authorizing; JWT sessions need database replacement or a revocation check.
- server-session (REASONED; authjs, owasp-docs): After token validation and allowlist authorization, create a server-side session and give the browser only a session cookie marked Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
- browser-token-storage (REASONED; oauth, owasp-docs): Do not store ID or access tokens in localStorage or script-readable cookies; this server-side login recipe has no browser need for them.
- client-secret-storage (REASONED; oauth, secret-rfc, owasp-docs, docker-build): Keep the web app client secret confidential. Prefer a secret manager (this guide's advice; OWASP lists it as an option). In containers, use an orchestrator-mounted secret or secret-store fetch where possible, and a runtime environment variable only if those are unavailable. Never commit the secret to a repository or bake it into an image (this guide's advice; Docker documents that build ARG and ENV persist in the final image).
- github-org-mfa (REASONED; github, github-2fa): GitHub OAuth has no ID token; active membership checks establish only membership. Inference: that alone does not prove MFA, as cited policies retain members without 2FA. Guide assessment: MFA depends on the effective org 2FA requirement and whether enabled. Membership API/app-check results for such members are unestablished; guide advice: verify the requirement and test such an account before relying on membership for MFA.
- github-org-mfa-api (REASONED; github-rest-api): GitHub's pinned REST API description says the list-members 2fa_disabled filter returns members without 2FA. It documents 204 from /orgs/&lt;org&gt;/members/&lt;username&gt; when requester and user are both organization members, and /user/memberships/orgs/&lt;org&gt; returning the authenticated user's membership if active or pending; neither states a 2FA condition. This is an API description, not observed behaviour.
- github-org-mfa-api-assessment (REASONED; github-rest-api): Guide assessment: GitHub's pinned REST API description treats accounts without 2FA as organization members, so an app treating org membership as MFA proof would accept such a member; whether a given app's check fails for them is unestablished.
- github-membership-2fa-schema (REASONED; github-rest-api): Source reading of GitHub's pinned REST API description, not observed behaviour: the org-membership schema from /user/memberships/orgs/&lt;org&gt;, its referenced organization-simple and nullable-simple-user schemas, and the team-membership schema list no 2FA property. Guide assessment: as described, neither membership response tells an app whether the member has 2FA.
- github-org-2fa-requirement (REASONED; github-rest-api): Pinned GitHub REST API description, not observed behaviour: GET /orgs/&lt;org&gt; two_factor_requirement_enabled true means members, billing managers, collaborators and others with repository access must enable 2FA; full details need an org owner and, for OAuth app tokens and classic PATs, admin:org. Guide advice: owners may check it as the org's requirement, never as proof of one member's MFA.
- github-user-2fa-field (REASONED; github-rest-api): Pinned GitHub REST API description, not observed behaviour: OAuth app tokens and classic PATs need read:user or user for GET /user to return the private user response, which includes two_factor_authentication (a required boolean there); tokens without them get the public response. Guide assessment: at most an account-level flag, not proof that a sign-in used a second factor or of one member's MFA.
- authjs-session-storage (REASONED; authjs): Auth.js stores an encrypted JWT or database session ID in an HttpOnly cookie; use database sessions or a server blocklist when copied-cookie revocation is required.
- mfa-session-check (REASONED; entra, okta): An app may additionally refuse an ID-token session showing no second factor only where the provider documents that claim; do not assume a portable MFA claim across providers.

# Identity-aware proxies: login in front of the app with no code change

An identity-aware proxy is a provider-run login gate in front of your app. This guide helps your AI assistant configure the AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Cloudflare Access, ngrok and Vercel versions securely, including no route around the proxy, signed identity assertions verified where provided, and authorization still checked.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/cloud-identity-proxies.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against AWS ALB (no recorded version), Vercel production-protection announcement 2026-09-09, and curl minimum write-out version 7.75.0; 5 further sources carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-05; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 51 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

An identity-aware proxy puts a login page in front of an application without changing the application: the cloud's load balancer, platform edge, or tunnel authenticates the user against an identity provider and forwards the request with the user's identity in headers. [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md) documents the pattern for Cloudflare Access; this guide covers the equivalents in AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, ngrok, and Vercel. The pattern fails in two ways: the origin stays reachable around the proxy, or the app trusts an identity header anyone can type. Both are addressed below.

## 1. Rules common to every proxy

1. **The origin accepts traffic only from the proxy.** Bind to loopback behind a tunnel, reference the load balancer's security group, or restrict ingress to the load balancer. If the app also answers directly, the login page is decorative ([cloud-firewalls.md](cloud-firewalls.md)).
2. **The app never trusts a plain identity header.** Where the proxy provides a signed assertion (AWS, Google Cloud, Cloudflare), verify its signature, issuer, audience, and expiry before using any claim. Where the platform documents that clients cannot set the identity headers (Azure), that guarantee holds only for requests that arrived through the platform.
3. **MFA comes from the identity provider behind the proxy, with one exception.** For ALB, IAP, Azure, ngrok, and Vercel, enforce the second factor at the IdP and the proxy inherits it. Cloudflare Access is the exception: it can enforce independent MFA (a TOTP authenticator app, or a WebAuthn security key or biometric) directly in Access without the IdP doing so ([mfa.md](mfa.md), [identity-providers.md](identity-providers.md)).
4. Authorization is still yours: the proxy proves who the user is, and the app or the proxy policy decides what they may do ([authentication.md](authentication.md)).
5. **Fail closed.** The auth layer must deny when it cannot reach a decision: missing auth configuration, an unreachable authorization service, and an unmatched route must never fall through to the app unauthenticated. Test this with a fresh, unauthenticated request against a protected route while the authorization service is unreachable, and require denial, not pass-through; an already-authenticated session is a separate question, since a proxy is not guaranteed to recheck the identity provider on every request.

## 2. AWS Application Load Balancer

A listener rule with an `authenticate-oidc` (any OIDC provider) or `authenticate-cognito` (Cognito user pool, including social and SAML federation) action, followed by a `forward` action. Both action types work only on HTTPS listeners. The `OnUnauthenticatedRequest` field takes `authenticate` (the default: redirect to the IdP), `allow` (forward without claims, for pages with a public view), or `deny` (HTTP 401). `SessionTimeout` defaults to 7 days and can be set as short as 1 second. The IdP must allow `https://<load-balancer-dns-or-cname>/oauth2/idpresponse` as a redirect URL.

```json
{ "Type": "authenticate-oidc",
  "AuthenticateOidcConfig": {
    "Issuer": "https://idp.example.com", "AuthorizationEndpoint": "...", "TokenEndpoint": "...",
    "UserInfoEndpoint": "...", "ClientId": "...", "ClientSecret": "REPLACE_WITH_LONG_RANDOM_VALUE",
    "SessionTimeout": 3600, "OnUnauthenticatedRequest": "deny" },
  "Order": 1 }
```

The load balancer forwards the user claims to targets in `x-amzn-oidc-data`, a JWT signed with ES256. The app must verify that signature (public key from `https://public-keys.auth.elb.<region>.amazonaws.com/<key-id>`, key ID from the JWT header), confirm that the `signer` field in the JWT header is your load balancer's ARN (ALB's audience binding is this signer ARN together with the `client` field, both in the JWT header, not a payload `aud` claim), and confirm the token's `exp` has not passed, before using any claim; AWS publishes the `aws-jwt-verify` library, which performs these checks for you. `x-amzn-oidc-accesstoken` and `x-amzn-oidc-identity` are unsigned legacy headers and cannot be verified, so never use them for identity. Restrict the targets' security group to accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group, and use an HTTPS target group if the claims must be encrypted on the last hop.

## 3. Google Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy

IAP protects App Engine, Cloud Run, Compute Engine, GKE, and on-premises applications served through a supported backend; it does not support backend buckets, so Cloud Storage served directly through a backend bucket is not IAP-gated (Cloud Storage served through an IAP-protected Cloud Run backend is). With Google Accounts or an external IdP through Workforce Identity Federation, a user reaches the app only if they hold the **IAP-secured Web App User** IAM role on the resource. With customer identities through Identity Platform, IAM does not govern access at all: the app must authorize on the claims in the verified IAP assertion, because the IAM role is not enforced in that mode.

IAP adds `x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion`, an ES256 JWT. Verify the signature against the keys at `https://www.gstatic.com/iap/verify/public_key-jwk`, check `iss` is `https://cloud.google.com/iap`, and check `aud` matches your resource (`/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/global/backendServices/SERVICE_ID` for a backend service, `/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/REGION/services/SERVICE_NAME` for Cloud Run, `/projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/apps/PROJECT_ID` for App Engine). The unsigned `x-goog-authenticated-user-email` and `x-goog-authenticated-user-id` headers can be forged by anyone who bypasses IAP; Google's docs describe the JWT as the secure alternative.

Bypass is the main risk. Google's docs say to verify whether backend resources can be reached directly when IAP is enabled on a load balancer, and that IAP on a load balancer secures only traffic through that load balancer, not traffic that reaches a Cloud Run service through its `run.app` URL. Either enable IAP directly on the Cloud Run service (the documented recommendation, no load balancer needed), or disable the default URL or restrict ingress so only the load balancer reaches it. For Compute Engine and GKE, firewall rules must block traffic that does not come through the load balancer.

## 4. Azure App Service and Azure Functions

Built-in authentication ("Easy Auth") is a platform module in front of the app; per the docs no SDK, language, or application code change is required. Providers: Microsoft Entra, Facebook, Google, X, GitHub, Apple (preview at the time of writing), and any OpenID Connect provider. Under **Settings > Authentication**, choose **Require authentication** to reject unauthenticated traffic (as an HTTP 302 redirect to the provider, recommended for websites; or 401, recommended for APIs; or 403 or 404), or **Allow unauthenticated requests** to let the app decide. Enabling the feature redirects all requests to HTTPS regardless of the app's enforce-HTTPS setting (`requireHttps` in the V2 configuration can turn this off; do not). Requiring authentication applies to every path; exceptions need a configuration file with excluded paths.

The app receives the identity in `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL` (Base64 JSON of the claims), `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-ID`, `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-NAME`, and `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-IDP`, with `/.auth/me` available when the token store is on. The docs state that external requests are not allowed to set these headers, so they are present only if App Service set them. With the Entra provider, any user in the tenant can obtain a token by default; restrict the app registration to assigned users if that is not intended.

**Azure Container Apps** uses the same authentication system, run as a sidecar container on each replica, with Microsoft Entra ID, Facebook, GitHub, Google, X, and custom OpenID Connect providers, and the same **Require authentication** / **Allow unauthenticated access** choice and `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-*` headers that external requests cannot set. The docs require HTTPS only: `allowInsecure` must be disabled on the ingress.

**Azure Static Web Apps** authenticates with GitHub and Microsoft Entra ID out of the box on all plans (a registered custom provider replaces the preconfigured ones; X is no longer preconfigured). Sign-in is at `/.auth/login/github` or `/.auth/login/aad`, signed-in users hold the `anonymous` and `authenticated` roles, and route rules in `staticwebapp.config.json` restrict paths by role. The preconfigured Entra provider accepts any Microsoft account; to limit sign-in to one tenant, configure a custom Entra provider.

## 5. Cloudflare Access

Set up the tunnel and Access policy per [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md). Then have the app validate the `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion` header (preferred over the `CF_Authorization` cookie, which is not guaranteed to be passed) against the public keys at `https://<team-name>.cloudflareaccess.com/cdn-cgi/access/certs`, checking that `aud` equals the application's AUD tag and `iss` is your team domain. Access rotates the signing key every 6 weeks with the previous key valid for 7 days, so fetch keys from the endpoint rather than hard-coding them.

## 6. ngrok

ngrok's traffic policy `oauth` action (providers include `google`, `github`, and `microsoft`) and `openid-connect` action (`issuer_url`, `client_id`, `client_secret`, `scopes`) redirect unauthenticated visitors to the provider, so a local tool becomes public only behind a login. Restrict who gets through with an expression on the identity the action exposes:

```yaml
on_http_request:
  - actions:
      - type: oauth
        config:
          provider: google
  - expressions:
      - "!actions.ngrok.oauth.identity.email.endsWith('@example.com')"
    actions:
      - type: deny
        config:
          status_code: 403
```

Use `!(actions.ngrok.oauth.identity.email in ['alice@example.com'])` for an explicit list; the negation matters, because the expression must be true for the `deny` to fire, so it has to match everyone you are turning away, not the one you are letting in. Leaving `client_id` and `client_secret` empty uses ngrok's managed OAuth application for the supported providers. Run with `ngrok http 3000 --traffic-policy-file policy.yml`; the older `--oauth`, `--oauth-allow-domain`, and `--oauth-allow-email` agent flags are marked deprecated in favour of traffic policy. Bind the app to `127.0.0.1` so the tunnel is its only path (rule 1); if the agent host is a cloud VM with the app on `0.0.0.0`, the login is decorative.

## 7. Vercel Deployment Protection

Vercel's protection guards a deployment from the public; it is not your application's user login. **Vercel Authentication** (all plans) admits logged-in team or project members with at least a viewer role, users granted access on request, holders of a shareable link, and automation with the bypass header. **Standard Protection** covers preview deployments and generated deployment URLs but not production domains; the **All Deployments** scope closes that gap, and Vercel's September 9, 2026 change made pairing it with Vercel Authentication free on every plan, including Hobby, rather than Pro and Enterprise only (per Vercel's Deployment Protection changelog; confirm current availability in your own dashboard). Until All Deployments protection is configured, the production domain stays public on every plan. A **Deployment Protection Exception** on a domain disables protection there for existing and future deployments, so review and remove any unintended exception rather than assuming All Deployments covers every URL. **Password Protection** is included on Enterprise and, at the time of writing, available on Pro at USD 20 per month per protected project (the older USD 150 per month Advanced Deployment Protection package is legacy, kept only for existing Pro teams), and is not offered on Hobby; Trusted IPs and Passport (your own IdP) are Enterprise only.

## Verify

REASONED: following block; the cited ALB, IAP and Azure authentication/header documentation defines origin isolation, anonymous denial and forged-header rejection.
```bash
# origin direct. Run this from a host OUTSIDE your cloud network (your laptop on a public connection,
# not the instance or a VPC peer), so the probe actually crosses the cloud boundary you are testing. Read err,
# not the number: it must name a refusal or timeout reaching YOUR address. An HTTP code means the origin
# answered. A resolver failure, a local socket error, or a timeout that did not come from the remote
# address is inconclusive, never a pass.
(                                                       # a subshell, so your own script arguments are untouched
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_PUBLIC_IP'   # replace inside the quotes, keeping them
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit; }
  case "$1" in
    *REPLACE_WITH_*|*YOUR_PUBLIC_IP*|"") echo "substitute your own address on the set -- line above; not probing" ;;
    *) curl -q -g -s -o /dev/null --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
         -w 'http=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "http://$1:3000/" ;;
  esac
)
# guard-conventions: allow probe of an illustrative example host; no reader-substituted placeholder in this probe's argv
curl -q -sSI https://app.example.com/                      # via proxy, no session: 302 to the IdP, or 401/403
# guard-conventions: allow probe of an illustrative example host; no reader-substituted placeholder in this probe's argv
curl -q -sS -D - -H "x-amzn-oidc-identity: admin" \
     -H "X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-NAME: admin" \
     -H "X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email: admin@example.com" \
     https://app.example.com/whoami                      # status line and body: the login redirect or a 401/403, never a 200 echoing "admin"
```

For this change, curl 8.18.0 ran the probe shapes against a loopback HTTP listener standing in for the example host (302 on the anonymous HEAD, 401 on `/whoami`) and against a closed loopback port: `-sI` and `-sSI` both printed the full status line and headers on the listener and both exited 7 on the closed port, where `-sI` printed nothing and `-sSI` printed `curl: (7) Failed to connect ...` on stderr; the forged-header probe printed only the body without `-D -` and the status line, headers and body with it; and the altered-assertion shape delivered `x-amzn-oidc-data` through `--header @-` from stdin (the listener received the header; the value was a dummy, not a real assertion) and exited 7 with the connect error against the closed port. Unsubstituted, empty and two-value guard pastes again printed their refusals without reaching a curl stub, in plain bash and under set -u, and a substituted address reached the stub once. These loopback runs record curl's output shape, not vendor proxy behaviour. A synthetic JSON/base64url claim mutation preserved encoding but mismatched its unchanged HMAC signature; this does not test vendor verifiers. Live exposed bypass or forged-identity acceptance and fixed isolation, anonymous challenge, valid-assertion acceptance and altered-assertion rejection remain unobserved. After logging in, confirm that the app's own identity check reads the signed assertion (`x-amzn-oidc-data`, `x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion`, `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion`) and rejects a forged one. Test directly, because the proxy overwrites the header, so a through-proxy test proves nothing: from the origin host, or a host inside the allowed security group, first send a request carrying a valid, unexpired assertion and confirm the app accepts it (the positive control), then send one whose signature is unchanged but a non-authorizing claim is altered while the token stays well formed (valid JSON and base64url), and require rejection. Both assertions are credentials (restoring the altered claim makes the copy valid again), so never place either in curl's argv, where other local accounts could read it through `ps` and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`: hold the assertion in the positional parameters of a subshell that first runs `trap - DEBUG RETURN ERR`, then `set +x +a +e`, and refuses an empty value or one containing a control character (CONTRIBUTING rule 7; it assumes a clean shell; this keeps the assertion out of argv only, not out of `set -x` tracing or your own account's view of the process, and one pasted on the subshell's `set --` line still enters shell history, so clear it afterwards), and feed it to curl on stdin: `printf 'x-amzn-oidc-data: %s\n' "$1" | curl -q -sS -D - --noproxy '*' --header @- http://127.0.0.1:3000/whoami`. Keep the token well formed, because an app that never checks the signature would still reject a token mangled into malformed JSON, which would not prove verification.

A 200 serving your app's own content means the platform URL bypasses the proxy; a 404 or a transport error is inconclusive, never a pass, because a missing service also returns 404.

- REASONED: fresh-request denial during an authorization outage, per the guide's cited AWS, Authenticate users using an Application Load Balancer and Azure App Service authentication and authorization. No controlled proxy, authorization service or protected route is available; this prose supplies no local outage command or configuration to execute. No outage was observed. The exposed state passes an unauthenticated request to the app; the fixed state denies it even when authorization is unavailable, without asserting that existing sessions terminate. Stop the authorization service, or break its configuration, and send a fresh, unauthenticated request to a protected route: it must be denied, never passed through to the app. This checks that an undecidable auth state fails closed; it does not test whether an already-established session survives the outage, since a proxy is not required to recheck the identity provider on every request.

## Common mistakes

- Enabling IAP or ALB authentication while the Cloud Run `run.app` URL, the instance's public IP, or a second listener still serves the app directly.
- Reading `x-amzn-oidc-identity`, `X-Goog-Authenticated-User-Email`, or a similar unsigned header as the user identity.
- Treating Vercel Authentication as end-user login, or leaving production on Standard Protection and assuming it is covered.
- Using the ngrok `oauth` action without a `deny` rule on email or domain, which lets anyone with a Google account in.

## About the AI assistant section below

This generated section holds the recorded versions, claim statuses and source mappings for AI assistants; use [the prompt at the top](#ai-assistant-prompt). This guide is guidance to verify against your own deployment, not a certification, an audit, or a guarantee of compliance with any standard.

**Version basis**

AI assistants must compare the versions listed below with current releases and treat this guide as guidance, re-verifying version-specific defaults when newer releases exist.

DEMONSTRATED refers to historical evidence in this guide; REASONED records source reasoning, not a live demonstration. Unknown means no version recorded.

Components (recorded basis):

- aws: AWS ALB (unknown)
- iap: Google Cloud IAP (unknown)
- azure: Azure authentication (unknown)
- ngrok: ngrok (unknown)
- vercel: Vercel (unknown)
- vercel-announcement: Vercel production-protection announcement (2026-09-09)
- cf: Cloudflare Access (unknown)
- curl: curl minimum write-out version (7.75.0)

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- origin (REASONED; aws, iap): Origins must accept only proxy traffic through loopback, security-group restriction or ingress controls; direct access bypasses login.
- assertions (REASONED; aws, iap, cf, azure): Verify signed identity assertions before use; Azure's protected-header guarantee applies only to requests through its platform.
- mfa-idp (REASONED; aws, iap, azure, ngrok, vercel): ALB, IAP, Azure, ngrok and Vercel inherit MFA from the identity provider; enforce it there.
- mfa-access (REASONED; cf): Cloudflare Access can enforce independent TOTP or WebAuthn MFA without IdP enforcement.
- authorization (REASONED; aws, iap, ngrok): Authentication proves identity; application or proxy policy must still authorize access.
- fail-closed (REASONED; aws, azure): Missing auth configuration, an unreachable auth service or unmatched route must never pass an unauthenticated request through.
- alb-actions (REASONED; aws): authenticate-oidc or authenticate-cognito precedes forward and works only on HTTPS listeners.
- alb-anonymous (REASONED; aws): OnUnauthenticatedRequest defaults authenticate; allow forwards without claims, and deny returns HTTP 401.
- alb-session (REASONED; aws): SessionTimeout defaults seven days and permits a one-second minimum; the example selects 3600 seconds.
- alb-callback (REASONED; aws): The IdP redirect URL is the load-balancer DNS/CNAME over HTTPS at /oauth2/idpresponse.
- alb-jwt (REASONED; aws): Verify ES256 x-amzn-oidc-data using the regional public-key endpoint and key ID; bind signer ARN/client in the JWT header and check expiry.
- alb-legacy (REASONED; aws): Unsigned x-amzn-oidc-accesstoken and x-amzn-oidc-identity must not supply trusted identity.
- alb-target (REASONED; aws): Restrict target security groups to the ALB security group; use HTTPS targets when claims need last-hop encryption.
- iap-backends (REASONED; iap): IAP protects supported App Engine, Cloud Run, Compute Engine, GKE and on-premises backends, not backend buckets.
- iap-iam (REASONED; iap): Google Accounts and Workforce Identity Federation require IAP-secured Web App User IAM access.
- iap-customer (REASONED; iap): Identity Platform customer identities bypass IAM authorization; the app must authorize verified assertion claims.
- iap-jwt (REASONED; iap): Verify ES256 x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion with Google's IAP JWKs, issuer https://cloud.google.com/iap and the resource audience.
- iap-audience (REASONED; iap): IAP audience paths differ for backendServices, regional Cloud Run services and App Engine apps.
- iap-unsigned (REASONED; iap): Unsigned authenticated-user-email/id headers are forgeable when IAP is bypassed; use the JWT.
- iap-run (REASONED; iap): Load-balancer IAP does not protect run.app; enable IAP on Cloud Run or disable the default URL/restrict ingress.
- iap-firewall (REASONED; iap): Compute Engine and GKE firewalls must block access that bypasses the load balancer.
- azure-providers (REASONED; azure): Easy Auth fronts the app without code changes; documented providers include Entra, Facebook, Google, X, GitHub, Apple preview and custom OIDC.
- azure-require (REASONED; azure): Require authentication rejects anonymously with 302, 401, 403 or 404; Allow unauthenticated requests delegates the decision to the app.
- azure-https (REASONED; azure): Enabling Easy Auth redirects to HTTPS regardless of the app setting; do not disable requireHttps in V2 configuration.
- azure-paths (REASONED; azure): Authentication covers every path unless excluded paths are configured.
- azure-headers (REASONED; azure): X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL carries Base64 claims with ID/NAME/IDP headers; external requests cannot set these platform headers.
- azure-me (REASONED; azure): /.auth/me is available with the token store enabled.
- azure-tenant (REASONED; azure): Entra defaults to allowing any tenant user to obtain a token; restrict the app registration to assigned users when needed.
- container-auth (REASONED; azure): Container Apps uses per-replica auth sidecars, supported social/Entra/OIDC providers, Require/Allow choices and protected principal headers.
- container-https (REASONED; azure): Container Apps authentication requires HTTPS-only ingress with allowInsecure disabled.
- static-login (REASONED; azure): Static Web Apps preconfigures GitHub and Entra on all plans at /.auth/login/github and /.auth/login/aad; custom providers replace defaults.
- static-roles (REASONED; azure): Signed-in Static Web Apps users have anonymous and authenticated roles; staticwebapp.config.json route rules restrict by role.
- static-tenant (REASONED; azure): The preconfigured Static Web Apps Entra provider accepts any Microsoft account; a custom provider is needed for one tenant.
- cf-jwt (REASONED; cf): Prefer Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion over the non-guaranteed CF_Authorization cookie; validate team certs, application AUD and team-domain issuer.
- cf-rotation (REASONED; cf): Access rotates signing keys every six weeks with seven-day previous-key validity; fetch endpoint keys instead of hard-coding.
- ngrok-login (REASONED; ngrok): Traffic-policy oauth or openid-connect redirects to the provider; OIDC uses issuer_url, client_id, client_secret and scopes.
- ngrok-deny (REASONED; ngrok): OAuth login alone admits unintended accounts; a deny expression must match identities outside the email/domain allowlist.
- ngrok-managed (REASONED; ngrok): Empty client_id/client_secret selects ngrok's managed OAuth app for supported providers.
- ngrok-cli (REASONED; ngrok): Use ngrok http 3000 --traffic-policy-file policy.yml; legacy OAuth allow-domain/email flags are deprecated.
- ngrok-origin (REASONED; ngrok): Bind the app to 127.0.0.1 so a direct VM address cannot bypass ngrok login.
- vercel-members (REASONED; vercel): Deployment Protection is not end-user login; Vercel Authentication admits members/viewers, approved requesters, share links and automation bypass.
- vercel-scope (REASONED; vercel, vercel-announcement): Standard Protection excludes production domains; configure All Deployments. The guide records free availability on every plan from September 9, 2026.
- vercel-exception (REASONED; vercel): A domain Protection Exception disables protection for existing and future deployments; remove unintended exceptions.
- vercel-password (REASONED; vercel): At writing, Password Protection is Enterprise-included or USD 20/month/project on Pro; USD 150 legacy is existing-Pro only; Hobby lacks it.
- vercel-enterprise (REASONED; vercel): Trusted IPs and Passport are Enterprise-only at the time of writing.
- verify-origin (REASONED; aws, iap, curl): An external direct-port-3000 probe must refuse/time out at the intended address; HTTP proves exposure and resolver/local errors are inconclusive.
- verify-anonymous (REASONED; aws, azure): Anonymous proxy requests must redirect to the IdP or return 401/403.
- verify-headers (REASONED; aws, iap, azure): Forged unsigned identity headers through the proxy must still yield a login challenge or denial, never admin identity.
- verify-signature (REASONED; aws, iap, cf): At the origin, accept a valid assertion then reject a well-formed changed claim with the original signature; proxy overwrite or malformed JSON proves nothing.
- verify-platform (REASONED; iap, vercel): Probe a real route at run.app or the Vercel production domain: require the platform challenge; app content bypasses auth and 404/transport errors are inconclusive.
- verify-outage (REASONED; aws, azure): Break authorization and require denial of a fresh unauthenticated request; established-session survival is a separate test.
