# Python web apps: TLS and authentication

Flask, FastAPI and Django are Python web frameworks, served by Uvicorn or Gunicorn. This guide helps your AI assistant deploy them securely, including loopback behind a TLS proxy or a managed platform's required listener, Django's HTTPS settings, authentication, and `http.server` only as a last resort, for curated files over SSH.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/python.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against Django documentation 6.1, Python http.server documentation 3.14.4, Python http.server source v3.14.4, Python standard library documentation 3.14, CPython ssl source and documentation v3.14.8, CPython secrets documentation and source v3.14.8, PyOTP v2.9.0, and qrcode v8.2, plus 6 more recorded bases; 5 further sources are pinned to a commit and 6 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-21; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 24 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

Covers Flask, FastAPI/Uvicorn, Gunicorn, and Django. This guide's preferred production layout: bind the app server to `127.0.0.1` and terminate TLS in a reverse proxy ([caddy.md](caddy.md), [nginx.md](nginx.md)) or behind [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md). For managed HTTP ingress, bind the listener required by your deployment; TLS termination depends on the platform and configuration described below ([paas.md](paas.md)). The app servers can also terminate TLS themselves, shown below. Certificates: [free-certificates.md](free-certificates.md) or [self-signed.md](self-signed.md).

## 1. TLS per server

Flask's built-in server (development only; it is not a production server, TLS or not):

```python
app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=8443, ssl_context=("cert.pem", "key.pem"))
# ssl_context="adhoc" generates a throwaway self-signed cert; requires the cryptography package
```

Gunicorn (Flask/Django/WSGI in production):

```bash
gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8443 \
  --certfile /etc/ssl/certs/server.crt \
  --keyfile  /etc/ssl/private/server.key \
  app:app
```

Uvicorn (FastAPI/ASGI):

```bash
uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8443 \
  --ssl-certfile /etc/ssl/certs/server.crt \
  --ssl-keyfile  /etc/ssl/private/server.key
```

This guide's advice: Bind to `0.0.0.0` only when either (a) the process itself terminates TLS with authentication in place, or (b) a platform terminates TLS at its ingress and reaches your app over a private or container network. Otherwise, on a host you expose directly, keep `127.0.0.1` and terminate TLS in a reverse proxy.

This guide's advice for managed platforms: do not add extra listeners; bind only the listener required by your deployment. The documented HTTP ingress mappings are:

- Render web services must bind `0.0.0.0`. Render recommends the `PORT` environment variable (at the time of writing, default port 10000, configurable), can usually detect another bound port, and requires the public HTTP server to use `PORT` when multiple ports are bound ([web services](https://render.com/docs/web-services)).
- Heroku assigns each web process its port through `PORT` ([runtime principles](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/runtime-principles)), and Heroku's Node.js deployment page says the web process must bind to that port or the dyno does not start ([deploying Node.js](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/deploying-nodejs)). Fir Private Spaces networking uses IPv6 by default; Heroku warns that IPv4-only assumptions do not bind properly and recommends an IPv6 or dual-stack listener, typically `::` ([generations](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/generations)). Heroku's HTTP routing page lists IPv6 as unsupported in the Cedar generation without naming a listener address ([HTTP routing](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/http-routing)). This guide's assessment: none of the Heroku pages checked (runtime principles, HTTP routing, generations, dynos, Procfile, Gunicorn deployment, Node.js deployment, the Python and Node.js getting-started tutorials and Node.js best practices, all listed in Sources) states a listener address for Cedar; apart from the Fir recommendation above, the addresses they show are local-development URLs and sample log output. That absence is not evidence that Heroku accepts any listener address.
- Fly Proxy HTTP services must be reachable over IPv4: use `0.0.0.0` and match the configured `internal_port` to the app listener ([service binding](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/2f68a40e09bb6ef4c4ac6f90c15c1cf5a176d7e9/networking/app-services.mdx#L33-L42)). IPv4-mapped IPv6 wildcard behaviour depends on the VM and runtime ([wildcard qualification](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/2f68a40e09bb6ef4c4ac6f90c15c1cf5a176d7e9/networking/app-services.mdx#L92-L92)).
- Railway domains route to a detected or selected internal target port ([target ports](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/domains/working-with-domains.md#L126-L146)). Railway says web servers should bind `0.0.0.0` and listen on the automatically injected `PORT` ([listener and port](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/troubleshooting/application-failed-to-respond.md#L46-L51)). Its edge proxy (tcp-proxy) terminates TLS; traffic is then forwarded over Railway's internal network to the deployment ([request flow](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/edge-networking.md#L40-L43)).

Render's load balancer terminates inbound HTTPS and forwards HTTP to the web service ([web services](https://render.com/docs/web-services)). Heroku's HTTP routing page describes a load balancer offering SSL termination and routers forwarding HTTP to web dynos; it notes that both Private Spaces generations have different routers, so this is not a complete account of Private Spaces routing ([HTTP routing](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/http-routing)). Fly Proxy's `tls` handler terminates TLS and forwards plaintext ([TLS handler](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/2f68a40e09bb6ef4c4ac6f90c15c1cf5a176d7e9/networking/services.mdx#L174-L176)); without handlers it passes TCP through, allowing the app to terminate TLS itself ([TCP passthrough](https://github.com/superfly/docs/blob/2f68a40e09bb6ef4c4ac6f90c15c1cf5a176d7e9/networking/services.mdx#L93-L97)). This guide's advice: plain HTTP is acceptable only behind protected ingress that terminates TLS; application authentication is still required ([paas.md](paas.md)).

## 2. Django settings for HTTPS

```python
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")  # only behind a proxy that STRIPS the client's value and sets its own
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 3600               # start small; raise to 31536000 (1 year) after HTTPS is confirmed working
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = False   # True ONLY after every subdomain also serves valid HTTPS; the commitment is irreversible for SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS
```

`SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` must be set only when a proxy you control, or a managed platform that reliably guarantees this, strips any client-supplied `X-Forwarded-Proto` from every request and sets it itself from the real connection scheme; otherwise a client can spoof it and make Django treat plain HTTP as HTTPS. Leave it unset if you are not behind such a proxy, and confirm the app is reachable only through that proxy, not directly. Run `python manage.py check --deploy` and fix what it reports.

## 3. Authentication

Follow [authentication.md](authentication.md). Framework specifics:

- Keep Django's built-in password hashing; do not replace it with custom code (this guide's advice).
- If your Flask or FastAPI application implements its own password accounts, provide its account storage and hash passwords with `argon2-cffi` or `bcrypt` (this guide's advice; follow the algorithm and legacy-bcrypt constraints in [authentication.md](authentication.md)):

```python
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher()
hash_ = ph.hash(password)
ph.verify(hash_, password)   # raises on mismatch
```

The [argon2-cffi 25.1.0 example](https://github.com/hynek/argon2-cffi/blob/25.1.0/README.md#L11-L28) documents these `PasswordHasher`, `hash` and `verify` calls and a `VerifyMismatchError` on mismatch. The [pinned bcrypt example](https://github.com/pyca/bcrypt/blob/2b4ba9ac84df972e8e81311d09559af8dc82ef33/README.rst#L62-L76) documents `hashpw(password, gensalt())` and `checkpw(password, hashed)`; these API examples do not establish framework user-store capabilities.

- Generate tokens and secrets with the standard library, and load them from the environment (this guide's advice):

```python
import secrets
token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
```

In [CPython v3.14.8](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Doc/library/secrets.rst#L91-L103), `token_urlsafe(nbytes=None)` returns URL-safe Base64 text from `nbytes` random bytes; the argument counts input bytes, not output characters. The explicit `32` above is this guide's example choice, not a size suitable for every secret. If the argument is omitted or `None`, it uses `DEFAULT_ENTROPY`, [32 bytes at this pin](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Lib/secrets.py#L31-L45); the [documented default can change](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Doc/library/secrets.rst#L125-L130), including in maintenance releases.

- FastAPI's `fastapi.security` classes (`HTTPBearer`, `APIKeyHeader`, `OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer`, and so on) extract the credential from the request and declare the OpenAPI security scheme; what they check varies by helper (an API-key helper checks only that a value is present; the HTTP and OAuth2 bearer helpers may also check the scheme), but none authenticate the credential (no signature, issuer, audience, or expiry check), and `OpenIdConnect` is documented as a stub that does not implement the scheme or use the discovery URL. Use them to extract the token, then validate it (signature, issuer, audience, expiry) with an OIDC library such as Authlib, and authorize per [oidc-integration.md](oidc-integration.md).
- Rate-limit login routes (this guide's advice; for example with a proxy-level limit or a library such as slowapi for Starlette/FastAPI ASGI apps' HTTP endpoints; endpoints using slowapi's `limit` decorator must take an explicit `request` argument, and slowapi does not support WebSocket endpoints).
- MFA: add TOTP with [pyotp](https://github.com/pyauth/pyotp) plus the [qrcode](https://pypi.org/project/qrcode/) package for enrolment QR codes; [django-otp](https://pypi.org/project/django-otp/) integrates this into Django. Requirements and options in [mfa.md](mfa.md).

## 4. Client-side TLS discipline

Never ship `verify=False` (requests/httpx) or `ssl._create_unverified_context` (this guide's advice). For an internal CA, point the client at it instead (this guide's advice):

```bash
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/ca.crt   # requests
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/path/ca.crt        # HTTPX with verify=True and trust_env=True; OpenSSL default CA file for ssl when its default verify paths apply (see caveat below)
```

HTTPX 0.28.1's SSL guide says `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` are not automatically used and shows an explicit context; its code path contradicts that: its sync and async transports pass `verify` and `trust_env` to `create_ssl_context`, which reads `SSL_CERT_FILE` when both are true. Its environment guide says environment variables are used by default but does not list `SSL_CERT_FILE`. This guide's advice: use the export above for that HTTPX code path; pass an explicit CA context for other configurations. With no CA specified and verification enabled, CPython's `ssl.create_default_context()` tries to load default CAs (CPython notes this may fail silently). `ssl.get_default_verify_paths()` reports OpenSSL's default verify paths and environment-variable names.

At CPython v3.14.8, [`SSLContext.load_default_certs()`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Lib/ssl.py#L542-L548) calls `set_default_verify_paths()`, whose [`_ssl.c` implementation](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Modules/_ssl.c#L4607-L4626) calls OpenSSL's `SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths()`. [`get_default_verify_paths()` in `_ssl.c`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Modules/_ssl.c#L5873-L5914) gets the file and directory environment-variable names from OpenSSL's `X509_get_default_cert_file_env()` and `X509_get_default_cert_dir_env()`; [`ssl.py`](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.14.8/Lib/ssl.py#L390-L405) returns those names and the resolved paths. [OpenSSL openssl-4.0.3](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-4.0.3/doc/man3/SSL_CTX_load_verify_locations.pod#L39-L49) documents that `SSL_CTX_set_default_verify_paths()` honours both `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` for its default CA file and directory, subject to its environment rules: [these variables are security-sensitive for CA loading](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-4.0.3/doc/man7/openssl-env.pod#L289-L298), and [security-sensitive environment variables are not consulted for set-user-ID or set-group-ID executables](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-4.0.3/doc/man7/openssl-env.pod#L9-L13).

This guide's inference: that CPython default-path call uses those OpenSSL overrides when linked to a library with the cited behaviour, subject to the executable exclusions above. This guide's assessment: a CPython build may link a different OpenSSL release from `openssl-4.0.3`; these lines do not establish platform-specific default stores (including Windows or macOS builds) or whether a deployed configuration takes this path and loads its intended CAs.

## 5. Do not quick-share files with `http.server`

`python -m http.server` is a common quick-share suggestion, and it is the wrong one on any reachable host. By default it binds every interface (as of Python 3.14.4), and it serves the current directory: source, `.env`, private keys, and database dumps are all downloadable by anyone who can reach the port. It also follows symbolic links, so a link in that directory hands out files from outside it, and the Python docs mark the module as not suitable for production. If you have no alternative, bind loopback and serve a directory that holds only what you mean to share:

```bash
cd /path/to/a/directory/with/nothing/private || exit
python -m http.server -b 127.0.0.1 8000
```

Reach it through an SSH tunnel, including one that runs over your tailnet, never a public bind.

## 6. Verify (REASONED: TLS, authentication and listener expectations follow the Sources below and linked deployment guidance; no deployment run or outcome is recorded in this guide. This metadata-only review has no deployed Python application, proxy or managed ingress to test.)

```bash
curl -q -sSI --noproxy '*' https://example.com/        # public HTTPS endpoint: must succeed without -k; if not, investigate the cert, chain, hostname, or your client trust store, never -k
# An unauthenticated request to a real protected path must be REJECTED and a valid credential ACCEPTED. --noproxy
# disables YOUR client proxy, not a reverse proxy in front of the app, so if the app sits behind an auth proxy this
# pair cannot tell whether the app or the proxy enforced it: confirm the layer by probing the app directly or in its logs.
curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' 'https://example.com/REPLACE_WITH_PROTECTED_PATH'        # no credentials: expect 401/403
curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' -H @cred.txt -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' 'https://example.com/REPLACE_WITH_PROTECTED_PATH'   # valid credential from a file (cred.txt holds a full header line, e.g. "Authorization: Bearer ..."): expect 2xx
ss -tlnp   # every listener: loopback for a same-host reverse proxy, or the platform's required address and port from section 1 on managed ingress
```

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- bind (REASONED; gunicorn, uvicorn, render, heroku, fly-pinned, railway): Guide advice: loopback behind same-host TLS proxies, no extra managed listeners, wildcard only for authenticated TLS ingress, direct or private; app auth required. Railway: 0.0.0.0 on injected PORT, edge TLS; Fly w/o handlers: TCP passthrough; Heroku web processes must bind PORT, IPv6/dual-stack advised for Fir Private Spaces; checked pages state no Cedar address (guide's view, not proof any address works).
- flask-tls (REASONED; werkzeug): Flask development server binds 127.0.0.1:8443 with cert/key ssl_context; adhoc requires cryptography and remains development-only.
- gunicorn-tls (REASONED; gunicorn): Gunicorn binds 0.0.0.0:8443 with --certfile and --keyfile for direct TLS.
- uvicorn-tls (REASONED; uvicorn): Uvicorn binds 0.0.0.0:8443 with --ssl-certfile and --ssl-keyfile for direct TLS.
- django-redirect (REASONED; django): Set SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT=True.
- django-proxy (REASONED; django): Set SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER only behind a trusted proxy that strips and replaces X-Forwarded-Proto; prevent direct bypass.
- django-cookies (REASONED; django): Set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE true.
- django-hsts (REASONED; django): Begin HSTS at 3600 seconds and include-subdomains false; raise duration and scope only after valid HTTPS is confirmed.
- deploy-check (REASONED; django): Run manage.py check --deploy and fix its findings.
- password (REASONED; django, argon, argon-api, bcrypt-api): Keep Django's built-in hashing; do not replace it with custom code (guide advice). For Flask/FastAPI apps implementing local password accounts, this guide advises account storage and argon2-cffi or bcrypt under authentication.md's constraints; argon2-cffi 25.1.0's PasswordHasher.verify raises VerifyMismatchError on mismatch, and these APIs do not establish framework user-store capabilities.
- secrets (REASONED; django, stdlib-docs, cpython-secrets): Generate secrets.token_urlsafe(32) and load secrets from the environment (guide advice); 32 counts random input bytes and is this guide's example choice, not a universal size. CPython v3.14.8 uses DEFAULT_ENTROPY (32 bytes) when omitted or None, but that default may change, including in maintenance releases.
- credential-extraction (REASONED; fastapi): FastAPI security helpers extract credentials and declare schemes; presence/scheme checks do not verify signature, issuer, audience or expiry.
- oidc (REASONED; fastapi, oidc-stub): OpenIdConnect is a stub and does not use its discovery URL; validate extracted tokens with an OIDC library and authorize separately.
- login-limit (REASONED; fastapi, slowapi): Rate-limiting login routes and a proxy-level limit are this guide's advice. slowapi v0.1.10 documents limits for Starlette/FastAPI HTTP endpoints; endpoints using its limit decorator must take an explicit request argument, and WebSocket endpoints are not supported.
- mfa (REASONED; django, pyotp, qrcode, django-otp): Use pyotp and qrcode, django-otp for Django, or linked MFA guidance.
- client-validation (REASONED; python, requests, httpx, cpython-ssl): Never ship requests/httpx verify=False or ssl._create_unverified_context; HTTPX documents verify=False and CPython defines _create_unverified_context. The prohibition is this guide's advice.
- client-ca (REASONED; cpython-ssl, openssl): CPython's ssl reports OpenSSL default verify paths and environment-variable names. With no CA specified and verification enabled, create_default_context tries default CAs; loading may fail silently. This guide's inference: the call uses SSL_CERT_FILE/SSL_CERT_DIR if OpenSSL behaves as cited. This guide's assessment: linked OpenSSL may differ; platform stores and deployed use remain unverified.
- client-ca-httpx (REASONED; httpx): HTTPX 0.28.1's transport passes verify and trust_env to create_ssl_context, which reads SSL_CERT_FILE when verify=True and trust_env=True; its SSL guide contradicts that source. Its environment guide says environment variables are used by default but does not list SSL_CERT_FILE.
- client-ca-advice (REASONED; requests, httpx, cpython-ssl, openssl): REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE selects a requests CA. OpenSSL openssl-4.0.3 honours SSL_CERT_FILE/SSL_CERT_DIR for its default CA file/directory except in set-user-ID/set-group-ID executables. This guide's advice: use the exports for requests, the stated HTTPX path and CPython's qualified default-path call, or an explicit context for other configurations.
- http-server-bind (REASONED; python-pin): As of Python 3.14.4, http.server binds every interface by default; explicitly bind 127.0.0.1:8000.
- http-server-files (REASONED; python): http.server serves the current directory and follows symlinks outside it; it is unsuitable for production. Share only a non-private directory through an SSH tunnel.
- verify-tls (REASONED; gunicorn, uvicorn): Public HTTPS must succeed without -k; certificate, chain, hostname and trust failures need investigation.
- verify-auth (REASONED; django, fastapi): A real protected route denies no credentials with 401/403 and accepts valid file-supplied credentials with 2xx; logs or direct probing distinguish app from proxy enforcement.
- verify-bind (REASONED; gunicorn, uvicorn): Inspect every listener for loopback behind a same-host proxy or the required managed-ingress address and port.

# Docker and Compose: exposure, TLS, and authentication

Docker runs apps in containers, packages bundling an app with what it needs, and Compose starts several containers from one file. This guide helps your AI assistant configure a deployment securely, including only the TLS proxy public, every other port kept private, and secrets kept out of images.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/docker.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against Docker Engine minimum boundary 28.0, Moby Docker service unit v28.3.3, Docker firewalld reload fix 28.3.3, systemd unit ordering v262, Git ignore rules v2.49.0, PostgreSQL 17, Caddy v2.11.4, and nginx authentication source release-1.26.3, plus 3 more recorded bases; 8 further sources are pinned to a commit and 8 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-19; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 27 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

Containers are where accidental exposure happens most. Two Docker behaviours cause it:

1. `ports: - "3000:3000"` (or `-p 3000:3000`) publishes on every host address, `0.0.0.0` and `[::]`, at the time of writing.
2. On Linux, Docker programs iptables/nftables directly, so published ports are reachable **even when UFW or firewalld says the port is blocked**. A `ufw deny 3000` rule does not protect a published container port.

## 1. Publish nothing except the TLS proxy

Bind anything that must be reachable from the host to loopback, and give everything else no `ports:` entry at all; containers on the same Compose network reach each other by service name without published ports.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    # no ports: entry; only the proxy is published
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    # no ports: entry; the app reaches it at db:5432 on the internal network
```

Where a host-published port is genuinely needed for local access:

```yaml
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
```

That host-IP restriction requires Docker Engine 28.0 or later, with the firewalld-reload caveat below. Before 28.0, under the default bridge configuration, a neighbour on the same layer-2 segment could reach a port mapped to a loopback address, a remote host could reach a container on a published port despite the host-IP binding, and an unpublished container port was reachable by routing directly to the container if the host's forwarding policy allowed it; 28.0 fixed all three. Check the running Engine version (`docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'`, not the client's); on an older engine, treat the address in a publish string as a convenience, not a boundary, and restrict the port in the `DOCKER-USER` chain below or upstream of the host (a cloud security group or a network ACL), since a host firewall like UFW or firewalld does not reach a published port (see the top of this guide).

On Linux, when Docker Engine runs in the host's network namespace with firewalld running, Engine 28.2.x and 28.3.0 through 28.3.2 failed to restore container-address filtering rules after a firewalld reload. A remote host with a route to the bridge network could then reach published ports at container addresses, including loopback-only publications; unpublished ports remained filtered. Where firewalld is used, run Engine 28.3.3 or later, which fixes this regression (CVE-2025-54388, GHSA-x4rx-4gw3-53p4). Rootless Mode and Docker Desktop are unaffected by this regression.

As this guide's assessment, where a port must be published on a routable interface, because other hosts need it but the whole internet does not, the most reliable restriction is upstream of the host, in a cloud security group or a network ACL: it does not depend on Docker's firewall backend, its userland proxy, or the host's boot order. See [cloud-firewalls.md](cloud-firewalls.md) for sourced AWS security-group, Google Cloud VPC firewall and Azure NSG rules; network-ACL configuration is not directly sourced here. On the host itself, filter it in the `DOCKER-USER` iptables chain (Docker's iptables backend only; its nftables backend has no such chain), whose rules Docker evaluates before its own accept rules. Match only new connections, so the rule does not also drop the replies to connections your own containers open, which arrive on the same interface and would otherwise lose their outbound access:

```bash
# IPv4, run as root; replace ext_if with your external interface and the subnet with your own
iptables -I DOCKER-USER -i ext_if -m conntrack --ctstate NEW ! -s 192.0.2.0/24 -j DROP
```

This runs after destination NAT, so an ordinary destination match sees a container's internal IP and port, not the published host IP or port; it also covers every published port arriving on that interface, so scope it to one service with conntrack's `--ctorigdstport` and `--ctdir ORIGINAL` if you need to. As this guide's reasoning, `iptables` covers IPv4 only. Cover native IPv6 forwarding with an equivalent `ip6tables` `DOCKER-USER` rule, but note a second path: publishing without a host IP on an IPv4-only bridge with `--userland-proxy=true` (the default) also makes the port answer on the host's IPv6 addresses through Docker's userland proxy (it maps IPv6 to the container's IPv4). As this guide's reasoning, that connection terminates on a host process, so it traverses the host `INPUT` chain, not `FORWARD`, and a `DOCKER-USER` rule (which lives in `FORWARD`) never sees it. Close that path by publishing to a specific address (`-p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000` or a chosen IPv4), disabling the userland proxy, or restricting the host's IPv6 `INPUT`. Probe IPv4 and IPv6 separately, each from an allowed and a disallowed source. Confirm with `sudo iptables -nvL DOCKER-USER`, watching its counters, and by probing the port from a host outside the allowed subnet, expecting a timeout, and one inside it, expecting a connection. As this guide's assessment, the rule does not survive a reboot and is not in place while the host boots; persist just the DOCKER-USER rules with a startup unit ordered after the Docker service, not a blanket `iptables-persistent` save (which, as this guide's assessment, also captures Docker's own dynamic chains and can break container networking on the next boot), and where the boot-time window matters, rely on the upstream control.

## 2. Terminate TLS in one proxy container

Caddy is the least configuration ([caddy.md](caddy.md)); nginx ([nginx.md](nginx.md)) and Traefik ([traefik.md](traefik.md)) work the same way. A complete pattern:

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:
```

`Caddyfile`:

```caddyfile
app.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:3000
}
```

Caddy obtains and renews the certificate automatically ([free-certificates.md](free-certificates.md) explains the ACME requirements). As this guide's recommendation, hosts with no inbound ports but a domain you can put on Cloudflare should use [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md); run the `cloudflared` connector as a container on the app's Compose network and point it at `http://app:3000`. As this guide's recommendation, hosts with no domain at all should use [tailscale.md](tailscale.md) (Serve for private tailnet access or Funnel for public access), or [self-signed.md](self-signed.md) for internal use. Docker documents service-name lookup on the shared Compose network; the `http://app:3000` origin is this guide's inference from that lookup and [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md)'s HTTP origin example, while the fetched Cloudflare origin parameters show an HTTPS service URL rather than this literal HTTP value. This guide does not show the tunnel-token setup; [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md) gives the protected `--token-file` path.

## 3. Authentication and secrets

- As this guide's assessment, the proxy is the natural place for a first authentication gate (basic auth per the proxy guides, or Cloudflare Access); the application still needs its own login for anything multi-user ([authentication.md](authentication.md)). The proxy is also where MFA attaches for human-facing services ([mfa.md](mfa.md)): Cloudflare Access policies can require a second factor, and an Authelia portal can handle authentication behind Caddy `forward_auth`, nginx `auth_request` or Traefik `forwardAuth`. Require MFA in the governing policy or portal; as this guide's assessment, basic auth alone is single-factor.
- As this guide's advice, pass secrets at runtime through environment files or Docker/Compose secrets. Docker's Compose documentation advises against using environment variables to pass sensitive information such as passwords into containers and recommends secrets instead, noting that environment variables are often available to all processes, that access to them can be hard to track, and that they can be printed in logs when debugging errors; the same page's `env_file` section also describes a separate environment file as a more organized and secure way to manage sensitive information, because the file need not sit in the project root. As this guide's assessment, environment files are the weaker of the two runtime methods named here. Compose mounts each secret as a file under `/run/secrets/`, named after the secret, supports secrets on Linux containers only, and grants access per service. Docker Swarm secrets are available only to swarm services, not to standalone containers; Docker documents them as encrypted in transit and at rest in the swarm, accessible only to services granted explicit access while their tasks run, and, in Linux containers, mounted decrypted in an in-memory filesystem, by default under `/run/secrets/`. Docker also documents that a container's environment is not set until the service configuration has an explicit entry for it, such as the `environment` or `env_file` attribute, and that the `.env` file in the project directory, the default method for setting variables, defines variables for interpolation in the Compose file, which an `environment` entry such as `DEBUG=${DEBUG}` can then pass into the container. As this guide's reasoning about Compose configuration, defining a value in `.env` does not by itself put it in the container's environment. The cited examples pass values through an `environment` entry or load an environment file through an `env_file` entry; interpolation can also place values elsewhere in the Compose file, such as an image tag. Never bake secrets into the image. Never put secrets in Dockerfile `ENV` or `ARG`: Docker documents that both are exposed in the final image; `ENV` also persists in containers from the image, and build arguments may persist in image metadata, provenance attestations and image history. As this guide's assessment, baking a key into an image ships it to every registry the image touches. `docker image history` shows the image's history, including creation commands; as this guide's assessment, the cited reference does not establish that every argument value is shown. For build-time secrets, use a temporary secret mount for the build instruction and do not copy or print the secret into the image.
- As this guide's advice, keep `.env` in `.gitignore` and untrack it if already tracked (Git ignores matching untracked files, while already tracked files are unaffected), and run containers as a non-root user (`USER` in the Dockerfile); as this guide's assessment, this means a compromised app is not root in the container. As this guide's advice, non-root is the start, not the whole of workload hardening: dropping capabilities (`cap_drop`), `--security-opt no-new-privileges` (or Compose `security_opt`), a read-only root filesystem (Compose `read_only`), and never mounting the Docker socket are in [container-hardening.md](container-hardening.md). Docker documents these option names, that only trusted users should control the daemon, and that Unix permissions can limit access to its control socket; the linked guide's hardening consequences, including the mounted-socket path, remain this guide's assessment. Git v2.49.0 documents that `git rm --cached` removes paths only from the index and leaves working tree files alone. As this guide's advice, rotate any secret that was ever committed; as this guide's reasoning, untracking does not remove the file from earlier commits. The cited Git lines describe index and working tree behaviour and do not discuss earlier commits or secret rotation.
- Databases in containers still need their own TLS and authentication when anything outside the Compose network connects: see [postgresql.md](postgresql.md), [mysql.md](mysql.md), [mongodb.md](mongodb.md), and [redis.md](redis.md).

## 4. Verify

REASONED: publication, redirect, authentication and external isolation checks; no exposed/fixed run is recorded in this guide. Expectations follow the cited Docker networking sources and linked proxy guides; the authoring environment has no authorized deployment or external probe hosts. For the unauthenticated API probe, expect 401 from Caddy or nginx basic auth; Caddy `forward_auth` admits auth-service 2xx, but its rejection status is not established by the fetched lines. Expect 401/403 from nginx `auth_request`; the cited Authelia nginx configuration converts its 401 to a 302 login redirect. Traefik `forwardAuth` passes through its auth service's non-2xx status, including a login redirect; Traefik `basicAuth` calls `RequireAuth`, whose response the fetched lines do not show, so 401 is this guide's expectation rather than a status established by the fetched middleware. For Cloudflare Access, this guide expects a 302 login redirect in the configuration described in [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md); the fetched Cloudflare lines do not establish that status. A 3xx passes only when its printed location is the gate's own login portal (for Cloudflare Access, your team's `*.cloudflareaccess.com`), never the application's own login. The command fails on any 2xx; any status other than the gate's expected rejection or a 3xx to its portal is not a pass; and an authorized request must succeed separately.

```bash
docker compose ps                     # project-scoped: only the proxy shows a published (0.0.0.0/[::] or a host IP) binding; review every container on the host, IPv6 included
ss -tulnp                             # host sockets (TCP and UDP); socket visibility varies by Docker version and config, so a socket listing alone does not prove reachability
curl -q -sI http://app.example.com/      # expect a redirect to https:// with Caddy automatic HTTPS, or after configuring nginx or Traefik to redirect
( set -o pipefail; curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code} loc=%{redirect_url}\n' https://app.example.com/api | awk '{ print; if ($1 ~ /^http=2/) { print "FAIL: unauthenticated /api returned " substr($1, 6); exit 1 } }' )  # unauthenticated: inspect the gate's rejection and portal location; then confirm an authorized request succeeds
```

REASONED: preceding block; publication and socket inventory, HTTPS redirect, unauthenticated API rejection and authorized API success follow the cited Docker networking sources and linked proxy guides, as do the external isolation probes this paragraph describes; no Docker runtime or external probe hosts are available, and no exposed/fixed result is recorded. Test from a second machine on a different network where possible; the UFW bypass means testing the firewall from the host itself proves nothing about published ports. The `curl` checks above exercise the proxy's redirect and auth, not the backend, so also probe each restricted host address and published port directly (for example port 3000) from an allowed and a disallowed source, IPv4 and IPv6 separately: a loopback-bound or firewalled backend must show unreachable while the proxy stays reachable.

REASONED: this firewalld reload check follows the Impact section of GHSA-x4rx-4gw3-53p4 and the pinned v28.3.3 rule-restoration source. It has not been demonstrated here because the authoring environment has no Docker runtime, firewalld or external test host. For a loopback-published HTTP backend using default NAT bridge filtering, confirm that the backend answers locally. From a second host with a route through the Docker host to the bridge subnet, run `curl -q -g --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 -v http://172.17.0.2:3000/`, replacing the address and port with the actual container address and container port. Repeat with a fresh connection after running `sudo firewall-cmd --reload` on the Docker host. Without another control masking the regression, an affected host changes from blocked to connectable; a fixed host remains blocked. Any successful TCP connection, including an HTTP 401 or 403 response, demonstrates reachability. A failed probe alone does not establish that the Engine is patched: confirm the route, target and backend health. Repeat for configured IPv6 addresses and the restricted host-address publications, and confirm that the TLS proxy remains reachable.

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- publish (REASONED; engine): Omitting the host address publishes 3000:3000 on 0.0.0.0 and [::].
- host-firewall (REASONED; engine): Docker programs firewall rules directly; UFW or firewalld blocking a host port does not establish published-port isolation.
- private-network (REASONED; compose, postgresql): Omit app/database ports; Compose peers use service names. The example uses postgres:17 at db:5432.
- loopback (REASONED; engine, boundary, reload, reload-advisory): Publish local access as 127.0.0.1:3000:3000; check the running server version. Engine 28.0 is the minimum boundary, with 28.3.3 or later required where firewalld is used.
- old-loopback (REASONED; boundary): Before 28.0, same-L2 neighbours could reach loopback publications under the default bridge configuration.
- old-host-bind (REASONED; boundary): Before 28.0, remote hosts could reach published container ports despite the host-IP binding.
- old-unpublished (REASONED; boundary): Before 28.0, direct routing could reach unpublished container ports; 28.0 fixed the stated default-bridge exposures.
- upstream (REASONED; engine, aws-firewall, gcp-firewall, azure-firewall): Use an upstream security group or network ACL for routable publications and boot-time protection. AWS security groups, Google Cloud VPC firewall rules and Azure NSGs have rolling sources; network-ACL configuration and boot-time independence remain this guide's assessment.
- docker-user (REASONED; engine): On the iptables backend, DOCKER-USER precedes Docker accepts; the nftables backend has no such chain. Match NEW traffic from outside the allowed subnet.
- dnat (REASONED; engine): DOCKER-USER sees post-DNAT container destinations; conntrack original destination port and ORIGINAL direction scope a published service.
- ipv6 (REASONED; engine, engine-pinned): As this guide's reasoning, native IPv6 forwarding needs ip6tables; Docker documents IPv6-to-IPv4 userland-proxy mapping when no host IP is given, the bridge is IPv4-only and `--userland-proxy=true` (the default), and places DOCKER-USER in FORWARD. As this guide's reasoning, the proxy path terminates on host INPUT and bypasses DOCKER-USER.
- proxy-path (REASONED; engine, engine-pinned): Close the userland-proxy path with an explicit publish address, disabled userland proxy or IPv6 INPUT restrictions; test both address families and sources. Docker documents the explicit-address option and conditional userland-proxy mapping; the INPUT restriction and probes are this guide's reasoning and advice.
- persistence (REASONED; engine, engine-pinned, moby-unit, systemd-unit): As this guide's advice, persist only DOCKER-USER rules after Docker startup, avoiding blanket dynamic-chain saves. Moby identifies docker.service and systemd documents After= ordering; as this guide's assessment, rule non-persistence, the boot-time gap, what iptables-persistent captures and its potential to break container networking have no direct source here.
- tls (REASONED; compose, caddy-image, caddy): Example caddy:2 publishes 80:80 and 443:443, mounts Caddyfile read-only and persists data/config, proxying app:3000 with automatic certificates.
- alternate-entry (REASONED; compose, cloudflared-image, cloudflare-tunnel, compose-pinned, tailscale-entry, self-signed-entry): As this guide's advice, hosts with no inbound ports and a domain they can put on Cloudflare use a cloudflared container, while hosts with no domain at all use Tailscale or internal self-signed TLS. Cloudflare documents a tunnel daemon that needs no firewall openings, a container image, an HTTPS origin service URL and a domain prerequisite; Docker documents Compose service-name lookup. The http://app:3000 origin target on a shared Compose network is this guide's inference, not shown literally by the fetched Cloudflare lines. The tunnel-token setup is not shown here; the Tailscale and OpenSSL references are rolling, and the self-signed fallback remains this guide's advice.
- auth (REASONED; compose, caddy, nginx-auth, traefik-auth, cloudflare-access, authelia-proxy): As this guide's assessment, proxy authentication and human MFA supplement application login. Caddy and nginx basic authentication reject missing credentials; nginx auth_request returns 401/403; Traefik basicAuth calls RequireAuth and forwardAuth passes through non-2xx; Cloudflare Access policies can require MFA, and Authelia can sit behind the proxy. Require MFA in the governing policy or portal; as this guide's assessment, basic auth alone is single-factor. The Caddy forward_auth rejection status, exact Traefik basicAuth status and Cloudflare Access anonymous status are not established by these fetched lines.
- secrets (REASONED; compose, docker-build, docker-secrets, git-ignore): Use runtime env files (guide advice; weaker: guide assessment), Compose secrets (Linux only) or Swarm secrets (swarm services only). Guide advice: keep .env in .gitignore (untracked files only); untrack if tracked. No Dockerfile ENV/ARG secrets; use temporary build secret mounts. Guide assessment: never bake/copy/print secrets into images; history source does not establish that every argument value is shown.
- env-git (REASONED; git-ignore): As this guide's advice, keep `.env` in `.gitignore` and untrack it if already tracked; Git ignores matching untracked files but not tracked files, and `git rm --cached` removes paths only from the index, leaving working tree files alone. As this guide's advice, rotate any secret ever committed; as this guide's reasoning, untracking does not remove it from earlier commits.
- workload (REASONED; compose, docker-workload): Guide advice: use non-root Dockerfile USER, drop capabilities, use no-new-privileges and a read-only root filesystem, never mount Docker's socket. Docker documents option names, that only trusted users should control the daemon and that Unix permissions can limit socket access; guide assessments: with non-root USER a compromised app is not container root; linked guide's hardening effects, mounted-socket path included.
- database (REASONED; compose): Database TLS and authentication remain necessary for connections from outside the Compose network; database vendor sources are in linked guides.
- verify-publish (REASONED; compose, engine): Compose ps is project-scoped; inventory every host container and TCP/UDP socket, including IPv6. Socket visibility alone does not prove reachability.
- verify-redirect (REASONED; compose, caddy): Verify that HTTP redirects to HTTPS: Caddy v2.11.4 configures an automatic HTTPS redirect; as this guide's configuration-dependent expectation, nginx and Traefik require a configured redirect. This is an expectation, not an observed deployment result.
- verify-auth (REASONED; compose, caddy, nginx-auth, traefik-auth, authelia-proxy, cloudflare-access): Verify unauthenticated HTTPS /api rejection with printed status and redirect location; the probe itself fails on any 2xx. A 3xx passes only when the location is the gate's own login portal, never the application's own login; verify authorized success separately. Caddy basic auth and nginx auth_basic expect 401; Caddy forward_auth admits auth-service 2xx, but its rejection status is not established by the fetched lines. nginx auth_request returns 401 or 403, while the cited Authelia nginx configuration turns 401 into 302 to its portal. Traefik forwardAuth passes through a rejecting auth service's status, including a login redirect; Traefik basicAuth's 401 is this guide's expectation because the fetched code calls RequireAuth, whose response these lines do not show. Cloudflare Access's anonymous 302 login redirect is this guide's assessment per cloudflare.md, not established by the fetched Cloudflare lines.
- verify-isolation (REASONED; engine): Probe each restricted host address and publication from allowed/disallowed sources in both families; backend isolation must coexist with proxy reachability.
- firewalld-reload (REASONED; reload, reload-advisory): Engine 28.2.x and 28.3.0 through 28.3.2 fail to restore container-address filtering after firewalld reload; 28.3.3 fixes CVE-2025-54388 (GHSA-x4rx-4gw3-53p4).
- firewalld-scope (REASONED; reload, reload-advisory): The regression affects Linux Engine in the host network namespace with firewalld: routed remote hosts can reach published container ports, including loopback publications; unpublished ports stay filtered. Rootless Mode and Docker Desktop are unaffected.
- verify-firewalld-reload (REASONED; reload, reload-advisory): Confirm local backend health, then curl the container address from a second host with a bridge-subnet route before and after sudo firewall-cmd --reload. Without masking controls, affected hosts change from blocked to connectable; fixed hosts stay blocked. Any TCP connection, including HTTP 401/403, shows reachability; failure alone does not prove patching. Check route, target, IPv6, restricted host publications and continued proxy reachability.
