A bare `401` proves less than it looks: a fronting authentication proxy can return it while the
underlying `users.anonymous.enabled` is still on, so pair the probe with an authenticated request
through the same route that should succeed, and read the anonymous and `policy.default` settings from
`argocd-cm`/`argocd-rbac-cm` directly. For Flux, test the webhook with an **unauthenticated** request, not merely an unsigned body, since a valid
`X-Gitlab-Token` or OIDC token authenticates without a signature. Paste the receiver's HMAC secret alone at the
block's hidden prompt: a multi-line paste leaves every line after the first for your shell to run.
For a `generic-hmac` receiver the
signature is `X-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC of the exact body under the receiver's secret>`; send identical
bytes without it (must be rejected) and then with it (must be accepted and trigger the reconciliation):

```bash
# REASONED: Flux webhook checks follow the cited receiver documentation; no live Flux is available.
# Read the HMAC key without echo.
# Python's hmac reads the key from stdin; only the non-secret request body is passed in argv.
# The hidden prompt keeps the key out of shell history and set +x keeps it out of set -x tracing.
# Stdin closes the argv channel only: the account owner and root can still read the key in the
# subshell and python3.
# The signature, a replayable HMAC for that exact body, goes to curl on stdin as a header line (-H @-)
# and the fixed, non-secret body as an argument. Stdin closes the argv channel only: the account owner
# and root can still read the signature in the subshell and curl.
(
  trap - DEBUG RETURN ERR  # assumes a clean shell (CONTRIBUTING rule 7): no inherited DEBUG trap, extdebug, function or alias
  set +x +a +e
  { unset -n hmac sig && unset -v hmac sig; } 2>/dev/null ||
    { echo 'a readonly hmac or sig is set in this shell; not probing'; exit 2; }
  { unset -n IFS; } 2>/dev/null || { echo 'a readonly IFS is set in this shell; not probing'; exit 2; }
  IFS= read -r -s -p 'receiver HMAC secret: ' hmac < /dev/tty || exit 2; echo
  [ -n "$hmac" ] || { echo 'supply the HMAC secret; not probing'; exit 2; }
  body='{"ref":"refs/heads/main"}'
  sig=$(set -o pipefail; printf '%s' "$hmac" | python3 -c \
    'import hmac, sys; print(hmac.new(sys.stdin.buffer.read(), sys.argv[1].encode(), "sha256").hexdigest())' "$body") ||
    { echo 'signature generation failed; not probing'; exit 2; }
  [ -n "$sig" ] || { echo 'signature generation failed; not probing'; exit 2; }
  url='https://flux-webhook.example.com/hook/REPLACE_WITH_PATH'
  printf '%s' "$body" | curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    -X POST --data-binary @- -w '\nno-sig http=%{http_code}\n' "$url"          # expect rejected
  printf 'X-Signature: sha256=%s\n' "$sig" | curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    -X POST --data-binary "$body" -H @- -w '\nsigned http=%{http_code}\n' "$url"  # expect accepted
)
```

Read the receiver's status without printing the default table, full status, condition messages, or
`.status.webhookPath` (status messages can carry the generated path, itself a capability for a `generic`
receiver): select the name and the Ready condition explicitly. The rejection status is type- and
version-dependent, so read it as rejected rather than a fixed code. A malformed-payload error or a
proxy-only rejection is inconclusive; repeat against the receiver origin from an authorized location.
Because these checks discriminate on a response rather than on silence, they take the plain form above;
a bare reachability probe of your own public address, whose pass is nothing answering, would instead
need the guarded-subshell form so an unsubstituted address cannot time out and read as closed.

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- git-boundary (REASONED; argo-docs, flux): Repository writers exercise reconciliation permissions; review platform changes, separate tenants and scope credentials.
- secret-storage (REASONED; argo-docs, flux): Protect bootstrap, registry, cluster, webhook and decryption credentials; commit only encrypted secrets and keep SOPS/age keys out of Git.
- egress (REASONED; argo-docs, flux): Restrict fetch, API, identity and notification egress; Argo repository allowlists do not constrain remote bases or Helm dependencies.
- argo-bootstrap (REASONED; argo-docs): Rotate the initial admin password before deleting argocd-initial-admin-secret; deletion alone does not rotate it.
- argo-sso (REASONED; argo-docs): The built-in admin is unrestricted; configure named SSO roles and IdP MFA, then set admin.enabled=false.
- argo-origin (REASONED; argo-docs, argo): Keep the ClusterIP origin private behind authenticated TLS and protect both REST/browser and CLI/gRPC routes.
- argo-server (REASONED; argo): Server defaults to 0.0.0.0:8080; the Service maps 80 and 443 to it.
- argo-tls (REASONED; argo, argo-docs): Server --insecure/server.insecure defaults false and disables backend TLS, not authentication; use only behind protected TLS termination.
- argo-client-tls (REASONED; argo-docs): argocd login --insecure skips client certificate verification; the server initially uses a self-signed certificate.
- argo-metrics (REASONED; argo): Server HTTP metrics on 8083 are unauthenticated and bind to --address, not --metrics-address.
- argo-profiler (REASONED; argo): Server and repo-server pprof paths return 401 unless the profiler file contains exactly true with no newline; enabled profiling has no caller authentication.
- argo-profiler-file (REASONED; argo): ARGOCD_ENABLE_PROFILER_FILE_PATH defaults to /home/argocd/params/profiler.enabled; the server mounts ConfigMap key server.profile.enabled there.
- repo-grpc (REASONED; argo): Repo-server gRPC binds 0.0.0.0:8081 with TLS by default; mTLS is skipped without the client CA, separate from the serving certificate.
- repo-http (REASONED; argo): Repo-server HTTP metrics and health bind 0.0.0.0:8084 without an authentication wrapper.
- repo-limits (REASONED; argo): Repo-server requires verified client certificates with a loaded client CA; missing or unstatable serving files trigger a session self-signed certificate, while an invalid present pair errors. No authorization interceptor appears, and the registered service handlers read no caller identity, so, from this source reading, any client completing the transport handshake can call its methods.
- controller-metrics (REASONED; argo): Application-controller metrics, health and file-gated pprof share one plain-HTTP mux on a hardcoded 0.0.0.0 host; --metrics-port (default 8082) sets only the port, and the command defines no bind-address flag.
- applicationset-webhook (REASONED; argo): ApplicationSet webhook binds :7000; its container and Service declare 7000.
- applicationset-metrics (REASONED; argo): ApplicationSet metrics bind :8080; its container and Service declare 8080.
- applicationset-health (REASONED; argo): ApplicationSet health probes bind :8081 without a container or Service port declaration; missing declarations do not close sockets.
- notifications (REASONED; argo): Notifications HTTP metrics bind 0.0.0.0:9001 without authentication; a metrics Service and TCP liveness probe exist without containerPort.
- dex-http (REASONED; argo): Dex starts only with nonempty generated configuration; HTTP defaults to TLS on 0.0.0.0:5556 using /tmp/tls.crt and /tmp/tls.key.
- dex-grpc (REASONED; argo, dex): Generated Dex gRPC uses 0.0.0.0:5557 without TLS or client-auth settings; Dex v2.45.1 source sets no transport credentials or authentication interceptor for this configuration, its API handlers read no caller identity, and GetClient returns client secrets, including Argo CD's static client; this assumes the deployed ghcr.io/dexidp/dex:v2.45.1 tag was built from Dex v2.45.1.
- dex-image (REASONED; argo, dex): Dex v2.45.1's release workflow builds pushed vX.Y.Z tags from the checked-out tree, tags the alpine variant through its semver rule, and, when publishing, cosign-signs and attests the pushed ghcr.io digest; Argo CD's base names ghcr.io/dexidp/dex:v2.45.1, no signature or attestation was verified, and whether that published image came from this workflow is not established.
- dex-telemetry (REASONED; argo): Dex telemetry uses HTTP on 0.0.0.0:5558; all three Dex ports have Services.
- redis-password (REASONED; argo, redis-image, redis-source): Redis receives --requirepass from argocd-redis/auth; secret-init generates and checks that Secret. The redis:8.2.3-alpine tag, taken as built from docker-library-redis v8.2.3, uses Redis wildcard bind defaults and patches protected mode off; this holds for the deployed public.ecr.aws image only if it was built from that recipe.
- redis-image-name (REASONED; argo, official-images, official-images-docs): The base Redis kustomization renames redis to public.ecr.aws/docker/library/redis, keeping 8.2.3-alpine, as the rendered install.yaml shows; Docker Official Images lists redis:8.2.3-alpine as built from docker-library-redis bcbc6921's alpine directory, but the pinned sources do not establish which recipe the ECR registry tag was built from.
- redis-argv (REASONED; argo, redis-source): Redis 8.2.3 has no password-specific redaction of its start-up arguments; on Linux, with set-proc-title at its default yes, its first title update zeroes the original argument area and any environment strings directly after it before listeners open, leaving heap and setenv() copies; whether that clears the REDIS_PASSWORD environment copy is not established.
- redis-tls (REASONED; argo): Base manifests configure no Redis TLS and the Argo Redis client defaults --redis-use-tls=false; protect traffic, Secret and cache.
- component-policies (REASONED; argo): Base policies restrict repo gRPC, Redis and Dex callers by component; enforcement needs a supporting CNI.
- broad-policies (REASONED; argo): Server policy allows all ingress; other metrics and ApplicationSet webhook allowances admit every namespace. Narrow existing additive allowances and egress separately.
- argo-anonymous (REASONED; argo, argo-docs): users.anonymous.enabled defaults off; anonymous callers otherwise inherit policy.default.
- argo-disable-auth (REASONED; argo): server.disable.auth defaults false; inspect effective args and environment because anonymous-off does not compensate for disabled authentication.
- argo-default-role (REASONED; argo, argo-docs): Base RBAC ConfigMap omits policy.default; the inspected loader supplies an empty role to the enforcer, which skips its additive default-role check. Default-role grants are additive and cannot be revoked by a later subject rule; define scoped policy.csv roles and group mappings.
- argo-rbac-wiring (REASONED; argo): argocd-server builds its enforcer for argocd-rbac-cm with the built-in policy and a claims enforcer, starts the ConfigMap loader, authenticates gRPC calls by default and stores claims, and passes the enforcer to API services; for example, application List filters on get and Create checks create. Per-handler coverage and runtime overrides remain unverified.
- argo-auth-overrides (REASONED; argo, grpc-middleware, grpc-go, grpc-middleware-prom): argocd-server's gRPC interceptors authenticate calls by default unless auth is disabled, but, from this source reading, the session, version and settings services override that function for every method and accept unauthenticated callers, settings only for Get; pinned go-grpc-middleware v2.3.3 calls an override on the service value grpc-go v1.81.1 passes. As read, the interceptors ahead keep it.
- argo-auth-chain-ahead (REASONED; argo, grpc-middleware, grpc-middleware-prom): Ahead of auth, argocd-server's unary chain runs the bug21955 workaround, v2.3.3 logging and providers/prometheus v1.1.0 metrics interceptors; read in the extracted modules, the two module interceptors wrap one shared v2.3.3 interceptor that reads only info.FullMethod and calls the handler with the context its reportable returns, and none of the three writes to UnaryServerInfo or its Server field.
- argo-grpc-middleware-pin (REASONED; argo, grpc-middleware, grpc-middleware-prom, grpc-go): Argo CD's go.sum lines for go-grpc-middleware/v2 v2.3.3, providers/prometheus v1.1.0 and grpc-go v1.81.1 match hashes a go mod download recorded over their zips on 2026-10-23. A diff -rq of each extracted zip against its tag's module directory reported no differing file; one-sided paths are or hold nested modules, or are the root LICENSE in the prometheus zip; no h1: hash was recomputed from git.
- argo-webhook (REASONED; argo-docs): /api/webhook accepts unauthenticated refresh events without a shared secret; configure one to limit spoofed reconciliation and resource exhaustion.
- argo-projects (REASONED; argo-docs): Restrict AppProjects including the built-in default project; project constraints do not reduce a compromised controller's Kubernetes credentials.
- argo-cluster-rbac (REASONED; argo-docs): Reduce controller and registered-cluster argocd-manager write permissions to needed namespaces/resources while retaining required read access.
- flux-api (REASONED; flux): Flux has no standalone management login/API; Kubernetes authenticates its custom-resource operations, while separate dashboards need their own controls.
- flux-bootstrap (REASONED; flux): GitHub bootstrap --token-auth retains a PAT in flux-system; --token-auth=false creates a read-only SSH deploy key by default. Protect bootstrap input and Secrets.
- flux-writeback (REASONED; flux): Image automation needs Git write access, including --read-write-key=true for the bootstrap key; scope the repository and protect update branches and objects.
- flux-artifacts (REASONED; flux): Source-controller serves fetched artifacts over internal HTTP; enforced NetworkPolicy, not ClusterIP alone, isolates them.
- flux-receiver-port (REASONED; flux): Webhook receiver listens on 9292 behind Service port 80; external exposure needs a route and TLS termination.
- flux-receiver-types (REASONED; flux): generic validates nothing; generic-hmac, GitHub, Bitbucket and Nexus use HMAC, while gitlab compares X-Gitlab-Token.
- flux-oidc (REASONED; flux, flux-oidc): generic-oidc, introduced in Flux 2.9, rejects secretRef and validates bearer tokens; constrain issuer validations and audience, whose default is notification-controller.
- flux-rbac (REASONED; flux): Only kustomize-controller and helm-controller hold cluster-admin; other controllers still have meaningful permissions including Secret access.
- flux-lockdown (REASONED; flux): Use scoped reconciliation ServiceAccounts, --no-cross-namespace-refs and --no-remote-bases; --default-service-account fills an omission, not an explicit serviceAccountName.
- verify-argo (REASONED; argo-docs, argo, curl): Anonymous application listing should fail with 401 while a valid token lists the expected application; repeat at origin and CLI/gRPC and inspect effective RBAC.
- verify-bootstrap (REASONED; argo-docs): Absence of the bootstrap Secret proves removal of that material, not password rotation.
- verify-inventory (REASONED; argo, flux): Inventory Services, routes, host ports, policies and component sockets; node-local ss and policy objects alone do not establish cluster isolation.
- verify-repo-metrics (REASONED; argo): Base policy permits HTTP 200 metrics to monitoring and unrelated pods; narrowed policy should admit only monitoring, with a successful positive control.
- verify-server-metrics (REASONED; argo): Repeat on server 8083: only authorized monitoring should receive metrics after narrowing ingress; a failed control is inconclusive.
- verify-profiler (REASONED; argo): From an allowed pod, pprof cmdline should return 401 disabled, 200 for exact true, then 401 for true plus newline; keep metrics as control.
- verify-flux (REASONED; flux, python, curl): Identical generic-hmac bodies without and with X-Signature should be rejected and accepted with reconciliation; status is type/version dependent. The cited curl curl-8_14_1 lines show --data-binary posting data exactly as specified, preserving newlines and carriage returns that --data strips from @file input, reading @- from stdin and @filename from a file, and posting like --data's POST request.
- verify-receiver-status (REASONED; flux): Read receiver name and Ready condition without exposing webhookPath or condition messages; origin checks distinguish receiver rejection from proxy rejection.

# Self-hosted CI runners: GitHub Actions and GitLab Runner

GitHub Actions self-hosted runners and GitLab Runner run CI jobs on machines you manage. This guide helps your AI assistant configure runners securely, including limits on whose code can start jobs, untrusted jobs on isolated disposable workers apart from deployment runners, narrow credentials, and egress enforced outside the job.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/self-hosted-ci-runners.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against GitHub Actions documentation (no recorded version), GitHub REST API 2026-03-10, GitLab Runner source v19.5.0, and Python tomllib minimum 3.11; 3 further sources carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-21; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 37 claims: 1 demonstrated by a check that ran and 36 reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

A self-hosted runner exists to execute CI job commands on your own machine, so the trust question is
not a bind address but who can cause code to run on it. Both GitHub Actions runners and GitLab Runner
are outbound-only for job transport: they poll their service over HTTPS (configure GitLab Runner to verify the
certificate) and open no inbound job-polling port, so no inbound opening is needed to receive jobs. Autoscaled
GitLab workers can still take private management connections from their runner manager, and a custom GitHub
autoscaler can run a separate webhook receiver; restrict any such management listener to its manager and
validate webhook signatures before processing. The controls are eligibility (whose code the runner will run),
credentials (what a job can reach), executor privilege (how isolated the job is from the host), and lifecycle
(what survives after a job). Get those wrong and an untrusted job is remote code
execution with the runner's permissions and network position: it can steal the credentials the job
legitimately receives, poison caches and tools that later trusted builds consume, and pivot from the
runner's place in your network, including the cloud metadata endpoint
([egress-metadata.md](egress-metadata.md)).
Isolate runners from production and from each other, and handle every token as [secrets.md](secrets.md)
describes. Run the job-executing process under a dedicated account with the least OS privilege it needs, keep
administrator and provisioning credentials off the worker, and treat rootful Docker access (including `docker`
group membership) as host administration confined to a disposable VM. Enforce worker egress outside the job's
control: allow the CI, artifact, registry, DNS and dependency destinations it needs and deny production
networks, runner-management services, other workers, and unused metadata endpoints over IPv4 and IPv6. IMDSv2
and metadata headers do not stop arbitrary job code that can request its own token, so test egress from the
actual job environment, including connections that bypass any proxy ([egress-metadata.md](egress-metadata.md)).

## GitHub Actions self-hosted runner

GitHub's own guidance is to "only use self-hosted runners with private repositories", because a fork of
a public repository "can potentially run dangerous code on your self-hosted runner machine by creating
a pull request that executes the code in a workflow". Keep self-hosted runners off public repositories.
Runner groups are the control: only private repositories can use a runner group by default, and the
override that admits public repositories should stay off. An ordinary fork `pull_request` run receives a
read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and, on the default fork settings, none of your other secrets, but the code
still executes on your host, so it can already read host-resident credentials, files, and reachable
services; host persistence (a poisoned tool or harvested credential left for a later, more privileged
job on the same machine) only compounds it. The `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` triggers can access secrets and a write token, so never check out
or execute untrusted pull-request code (or scripts from untrusted artifacts or caches) in those privileged
workflows; a fresh ephemeral runner does not protect credentials supplied to the same job. Keep privileged
workflows on separate, trusted, ephemeral workers, and review the private-repository fork-workflow settings,
which can themselves grant write tokens and secrets.

Several credentials pass through a runner, and they are not interchangeable. The registration token is
a short-lived bootstrap value (documented one-hour lifetime); generate it on demand, never bake it into
an image, and note that its expiry does not deregister a runner already registered with it. Keep the
admin-scoped credential that generates it (a GitHub App installation or a PAT) off the runner host and in a
separate management service, since it outranks anything the runner holds; use the endpoint's documented minimum
(organization registration or JIT endpoints need `Self-hosted runners: write`, repository endpoints need
`Administration: write`) and expire or revoke it when no longer needed. A JIT
configuration (the `encoded_jit_config` the generate-jitconfig API returns) provisions a runner that
executes at most one job; protect the whole response. Once configured, the runner stores its own
authentication credential locally, so protect the install directory and any backups. `GITHUB_TOKEN` is
a per-job token scoped to the workflow's repository; set the default workflow permissions to read-only
and grant more only to the trusted job with an explicit `permissions:` key. Treat OIDC as another job
credential: grant `id-token: write` only to the deployment job that needs it, keep it out of the default
permissions, and configure the cloud provider to validate the issuer, audience and a narrowly scoped subject
for the intended repository and trusted branch or protected environment ([machine-auth.md](machine-auth.md)),
since any code in an authorized job can mint that token and use the cloud credentials it buys. Run the runner
service as a dedicated unprivileged user, never root and never in the `docker` group (membership is
root-equivalent), because a job executes with that account's authority ([docker.md](docker.md)). Prefer ephemeral or JIT
runners so one job cannot poison the next, run untrusted CI on a pool kept separate from deployment and
signing runners, and remember that deregistering an ephemeral runner does not destroy its disk: tearing
down the machine is your job. Labels only route jobs to runners; they do not authorize, so never treat
a label as a security boundary.

## GitLab Runner

The executor decides how much of the host a job controls, and it is the first thing to get right. The
shell executor runs the job directly as the runner's user with no isolation. The Docker executor is a
real boundary only when it is unprivileged: GitLab warns that with `privileged = true` "you are effectively
disabling all the container's security mechanisms", exposing the host to privilege escalation and container
breakout. Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` (or reaching a rootful daemon over TCP)
hands over the daemon's host even with `privileged = false`. For untrusted work use an unprivileged Docker or a hardened Kubernetes executor on isolated disposable workers,
never shell on a shared host, never the socket, and never `services_privileged`; build images without the host
daemon rather than mounting it. Deny job access to the host Docker daemon, sensitive host mounts, host
PID/network namespaces, unnecessary devices and elevated capabilities; for Kubernetes enforce non-privileged
containers, disable privilege escalation, restrict the service-account RBAC, and disable automatic
service-account-token mounting where jobs do not need it, and prevent job configuration from overriding those
restrictions. Containers share the host kernel, so use separate disposable VMs or nodes where that boundary is
insufficient. Make workers disposable, one job each, with an autoscaling executor, since a persistent worker
lets one job poison the next.

The tokens are distinct credentials. The legacy registration token was disabled by default in GitLab 17.0; removal is currently scheduled for GitLab 20.0. Use
the runner authentication token, which lives in `config.toml`, so protect that file and its backups and rotate
the token on any exposure, because a cloned runner using the same token silently steals the jobs meant for the
original. The access token that creates a runner (through `POST /user/runners`, needing the `create_runner`
scope) is a separate, more powerful credential: keep it off the worker, and set runner scope and protection at
creation rather than assuming legacy registration arguments still configure them. `CI_JOB_TOKEN` carries the triggering user's access to the resources it
supports for the job's
lifetime, and it is also `CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD` and is embedded in `CI_REPOSITORY_URL`, so restrict inbound
job-token access on each target project that holds sensitive resources: that allowlist controls whose job
tokens may reach the target, not where this job's token may go, and some resources stay reachable outside it
unless you also restrict their feature visibility. An instance-wide runner on an installation with public
projects accepts strangers' code just as a public-repository GitHub runner does. A project-scoped runner limits
which project can assign it, not the provenance of the code it runs: a parent-project member can launch a fork
merge-request pipeline using the fork's configuration with parent-project resources, so review that code before
launching it or disable `ci_allow_fork_pipelines_to_run_in_parent_project`. Any user with the Developer role can
compromise a non-ephemeral runner, so use protected runners with `access_level: ref_protected` for protected
refs and keep them separate from the pool that tests forked merge requests. The runner opens no inbound listener unless you configure one. The Prometheus metrics endpoint (set through
`listen_address` or `gitlab-runner run --listen-address`, and also via Helm/Operator config) has no built-in
authorization and also exposes profiling endpoints; `9252` is the allocated port, not proof of the configured
one. The optional `[session_server]` listener uses TLS and must be reachable by GitLab at its configured
address (`8093` is an example), so restrict it to the required GitLab traffic rather than only to monitoring
clients. Enable neither unless needed, and firewall each to the clients that need it when you do.

```bash
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_METRICS_URL'

  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'exactly one URL required; not probing'; exit 2; }
  case "$1" in
    *REPLACE_WITH_*|'') echo 'substitute the URL inside the quotes; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  case "$1" in
    http://*|https://*) ;;
    *) echo 'HTTP or HTTPS URL required; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "$1"
)
```

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- job-transport (REASONED; github, gitlab): Both runners poll over HTTPS without an inbound job-polling port; verify GitLab TLS and restrict separate autoscaler management or webhook listeners.
- worker-account (REASONED; github, gitlab, docker): Use a dedicated least-privileged account, keep provisioning credentials off workers and confine rootful Docker access to disposable VMs.
- worker-egress (REASONED; github, gitlab, aws): Enforce job egress outside job control, isolate production and other workers, and deny unused metadata over both families; IMDSv2 does not stop arbitrary authorized job code.
- github-eligibility (REASONED; github): Keep self-hosted runners off public repositories; runner groups admit only private repositories by default and the public override should stay off.
- fork-token (REASONED; github): Ordinary fork pull_request jobs normally receive a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no other secrets, but can still read host credentials and reachable services.
- privileged-triggers (REASONED; github): pull_request_target and workflow_run can access secrets and write tokens; never execute untrusted PR code, artifacts or caches in these jobs.
- private-forks (REASONED; github): Review private-repository fork settings, which can grant write tokens and secrets; separate trusted privileged workers from untrusted CI.
- registration-token (REASONED; github-api): Registration tokens last one hour; generate on demand, never bake into images, and do not confuse expiry with runner deregistration.
- registration-manager (REASONED; github-api): Keep the App/PAT generating registration or JIT credentials off workers; organization endpoints need Self-hosted runners: write, repository endpoints Administration: write.
- jit (REASONED; github-api): Protect encoded_jit_config and the whole response; JIT runners execute at most one job.
- runner-credential (REASONED; github): Protect the installed runner authentication credential, directory and backups.
- github-job-token (REASONED; github): GITHUB_TOKEN is repository-scoped and per-job; set read-only defaults and grant only trusted jobs additional permissions.
- oidc (REASONED; github): Grant id-token: write only where needed; the cloud trust must restrict issuer, audience and repository/branch or protected-environment subject.
- github-lifecycle (REASONED; github, github-api): Prefer ephemeral/JIT workers and destroy their machines and storage; deregistration does not destroy disks, and labels route rather than authorize jobs.
- shell-executor (REASONED; gitlab): The GitLab shell executor runs as the runner user without isolation; avoid it for untrusted jobs on shared hosts.
- docker-executor (REASONED; gitlab, docker): Use unprivileged Docker; privileged=true or services_privileged and host Docker socket/TCP access can expose the host despite privileged=false.
- executor-host-access (REASONED; gitlab, gitlab-runner): Deny sensitive host mounts, host PID/network namespaces, unnecessary devices and capabilities; build without the host daemon.
- kubernetes-executor (REASONED; gitlab): Enforce nonprivileged containers, no privilege escalation, scoped ServiceAccounts and no unnecessary token mounting; prevent job overrides.
- gitlab-disposal (REASONED; gitlab): Containers share the kernel; use disposable separate VMs/nodes as needed and one-job autoscaling workers. Instance and Docker Autoscaler GA is recorded as Runner 17.1.
- gitlab-registration (REASONED; gitlab): Legacy registration tokens were disabled by default in GitLab 17.0, with removal scheduled for 20.0; use runner authentication tokens.
- gitlab-runner-token (REASONED; gitlab): Protect and rotate the runner authentication token in config.toml and backups; a cloned runner can steal assigned jobs.
- gitlab-creation (REASONED; gitlab): POST /user/runners needs create_runner scope; keep that access token off workers and set scope/protection at creation.
- gitlab-job-token (REASONED; gitlab): CI_JOB_TOKEN carries supported triggering-user access during the job and appears as CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD and inside CI_REPOSITORY_URL.
- gitlab-allowlist (REASONED; gitlab): Target-project inbound job-token allowlists limit who may access that target, not job egress; also restrict resource feature visibility.
- gitlab-forks (REASONED; gitlab): Instance runners on public installations accept strangers; project scope does not establish code trust. Review parent-launched fork pipelines or disable ci_allow_fork_pipelines_to_run_in_parent_project.
- gitlab-protected (REASONED; gitlab): Developer access can compromise persistent runners; release runners need ref_protected and a pool separate from fork-merge-request testing.
- gitlab-metrics (REASONED; gitlab): Optional listen_address metrics and profiling have no built-in authorization; 9252 is allocated, not proof of the configured port.
- gitlab-session (REASONED; gitlab): Optional session_server uses TLS and must admit required GitLab traffic at its configured address; 8093 is an example, not an established default.
- verify-eligibility (REASONED; github-api): Fully paginate groups, selected repositories and public repositories' own runners; visibility=all alone is not public eligibility, and inherited access needs review.
- verify-permissions (REASONED; github): Inspect organization and repository workflow-token defaults and PR approval settings; explicit workflow permissions can raise grants and id-token is separate.
- verify-assignment (REASONED; github-api, github): A controlled fork workflow should run when exposed and lose assignment when restricted, while an allowed private job still runs; skipped/pending/offline/timeout is inconclusive.
- verify-config (DEMONSTRATED; python, gitlab, gitlab-runner): Python 3.14.4 synthetic fixtures reported exposed/fixed Docker, Kubernetes and autoscaler values; wrong types passed through, misplaced keys printed null, and empty/error cases differed in output and exit status.
- verify-daemon (REASONED; gitlab, docker): Resolve docker.host through DOCKER_HOST or the default socket when absent; flag actual job access to a rootful daemon, not tcp:// alone.
- verify-autoscaler (REASONED; gitlab): For Instance/Docker Autoscaler require capacity_per_instance=1 and max_use_count=1 explicitly as integers; absent or other values are findings.
- verify-gitlab-api (REASONED; gitlab): Read inbound allowlists and require release-runner ref_protected against exposed controls; gitlab-runner verify proves authentication only.
- verify-lifecycle (REASONED; github-api, gitlab, github): Check complete deregistration listings and infrastructure disposal; persistent-worker canary must survive in the control, but absence alone does not prove destruction or clean shared caches.
- verify-listeners (REASONED; gitlab): Inventory namespaces and publications, require the permitted-client response, then test disallowed access; any HTTP response proves reachability, failure needs corroborating firewall denial.

# Full-stack JS frameworks: SvelteKit, Nuxt, Vite

SvelteKit and Nuxt are JavaScript frameworks for web apps with server code; Vite is a build tool. This guide helps your AI assistant deploy them securely, including SvelteKit's loopback bind and proxy trust, no secrets in public config, auth on every server entry point, and no Vite server in production.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/frontend-frameworks.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against SvelteKit adapter-node @sveltejs/adapter-node@5.5.7, SvelteKit routing and hooks documentation @sveltejs/kit@2.70.3, Nuxt lockfile v4.0.0, Nuxt documentation 4.x, Nuxt output source v4.0.0, Vite bind source v8.3.1, and h3 request and Node adapter source at release commit 1.15.3, plus 2 more recorded bases; 1 further source is pinned to a commit and 4 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-18; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 20 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

SvelteKit, Nuxt, and Vite-based apps built by AI assistants inherit the same traps as [nextjs.md](nextjs.md): a server bind that can default wide open (SvelteKit's Node adapter binds `0.0.0.0` as of adapter-node 5.5.7, though Vite's dev server defaults to `localhost` as of Vite 8.3.1), a proxy that has to be explicitly trusted before secure cookies and correct origins work, and a public-env prefix that ships anything given it straight to the browser. Each framework also has more than one server entry point (endpoints, server routes, load functions), and a check placed in only one of them leaves the others open, exactly as with Next.js layouts versus Server Actions.

## SvelteKit (`adapter-node`)

The built server "will accept connections on `0.0.0.0` using port 3000" by default (host and port as of adapter-node 5.5.7; the port default applies only when `SOCKET_PATH` is unset or empty, and none of this applies when systemd socket activation hands the process a socket); override with `HOST` and `PORT`:

```bash
HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=3000 node build
```

Behind a reverse proxy, set `ORIGIN` (for example `ORIGIN=https://app.example.com`) so SvelteKit computes the correct origin for redirects and cookies. `PROTOCOL_HEADER` and `HOST_HEADER` (for example `x-forwarded-proto` and `x-forwarded-host`) let it read the real scheme and host from the proxy; the docs caution to set these only behind a trusted reverse proxy, since an untrusted client could otherwise spoof them. `ADDRESS_HEADER` and `XFF_DEPTH` do the same for the client's real IP.

CSRF: `csrf.checkOrigin` (default `true`, deprecated in the current reference) checks the `Origin` header for a POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE form submission whose `Content-Type` is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, or `text/plain`, rejecting a mismatch with "Cross-site POST form submissions are forbidden." It does not inspect a JSON body or any other content type reaching a `+server.js` endpoint or form action, so those still need their own origin or session check. The docs point to `csrf.trustedOrigins` instead: an allowlist (default empty) of specific origins permitted to submit forms cross site; only `'*'` trusts every origin, and the docs call that generally not recommended.

Public env: only variables prefixed `PUBLIC_` (`env.publicPrefix`) are "statically injected into your bundle at build time" and reachable from `$env/static/public`; anything else throws if imported from client code. Keep secrets in modules SvelteKit treats as server-only, either `$env/static/private` / `$env/dynamic/private`, a `.server.js` filename, or anything under `$lib/server/` ([secrets.md](secrets.md)); SvelteKit statically traces import chains and fails the build if client code imports one, even through a dynamic `import()`.

None of this gates a request for you by default. The pinned SvelteKit load documentation and server/client source show layout and page `load` functions run concurrently unless a child calls `await parent()`, and a layout `load` does not run on every request. A `+layout.server.js` guard therefore cannot be relied on to protect a sibling `+page.server.js` load function before it uses protected data; the routing documentation says `+layout` has no effect on `+server.js`, and the form-actions documentation says actions are exported from `+page.server.js`. SvelteKit page dispatch calls form actions before page loads, so a layout guard cannot be relied on to protect a form action. Guide advice: check the session before protected work in each page load, form action and `+server.js` endpoint, the same pattern as the Next.js Data Access Layer in [nextjs.md](nextjs.md). The pinned hooks documentation describes `handle` in `hooks.server.js` for server requests, including prerendering, and returning a `Response` before `resolve` renders the route. The runtime invokes `handle` after checks that can return first, including cross-origin remote and form requests, hash-routing rejections and rerouted prerendered resources; it therefore does not run for every request received by the SvelteKit server. In adapter-node 5.5.7, client assets and already prerendered pages are served before SSR and do not reach `handle` through that adapter. Guide advice: use `handle` to check the session and block unauthorized SvelteKit requests that reach it; a hook that only redirects unauthenticated page navigation or only attaches identity to `event.locals` leaves directly reached `+server.js` endpoints and form actions open unless they check it. For a client-initiated remote function request, the runtime takes the page path and search from request headers and resolves `event.url`, `route` and `params` in `handle` from that path; the pinned hooks documentation describes these as calling-page fields rather than the generated endpoint. The pinned remote-functions documentation says the same about these `RequestEvent` properties inside remote functions. Both warn never to use these fields to authorize data access because request values can be manipulated. Guide advice: do not rely on those fields alone to decide what is authorized; check the session and enforce authorization for the specific resource where it is served, since a session check alone does not authorize access to that resource. Wire real authentication with an identity provider or library per [oidc-integration.md](oidc-integration.md), not a client-side redirect alone.

## Nuxt (Nitro server routes)

Files under `server/api/`, `server/routes/`, and `server/middleware/` are auto-registered Nitro handlers exported with `defineEventHandler()`, and a handler in `server/middleware/` runs before every other server route. Nuxt ships no built-in authentication. A middleware handler can enforce access if it throws (for example `createError` with a 401 or 403) or otherwise ends the request there; one that only attaches `event.context.auth` for other handlers to read has not enforced anything, and every handler that reads it still has to check it itself:

```ts
// server/api/admin.ts: the route checks for itself; the middleware only sets event.context.auth
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (!event.context.auth?.user) {
    event.node.res.statusCode = 401
    return { message: 'Not authenticated' }
  }
})
```

`runtimeConfig` splits the same way as Next's env prefix: keys directly on `runtimeConfig` are "only available within server-side"; keys under `runtimeConfig.public` are "also exposed to the client-side." Environment variables override both, using an uppercase `NUXT_` prefix with underscores between key segments: private keys just need `NUXT_` (for example `NUXT_API_SECRET`), public keys need `NUXT_PUBLIC_` (for example `NUXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE`). The docs warn not to "expose runtime config keys to the client-side by either rendering them or passing them to `useState`" even when they are private on the server.

## Vite (dev and preview servers)

Both are development tooling, not a production server: the `vite preview` docs say plainly "do not use this as a production server as it's not designed for it." Deploy the built `dist/` behind a real server, CDN, or your platform's hosting per [paas.md](paas.md) instead.

`server.host` defaults to `'localhost'` (as of Vite 8.3.1); setting it to `true` or `0.0.0.0` makes the dev server listen on all addresses, including the LAN, which is fine for testing from a phone on a trusted network but should not be left on elsewhere. `server.allowedHosts` defaults to `[]`, which still auto-permits localhost, `.localhost`, and IP addresses; setting it to `true` disables the check entirely, and the docs warn this "allows any website to send requests to your dev server and download your source code and content" (DNS rebinding). Prefer an explicit hostname allowlist over `true`.

Run from the project root after a production build. REASONED: scan coverage and the dist/server classification per the design of the block itself and the cited output-path sources; at marking time the scan ran against local fixture trees, where a secret planted under dist/assets was reported as a FINDING, a tree without it reported clean, a plant only under dist/server was reported as server output, with no listed directory the block refused as inconclusive, and with dist/assets a symlink to an external fixture directory holding the planted value the scan followed the link and reported dist/assets/x.js as a FINDING; no real framework production build is available in the authoring environment, so none was scanned. The block always scans all of `dist`, following symlinks, so it never misses a browser-served file. In a Vite SSR layout, where `dist/server` holds the server build, a result whose matches are all under `dist/server/` is reported as server output rather than as a client leak, and any other result is a FINDING, with its `dist/server/` matches labelled as server output. Confirm that `dist/server` is server-only in your deployment before treating a server-output result as clean. REASONED: following block; private-route denial, client-secret scanning, Host handling and proxy cookies/redirects. No deployed framework application or run outcome is recorded here; expectations are reasoned from the guide and its cited framework and grep documentation.

```bash
curl -q -si https://app.example.com/api/private | head -1   # 401 with no session cookie, on all three frameworks
ls -d build/client build/prerendered .output/public dist 2>/dev/null  # confirm browser-served output paths
# Use the browser-served paths above; adapt both lists for custom output or SSR before running.
# Search client assets and prerendered pages for the literal secret with a fixed-string match. The secret is prompted
# (input hidden) and reaches grep on stdin (-f - reads the patterns from stdin), never grep's argv; -l prints only
# file names, so a finding does not echo the secret. -R follows symlinks, so a linked asset is searched too; -D skip
# skips FIFOs, sockets and devices, so a linked pipe cannot stall the scan. Only the listed directories that exist
# are searched; adapter-node can produce two. The block refuses when none exists. grep's exit status is read
# separately, so an inherited `set -e` cannot abort on a clean result: 0 is a finding, 1 is clean, anything else is
# an error, with grep's own diagnostics left visible. Paste this subshell by itself: without bracketed paste, a line
# pasted after its closing ) becomes the search value instead, and its clean result then means nothing.
(
  trap - DEBUG RETURN ERR  # assumes a clean shell (CONTRIBUTING rule 7): no inherited DEBUG trap, extdebug, function or alias
  set +x +a +e
  set --
  for d in build/client build/prerendered .output/public dist; do [ -d "$d" ] && set -- "$@" "$d"; done
  [ "$#" -gt 0 ] || { echo 'inconclusive: no listed browser-served output directory here; build first and check the paths'; exit 2; }
  { unset -n client_secret && unset -v client_secret; } 2>/dev/null ||
    { echo 'cannot initialize secret input; not scanning'; exit 2; }
  { unset -n IFS; } 2>/dev/null || { echo 'a readonly IFS is set in this shell; not scanning'; exit 2; }
  IFS= read -r -s -p 'Secret value to search for (input hidden), then Enter: ' client_secret < /dev/tty || exit 2
  printf '\n'
  case "$client_secret" in
    ''|*[[:cntrl:]]*) echo 'the full secret value is required; not scanning'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  # File names are not secret: capture them so matches under dist/server/ (a Vite SSR server build) are reported apart.
  if hits=$(printf '%s\n' "$client_secret" | grep -RlF -D skip -f - -- "$@"); then rc=0; else rc=$?; fi
  case "$rc" in
    0)
      # FINDING is the default; only a positively classified all-dist/server/ result is reported as server output.
      client_hits=$(printf '%s\n' "$hits" | grep -av '^dist/server/' || :)
      server_hits=$(printf '%s\n' "$hits" | grep -a '^dist/server/' || :)
      printf '%s\n' "$hits"
      if [ -z "$client_hits" ] && [ -n "$server_hits" ]; then
        echo "server output only: every match is under dist/server/, which a Vite SSR build does not serve to browsers; confirm dist/server is server-only in your deployment before treating this as clean"
      else
        echo "FINDING: the secret is in the built client output"
        [ -z "$server_hits" ] || echo "(of the files listed, those under dist/server/ are server output)"
      fi
      ;;
    1) echo "clean: secret not found in $*" ;;
    *) echo "error: grep exited $rc, result inconclusive" ;;
  esac
)
curl -q -si https://app.example.com/ -H "Host: evil.example.com" | head -1   # the deployed application must not trust a spoofed Host
```

The account-owner and transformation limits stated in this paragraph are documented, not demonstrated. The secret reaches grep on stdin, never argv; the hidden prompt keeps it out of shell history and the block's `set +x` keeps it out of `set -x` tracing, but this does not hide it from the account owner or root. Paste the secret alone at the hidden prompt: a multi-line paste leaves every line after the first for your shell to run. A clean grep result here is evidence, not proof: it means the literal value did not match in the directories searched, not that the secret cannot be present in some other form. A bundler could split, encode, or otherwise transform it, so check the exit code and confirm the directory actually exists rather than reading silence alone as clean.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a SvelteKit `handle` hook that only redirects an unauthenticated page navigation, or a Nuxt `server/middleware/` that only attaches `event.context.auth`, as if it already enforced access, while the `+server.js` endpoint, form action, or `server/api/` route trusts that it happened and skips its own check.
- Leaving `server.allowedHosts` at `true`, or `server.host` wide open, past a local demo.
- Naming a secret `PUBLIC_...` or `NUXT_PUBLIC_...` out of habit from a genuinely public value.

- svelte-public (REASONED; svelte): PUBLIC_ via env.publicPrefix exposes static public env values at build; keep secrets out.
- svelte-private (REASONED; svelte): Private env modules, .server.js and lib/server are server-only; client import chains, including dynamic imports, fail builds.
- svelte-routes (REASONED; svelte, svelte-kit-pin): Pinned load docs and the SvelteKit client and server paths show layout `load` does not run on every request and layout/page `load` run concurrently unless a child calls `await parent()`; routing docs say `+layout` has no effect on `+server.js`; form-actions docs and page dispatch show actions are exported from `+page.server.js` and run before page loads. Guide advice: do not rely on a layout guard to protect a sibling page load, form action or directly reached endpoint; check the session before protected work in each.
- svelte-handle (REASONED; svelte, svelte-kit-pin, adapter): Pinned hooks docs describe `handle` for SvelteKit server requests, including prerendering; runtime source calls it after checks that can reject requests before the hook and lets it return before `resolve`. In adapter-node 5.5.7, client assets and already prerendered pages are served before SSR, so they do not reach `handle` through that adapter. For client-initiated remote function requests, runtime source takes the calling-page path and search from request headers and resolves `route` and `params` from that path; pinned remote-functions docs describe the same fields on `RequestEvent` inside remote functions, and both docs warn never to use these request-derived fields to authorize data access. Guide advice: use `handle` to block unauthorized SvelteKit requests that reach it; a redirect-only or `event.locals`-only hook leaves directly reached endpoints and form actions open unless they check the session; do not rely on calling-page fields alone, and authorize each specific resource where served because a session check alone does not authorize it.
- nuxt-handlers (REASONED; nuxt): Nuxt auto-registers server/api, server/routes and middleware; middleware runs first, but context.auth alone enforces nothing. Throw/end requests or check each handler.
- nuxt-auth (REASONED; nuxt): Nuxt ships no built-in authentication; enforce access server-side, not with client redirects.
- nuxt-private (REASONED; nuxt): Direct runtimeConfig keys are server-only with NUXT_ overrides; rendering or passing to useState can disclose them.
- nuxt-public (REASONED; nuxt): runtimeConfig.public is client-exposed with NUXT_PUBLIC_ overrides, not proxy/cookie configuration.
- vite-production (REASONED; vite): Vite dev/preview is development tooling; deploy dist through a production server, CDN or platform.
- vite-bind (REASONED; vite-pin, vite): Vite 8.3.1 server.host defaults localhost; true/0.0.0.0 exposes all addresses and should not remain beyond trusted-network tests.
- vite-hosts (REASONED; vite): server.allowedHosts defaults empty with localhost, .localhost and IPs allowed; true disables protection and permits DNS rebinding. Prefer explicit names.
- verify-private (REASONED; nuxt, svelte): Guide expects anonymous /api/private 401; enforcement needs app/server handlers, not client redirects.
- verify-secret (REASONED; grep, adapter, nuxt-output, nitro-output, vite-pin, vite, nitro-output-docs): Scan browser-served output: adapter-node build/client and build/prerendered, Nuxt .output/public, Vite dist, scanned whole following symlinks; only a result with every match under dist/server/ is reported as server output, else FINDING with dist/server/ matches labelled. Adjust paths for custom layouts/SSR; reject absence. Prompt full literal secret; grep stdin: 0 finding, 1 no match, others errors. Clean cannot rule out transformed secrets or runtime responses; hidden input and set +x keep the secret from argv, history and tracing, not the account owner or root.
- verify-host (REASONED; vite, adapter, nitro-node, svelte-kit-pin, h3-pin, node-http, nuxt-lock): The deployed application must not trust a spoofed Host. The supplied Vite allowlist reference covers its dev server. Guide assessment: for this probe, exposed means the application responds to the spoofed Host, so curl prints its first response line. Fixed means a fronting proxy or server refuses the unknown Host before the application; apply the default-server refusal pattern in [nginx.md](nginx.md) to the probed HTTPS listener. With a refusal response, curl prints its status line; with nginx return 444 closing without a response, this silent curl pipeline prints nothing. Neither a status line nor silence alone proves which layer handled the request or whether the application builds URLs or redirects from Host. Correlate proxy and application logs with the probe and a working allowed-host control; inspect response headers and generated URLs separately to judge Host use. In the traced adapter-node 5.5.7 and SvelteKit Node request conversion, ORIGIN or configured/request headers form the request URL; these files do not apply a Host allowlist. In the traced nitropack 2.12.0 node-server and app construction, the h3 app is passed to Node HTTP or HTTPS without a Host allowlist. Nuxt v4.0.0 resolves h3 1.15.3; its traced request utilities read Host or optionally forwarded Host and construct a URL without an allowlist; the release commit exports toNodeListener, which creates an event and calls app.handler, matching the adapter Nitro imports. Node v22.22.1 documents a default missing-Host rejection for HTTP/1.1, not an allowed-host list. Guide assessment: these source paths do not establish a universal Host rejection outcome or how the hosting platform treats Host and forwarded headers.
- verify-proxy (REASONED; svelte, nuxt, adapter, nuxt-output, nitro-node): Check Secure cookies and HTTPS redirects with SvelteKit ORIGIN; verify Nuxt for its deployment preset and hosting platform, not NUXT_PUBLIC_. Adapter-node 5.5.7 uses ORIGIN or configured/request headers for the request origin; with ORIGIN and PROTOCOL_HEADER unset, it defaults to https and uses the request Host header unless HOST_HEADER supplies one. Nuxt 4.0.0 pins nitropack 2.12.0, which falls back to its node-server preset for a non-static production build with no preset named or matched; that preset passes the h3 app through toNodeListener to a Node HTTP or HTTPS server. Guide assessment: Nuxt's own trusted-proxy and origin handling come from its deployment preset and hosting platform rather than one documented app-level variable; the cited lines do not establish how h3 1.x or the hosting platform treats Host and forwarded headers or a deployed cookie and redirect outcome.

# Containers: non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only root, and network segmentation

Container hardening means running each container with as few rights as possible, so an attacker inside one gains little. This guide helps your AI assistant apply it, including non-root users, dropped capabilities and read-only root filesystems in Docker, Compose and Kubernetes, plus NetworkPolicy where the cluster's network plugin enforces it.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/container-hardening.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against Docker documentation (no recorded version), Docker Compose source and reference v2.32.4, Kubernetes Pod Security Admission 1.34, kubectl source v1.34.0, Linux process status and capabilities manuals man-pages-6.19, JSON Merge Patch RFC 7396, and BusyBox source 1_36_1; 4 further sources are pinned to a commit and 1 carries no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-21; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 23 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

A model server, chat UI, or proxy is the thing most likely to face untrusted input, so treat its container as compromised eventually and limit what that gets an attacker: not root, not the host's capabilities, not a writable filesystem, and not a route to the rest of the network.

## Docker and Compose

- **Run as non-root.** `USER <user>[:<group>]` in the Dockerfile sets the default user for later `RUN` instructions and for `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` at runtime (per the Dockerfile reference); a user with no primary group runs with the `root` group, so set both. Compose's `user:` overrides that per service; unset in both places, the container runs as root (per the Compose file reference).
- **Read-only root filesystem.** `read_only: true` on a Compose service creates it with a read-only root filesystem; mount a small `tmpfs` for any path the process must write to.
- **Drop capabilities.** `cap_drop: [ALL]` removes every Linux capability; add back only the specific one a service needs with `cap_add`.
- **No privilege escalation.** `security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]` stops a `setuid` binary from gaining more privilege than the process already has (this maps to Docker's engine-level `--security-opt no-new-privileges`; the spellings `no-new-privileges`, `no-new-privileges=true`, and `no-new-privileges:true` are equivalent).
- **Never mount the Docker socket into a container.** In Docker's default rootful configuration, control of the daemon lets a user start a container that can alter the host filesystem without restriction; membership of the `docker` group grants root-level privileges. Rootless mode runs the daemon and containers without root privileges. Docker documents that a container with the mounted `/var/run/docker.sock` and a Docker client can control the host daemon, and documents the `--privileged` and host bind-mount options. This guide's assessment: a container holding the socket can start a privileged sibling or bind-mount host `/` and escape to the host; Rootless mode narrows the host privilege available through this path but does not make the mount safe.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    user: "10001:10001"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: [/tmp]
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true]
```

## Kubernetes securityContext

The same controls, per-Pod or per-container, in the Kubernetes securityContext documentation:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        runAsGroup: 10001
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: [ALL]
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
```

`runAsNonRoot: true` refuses to start the container if its effective user is root; pin `runAsUser` and `runAsGroup` too, since an unset primary group defaults to GID 0 (the runtime default). `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` applies the runtime's default syscall filter instead of running unconfined.

Enforce this with Pod Security Admission's `restricted` level, set as the namespace label
`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` (per the Pod Security Standards documentation); the label
applies to that namespace only, not the whole cluster. `restricted` requires, among its controls: no
privileged containers, no host namespaces or host ports, non-root execution, all capabilities dropped, and a
seccomp profile that is not `Unconfined`. A Pod violating any of these is rejected at admission, not merely
flagged, for Pods created after the label is set; adding the label to a namespace that already runs violating Pods does not evict them (it only warns), so recreate those workloads. The `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` setting above is a separate, per-container recommendation this
guide makes; it is good practice, but it is not one of the controls `restricted` itself requires.

## Network segmentation

A NetworkPolicy is additive and does nothing without an enforcing CNI (per the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy documentation; confirm yours enforces it before relying on this). Start default-deny, then allow only the specific path the app needs:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny-all }
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-app-egress-to-db }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: app } }
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: UDP, port: 53 }, { protocol: TCP, port: 53 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: db } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-db-ingress-from-app }
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: db } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { role: app } } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 5432 }]
```

A connection needs both sides to allow it: the egress policy on the source pod and the ingress policy on
the destination pod (per the Kubernetes NetworkPolicy documentation). With all three policies applied, an
`app` pod can resolve names through the cluster's DNS and reach the `db` pod on port 5432; the `db` pod
accepts connections only from pods labeled `role: app` on port 5432; every other path the namespace's own policies govern is refused. (NetworkPolicy handling of `hostNetwork` pods and of traffic on a pod's own node is implementation-dependent, and the DNS rule above allows port 53 to every pod in `kube-system`, not only CoreDNS, so narrow the DNS peer selector to your resolver where you can.) Databases
still need their own TLS and auth on top ([postgresql.md](postgresql.md), [mysql.md](mysql.md),
[mongodb.md](mongodb.md), [redis.md](redis.md)); a NetworkPolicy is a layer, not a substitute.

## Verify

REASONED: identity, filesystem, runtime security context and segmentation checks; no exposed/fixed run is recorded in this guide. Expectations follow the cited Docker, Kubernetes and Linux man-pages sources; the authoring environment has no authorized Docker workload or Kubernetes cluster. This guide's assessment: the Compose `app` service's image must supply id, sh and touch, and the Pod's container image must supply id, sh and grep -E for these commands; the exact touch error depends on the Compose `app` service's image and probe path.

```bash
docker compose exec app id                          # uid is not 0 (run from the Compose project; this guide advises using the actual container name with bare `docker exec` rather than the `app` service name)
docker compose exec app sh -c 'touch /app/probe && echo WRITABLE || echo blocked'
                                                    # with read_only: true expect "blocked" (typically EROFS; the exact error is image-dependent). But `touch` also
                                                    # fails on a MISSING or non-writable /app (ENOENT/EACCES), which prints
                                                    # "blocked" on a WRITABLE fs too, and this line exits 0 either way (read the
                                                    # printed word, it is not an exit-status test), so prove the discrimination:
                                                    # set read_only: false and recreate (docker compose up -d --force-recreate
                                                    # app), run the same line, confirm it prints WRITABLE (the path exists and
                                                    # the user owns it), then restore read_only, recreate again, and confirm
                                                    # "blocked". Probe a path the container user owns, not `/` (a non-root
                                                    # user cannot write `/` on a writable fs either) and not a tmpfs you
                                                    # mounted (writable by design)
kubectl get pod app -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext}'   # the DECLARED context, not runtime proof; also inspect the running process:
kubectl exec app -- sh -c 'id; grep -E "NoNewPrivs|Seccomp|CapEff|CapBnd" /proc/1/status'   # expect uid!=0, NoNewPrivs:1, Seccomp:2 (a filter is active, not 0=unconfined), and CapEff+CapBnd 0000000000000000 (this guide's expected runtime state under drop:[ALL] is zero effective AND bounding sets; CapEff alone is not enough). Assumes the container's own PID namespace; with shareProcessNamespace PID 1 is the pod sandbox (shown as /pause in the cited example), so pick the app PID and inspect its /proc/<pid>/status

# resolve the db Service's ClusterIP once and probe that same IP from both pods below; the
# role: other pod has no DNS egress under the policies above, so a probe by hostname would fail on
# name resolution rather than on the NetworkPolicy, and access by IP could still work even if
# the policy were not enforcing anything
DBIP=$(kubectl get svc db -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')

# A probe pod needs its own admission-compliant securityContext under the restricted PSA level (Pod Security
# Standards). This guide's advice: make a real TCP connect to the db's actual port (a Postgres port does not
# speak HTTP, so wget cannot test it).
# This guide's advice: quote the address into the JSON: unquoted, `10.96.0.5` is a bare token and the array is not valid
# JSON, so kubectl rejects the override and neither probe below runs. Keep the override's container name
# matching the pod name (this guide's advice): kubectl v1.34.0 `kubectl run --overrides` uses an RFC 7396 JSON
# merge patch by default (`--override-type=merge`), which replaces the whole `containers` array with the one in your override, so the
# override's container name is the one that remains (RFC 7396).
# kubectl run passes the pod name to its generator, generates the Pod, then applies the override; run.go
# does not show the generator's container-naming rule. Keep the names matching to avoid confusion (this guide's advice).
# BusyBox 1.36.1 source offers -z (zero-I/O scanning) in the 1.10-compatible nc applet with NC_EXTRA, and -w sets
# a connect timeout. At official-images d6d62c71, the amd64 busybox:1.36 image is the glibc variant published
# (imported, `Builder: oci-import`) from artefacts committed at docker-library/busybox c1375496, and its root
# filesystem has bin/nc as a link to the BusyBox binary. That commit's Dockerfile.builder applies one patch before
# `make defconfig` (no-cbq.patch, which changes only networking/tc.c and no nc file or NC option), and its config
# step changes no NC option. This guide's inference: that build produced the image's root filesystem. Tags move, so
# this tag-to-commit mapping holds as of that official-images commit, and only amd64 was examined. This guide's
# inference: with the 1.36.1 Kconfig defaults (NC_EXTRA and NC_110_COMPAT default y), the amd64 image's nc applet
# should accept -w and -z; that is not read from the built .config.
# This guide's advice: confirm that image accepts `nc -z -w 3` and makes a TCP connect before relying on the probe.
# Build the override per pod:
probe_override() {
  printf '%s' '{"spec":{"securityContext":{"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":10001,"runAsGroup":10001,"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}},"containers":[{"name":"'"$1"'","image":"busybox:1.36","securityContext":{"allowPrivilegeEscalation":false,"capabilities":{"drop":["ALL"]}},"command":["nc","-z","-w","3","'"$DBIP"'","5432"]}]}}'
}

kubectl run probe-permitted --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=role=app \
  --overrides="$(probe_override probe-permitted)" -- true
                                                     # from a pod labeled role=app, by IP: must succeed FIRST. This is the
                                                     # positive control. If it fails, the policy, the override, or this
                                                     # image's `nc` is the problem, and the forbidden probe below proves
                                                     # nothing: a refusal you cannot distinguish from a broken probe is
                                                     # not evidence

kubectl run probe-forbidden --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=role=other \
  --overrides="$(probe_override probe-forbidden)" -- true
                                                     # from a pod without that label, same IP: must time out or be refused
                                                     # at TCP, not fail on DNS. Read this as an END-TO-END denial: role=other
                                                     # cannot reach the db, but the refusal could be its own default-deny
                                                     # egress OR the db's ingress (either alone would refuse it), so it
                                                     # proves the combined segmentation, not either layer in isolation.
                                                     # Isolating which layer blocks (e.g. that the db ingress admits ONLY
                                                     # role=app) needs more elaborate per-layer probes, each with its own
                                                     # positive control, and is CNI-dependent, so validate the whole policy
                                                     # set on your CNI rather than reasoning rule by rule
```

- rfc7396: JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396)
- busybox-1361: BusyBox source (1_36_1)
- busybox-library: Docker Official Images busybox library (d6d62c71a83290283aa58c5041a156415cfd37d9)
- busybox-image: Docker busybox image build files (c1375496373e76f680b1ef5f713500e98921a45c)

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- docker-user (REASONED; docker): Dockerfile USER sets build/runtime identity; set user and group, since no primary group uses root. Compose user overrides it; unset in both runs as root.
- docker-rootfs (REASONED; docker): Compose read_only makes the root filesystem read-only; provide tmpfs only for required writable paths.
- docker-capabilities (REASONED; docker): cap_drop: [ALL] removes capabilities; add back only specific required capabilities with cap_add.
- docker-escalation (REASONED; docker): no-new-privileges prevents setuid privilege gain; the guide lists bare, equals-true and colon-true spellings as equivalent.
- docker-socket (REASONED; docker, docker-daemon): Never mount /var/run/docker.sock. In Docker's default rootful configuration, daemon control lets a user start a container that can alter the host filesystem without restriction, and docker-group membership grants root-level privileges; Rootless mode runs the daemon and containers without root privileges. Docker documents mounted-socket daemon control with a Docker client, and documents --privileged and host bind mounts; a socket-holding container starting a privileged sibling or bind-mounting host / to escape is this guide's assessment. Rootless mode narrowing the available host privilege but not making the mount safe is this guide's assessment.
- kube-user (REASONED; kubernetes): runAsNonRoot rejects root; pin runAsUser and runAsGroup to 10001, with the guide noting runtime-default GID 0 if unset.
- kube-rootfs (REASONED; kubernetes): Set readOnlyRootFilesystem per container; this is a separate recommendation, not a restricted Pod Security requirement.
- kube-escalation (REASONED; kubernetes): Set allowPrivilegeEscalation: false in the container securityContext.
- kube-capabilities (REASONED; kubernetes): Drop ALL capabilities in the container securityContext.
- kube-seccomp (REASONED; kubernetes): RuntimeDefault selects the runtime syscall filter instead of Unconfined.
- admission (REASONED; kubernetes, kubernetes-134): Namespace enforce: restricted rejects new violating Pods: privileged mode, host namespaces/ports, root, missing capability drops or Unconfined seccomp.
- existing-pods (REASONED; kubernetes, kubernetes-134): Adding the namespace label warns about existing violating Pods without evicting them; recreate workloads.
- policy-semantics (REASONED; kubernetes): NetworkPolicies are additive and require an enforcing CNI; both source egress and destination ingress must allow a connection.
- default-deny (REASONED; kubernetes): The empty podSelector with Ingress and Egress isolates all pods selected in the namespace before narrow allowances.
- dns (REASONED; kubernetes): The app egress rule permits UDP/TCP 53 to all kube-system pods, not just CoreDNS; narrow it to the actual resolver.
- database-path (REASONED; kubernetes): Allow app egress to role: db and db ingress from role: app on TCP 5432; other paths governed by these namespace policies are refused.
- policy-limits (REASONED; kubernetes): hostNetwork and same-node traffic handling are implementation-dependent; database TLS/authentication remain separate controls.
- verify-user (REASONED; docker, compose-2324): Compose exec targets the app service in the resolved project and id must report a nonzero UID; using the actual container name for bare docker exec is this guide's advice.
- verify-rootfs (REASONED; docker, compose-2324): With read_only false, touch on an existing owned path must print WRITABLE; after docker compose up -d --force-recreate with read_only true, it must print blocked. ENOENT or EACCES can also print blocked on a writable filesystem, so blocked alone is not proof of a read-only root. This guide's assessment: the errno, including typical EROFS, depends on the image and path; the probe's exit 0 does not discriminate.
- verify-context (REASONED; kubernetes, kubectl-134, procfs-619, kubernetes-website): kubectl get reads the declared context; kubectl exec inspects the application process for nonzero UID, NoNewPrivs:1, Seccomp:2 and zero effective/bounding capabilities. Clearing CapBnd under drop:[ALL] is this guide's expected runtime state; with shareProcessNamespace, PID 1 belongs to the pod sandbox, so select the application PID.
- verify-probe (REASONED; kubernetes, kubectl-134, rfc7396, busybox-1361): Resolve the db ClusterIP once; keep matching container names and restricted-compliant overrides for busybox:1.36 probes. Pinned kubectl and BusyBox sources explain merge and nc flags; no probe run is recorded, so this guide advises confirming that the image accepts nc -z -w 3 and makes a TCP connect before relying on it.
- probe-image (REASONED; busybox-1361, busybox-library, busybox-image): As of official-images d6d62c71 (tags move), amd64 busybox:1.36 is the glibc variant imported from docker-library/busybox c1375496 artefacts, bin/nc linked to BusyBox. That commit's build patches only networking/tc.c and keeps defconfig's NC options; this guide infers it made the image and, from 1.36.1 Kconfig defaults, not the built .config, that its nc accepts -w and -z; only amd64 was examined.
- verify-segmentation (REASONED; kubernetes): The role: app TCP probe must succeed first; role: other to the same IP must fail at TCP, not DNS. This tests combined segmentation, not either policy layer independently.

==> nextjs.md
