- error-reporting (REASONED; php8): error_reporting defaults E_ALL since PHP 8.0.0; retain reporting into logs. Package/template/deployment overrides can differ.
- php-banner (REASONED; php8, php): expose_php defaults On; Off suppresses PHP own X-Powered-By header, not other layers or all application identification.
- production-template (REASONED; template84): PHP 8.4 production template disables display and enables logging, but uses E_ALL &amp; ~E_DEPRECATED and leaves expose_php enabled.
- disable-functions (REASONED; php8): disable_functions defaults empty; test the listed process-function restrictions. Since PHP 8.0 definitions disappear and userland can redefine them; internal functions only, not a security boundary.
- url-fopen (REASONED; php): allow_url_fopen defaults On; disable unnecessary URL wrappers after compatibility tests, not as a general egress policy.
- url-include (REASONED; php): allow_url_include defaults Off, deprecated since PHP 7.4; retain Off. URL includes also require allow_url_fopen.
- basedir (REASONED; php8): open_basedir defaults NULL; allow required paths, retain OS isolation and account for disabled realpath caching. PHP 8.3 rejects runtime .. components.
- fpm-extensions (REASONED; php8): PHP 8.x FPM security.limit_extensions defaults .php .phar; restrict to .php, which still permits uploaded PHP dispatched by the server.
- upload-execution (REASONED; php8, laravel): Separate writable uploads from code, preferably outside the document root; server mappings must forbid PHP execution, including aliases/symlinks.
- laravel-storage (REASONED; laravel): Laravel 12.x local disk defaults storage/app/private; public disk uses storage/app/public via public/storage, which does not itself prevent PHP execution.
- upload-size (REASONED; php8): upload_max_filesize defaults 2M per file; post_max_size must allow multipart overhead.
- post-size (REASONED; php8): post_max_size defaults 8M; excess leaves POST and FILES empty and must be rejected by the app.
- upload-count (REASONED; php8, php): max_file_uploads defaults 20; twenty maximum-sized files need not fit the POST limit.
- memory-limit (REASONED; php8): memory_limit defaults 128M, should generally exceed post_max_size, and -1 removes the bound.
- input-vars (REASONED; php8): max_input_vars defaults 1000 separately for GET, POST and COOKIE; excess is warned/truncated, not a general JSON limit.
- execution-time (REASONED; php8): max_execution_time defaults 30 for web and 0 for CLI; platform/build accounting can exclude I/O, not a portable wall-clock deadline.
- input-time (REASONED; php8, template84): max_input_time defaults -1, using max_execution_time; 0 is unlimited. Example and production template select 60 seconds.
- upload-time (REASONED; php): Test slow/multiple uploads and coordinate server size/time limits. Per-request bounds do not replace capacity controls or rate limiting.
- fpm-timeout (REASONED; php8): request_terminate_timeout defaults 0, disabled; example selects 60s as app policy and kills overlong workers.
- fpm-finished (REASONED; php8): request_terminate_timeout_track_finished defaults no; yes extends the limit past fastcgi_finish_request and into shutdown work.
- session-gc (REASONED; php8, php): Native gc_maxlifetime defaults 1440 seconds; probabilistic collection is not auth expiry. Use timestamp expiry/cleanup; shared paths can inherit shorter lifetimes.
- session-lifetime (REASONED; php8, laravel): Native cookie_lifetime defaults 0, a browser-session cookie; Laravel uses config/session.php rather than native storage/lifetime directives.
- session-only-cookies (REASONED; php8): session.use_only_cookies defaults 1; retain it to exclude GET/POST IDs. Disabling it is deprecated from PHP 8.4.
- session-storage (REASONED; php8): Default files handler needs a private worker-writable directory outside the document root; dedicated-account mode 0700, default file mode 0600, separate untrusted-app identities.
- session-sid-length (REASONED; php8, template83): PHP 8.x session.sid_length defaults 32; changes are deprecated from 8.4. PHP 8.3 production template sets 26.
- session-sid-bits (REASONED; php8, template83): PHP 8.x session.sid_bits_per_character defaults 4; changes are deprecated from 8.4. PHP 8.3 production template sets 5.
- verify-listener (REASONED; php8): Inventory all FPM listeners: Unix socket or loopback TCP 9000 only.
- verify-tls (REASONED; curl): The TLS probe distinguishes cited exit=60 certificate failure from reasoned exit=0 success without -k; linked fronting-server guides supply TLS configuration.
- verify-cookies (REASONED; php8, laravel): Inspect login Set-Cookie for Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax.
- verify-auth (REASONED; laravel): Anonymous protected routes must deny or redirect to login without protected content; require authorized success and isolated auth-removal control. Unrelated redirects/errors and anonymous Set-Cookie do not establish authentication.
- verify-config (REASONED; php, php8): Inspect CLI ini/settings against installed E_ALL; CLI does not establish web SAPI/FPM settings. Do not publish phpinfo.
- verify-banner (REASONED; php): Fixture should give HTTP 200; expose_php On should show PHP header unless stripped, Off must hide it. Proxy stripping in both states needs SAPI inspection.
- verify-error (REASONED; php8, php): Native warning fixture must disclose canary with display_errors On, then return reached marker without diagnostics and log the warning after hardening. Errors/missing logs/blank bodies are inconclusive; startup/parse errors untested.
- verify-laravel-error (REASONED; laravel): Repeat body probe with controlled Laravel exception, rebuild config cache after APP_DEBUG changes, and require generic response plus protected log; native fixture does not test framework errors.
- verify-curl-version (REASONED; curl): The exitcode and errormsg write-out variables require curl 7.75.0 or later per the curl manual.

# Ruby on Rails and Puma: TLS and authentication

Ruby on Rails is a Ruby framework for building web apps, and Puma is a web server that runs them. This guide helps your AI assistant deploy them securely, including Puma bound privately behind a TLS reverse proxy, Rails told about that proxy, authentication, and certificate checks in outbound calls.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/ruby.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
```

Written against Rails documentation (no recorded version), Action Pack 7.1, and Puma defaults v8.0.2; 5 further sources are pinned to a commit and 3 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-09-26; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 26 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

Puma's default bind is `tcp://[::]:9292` when the host has a non-loopback IPv6 address, otherwise `tcp://0.0.0.0:9292` (as of v8.0.2): every interface, plain HTTP. Rails encrypts its session cookie but still sends it in clear unless HTTPS is enforced. Preferred layout: bind Puma to loopback and terminate TLS in a reverse proxy ([nginx.md](nginx.md), [caddy.md](caddy.md), [apache.md](apache.md)) or behind [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md), with a certificate from [free-certificates.md](free-certificates.md). Puma can also terminate TLS itself, shown below.

## 1. Bind Puma privately

```ruby
# config/puma.rb
bind "tcp://127.0.0.1:3000"
# or: bind "unix:///var/run/puma.sock"
# Puma terminating TLS itself (only when no proxy is in front):
# bind "ssl://0.0.0.0:8443?key=/etc/ssl/private/server.key&cert=/etc/ssl/certs/server.crt"
```

`bind` accepts only `tcp://`, `unix://`, and `ssl://` URIs. The `ssl://` query string also takes `ca=` and `verify_mode=` for client certificates ([machine-auth.md](machine-auth.md)).

## 2. Rails behind the proxy

```ruby
# config/environments/production.rb
config.force_ssl = true      # ActionDispatch::SSL: HTTPS redirect, HSTS per config.ssl_options (default hsts: { subdomains: true })
config.assume_ssl = true     # Rails 7.1+: the proxy terminated TLS and forwards plain HTTP
config.hosts << "app.example.com"   # Host header allowlist (DNS rebinding)
config.session_store :cookie_store, key: "_app_session", secure: true, httponly: true, same_site: :lax, expire_after: 14.days
```

`config.action_dispatch.trusted_proxies` already covers loopback, private, and link-local ranges, so a same-host proxy needs nothing more. A proxy on a public address must be listed as an enumerable, for example `config.action_dispatch.trusted_proxies = [IPAddr.new("203.0.113.10")]`; a single value is not supported. Without any proxy, `X-Forwarded-For` is client-controlled, so do not trust `request.remote_ip` for rate limits or allowlists. `config.action_dispatch.cookies_same_site_protection` defaults to `:lax` from `load_defaults 6.1`.

## 3. Authentication

Follow [authentication.md](authentication.md). Rails specifics:

- Rails 8.0 and later: `bin/rails generate authentication` "Generates a basic authentication system with users, sessions, and password reset", built on `has_secure_password`. Prefer it to hand-rolled login code.
- `has_secure_password` needs `gem "bcrypt", "~> 3.1.7"` and a `password_digest` column; `user.authenticate(password)` returns the user or `false`. It validates presence and the 72-byte bcrypt limit; add your own minimum length.
- Rate-limit login in the controller (needs an `ActiveSupport::Cache` store; defaults to `config.action_controller.cache_store`):

```ruby
class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create
end
```

- For path-level throttles and blocklists, [Rack::Attack](https://github.com/rack/rack-attack) (`gem "rack-attack"`, configured in `config/initializers/rack_attack.rb`; its railtie adds the middleware in Rails).
- Secrets live in `config/credentials.yml.enc`, edited with `bin/rails credentials:edit`; the decryption key is `config/master.key` (Rails adds it to `.gitignore`) or `ENV["RAILS_MASTER_KEY"]`, which takes precedence. Set `config.require_master_key = true` so a deployment without the key refuses to boot instead of running half-configured.
- MFA: Rails has no built-in second factor. Add TOTP in the app or front it with an identity layer; options in [mfa.md](mfa.md). OIDC login follows [oidc-integration.md](oidc-integration.md).

Sidekiq's Web UI is a common blind spot. Mounted the usual way it has no authentication of its own:

```ruby
# config/routes.rb -- unsafe as written
require "sidekiq/web"
mount Sidekiq::Web => "/sidekiq"
```

Anyone who reaches `/sidekiq` can read the arguments of the jobs it lists, which routinely carry tokens, email addresses, and record IDs, and can retry, kill, or clear queues. Gate the mount; these route snippets go inside your `Rails.application.routes.draw` block. With Devise, wrap it in an `authenticate` constraint so only a signed-in admin reaches it:

```ruby
authenticate :user, ->(u) { u.admin? } do
  mount Sidekiq::Web => "/sidekiq"
end
```

Without Devise, put HTTP Basic Auth in front of the Rack app, a separate credential kept out of source and compared in constant time (the SHA256 digests give `secure_compare` equal-length inputs, and `&` avoids a short-circuit that would leak which half matched):

```ruby
# config/initializers/sidekiq.rb
require "sidekiq/web"
Sidekiq::Web.use(Rack::Auth::Basic) do |user, password|
  ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(
    ::Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(user), ::Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_USER"))) &
    ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(
      ::Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(password), ::Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_PASSWORD")))
end
```

Never mount it bare, and keep it off the public internet even behind auth.

## 4. Client-side TLS discipline

```ruby
Net::HTTP.start("api.example.com", 443,
                use_ssl: true,                                  # verify_mode defaults to OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_PEER
                ca_file: "/etc/ssl/certs/internal-ca.pem") do |http|   # internal CA; or set SSL_CERT_FILE in the environment
  http.request(Net::HTTP::Get.new("/"))
end
```

`Net::HTTP.start` takes `use_ssl`, `ca_file`, `verify_mode`, and the other SSL settings in its options hash and applies them when it opens the connection. Assigning `http.ca_file` inside the block comes after the handshake and does not affect it; to set attributes on an instance, use `Net::HTTP.new` and set them before calling `start`.

Never set `verify_mode = OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_NONE`. Ruby's default SSL context loads the system store through `set_default_paths`, and OpenSSL reads `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` to locate that store, so an internal CA goes there (see [self-signed.md](self-signed.md)) rather than into a disabled check.

## Verify

REASONED: following block; Puma binds, Rails HTTPS/cookies/login, Sidekiq denial and master-key tracking. No application deployment or run outcome is recorded here; these checks are reasoned from the cited Puma, Rails and Sidekiq sources.

```bash
ss -tlnp   # read every listener; puma/ruby: 127.0.0.1:3000 only
curl -q -sI http://app.example.com/                                 # 301 to https:// (force_ssl)
curl -q -sI https://app.example.com/ | grep -iE 'strict-transport|set-cookie'   # HSTS; secure; httponly; samesite=lax
curl -q -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://app.example.com/dashboard    # 302 to login, or 401
curl -q -sS -i https://app.example.com/sidekiq
# if you run Sidekiq Web, read the headers, not just the code: Basic Auth answers 401 with a
# WWW-Authenticate: Basic header; the Devise constraint answers 302 with a Location pointing at your
# login path (a bare 404 is inconclusive, it also means nothing is mounted there). A 200 that returns
# the Sidekiq dashboard is the exposure. Then confirm an authorized request does reach it
git ls-files config/master.key                                   # prints nothing
```

# Host baseline: SSH, firewall, updates

A host baseline is the hardening of a server: who can log in, which ports are open, and how it is patched. This guide helps your AI assistant apply it, including key-only SSH without root login, a default-deny inbound firewall, bans after repeated failed logins, and automatic security updates.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/host.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against OpenSSH documentation (no recorded version), OpenSSH 8.2 server manual V_8_2_P1, OpenSSH 8.1 server manual V_8_1_P1, OpenSSH 9.9 source V_9_9_P2, DNF 4.14.0, cloud-init 26.2 and 20.1, iproute2 ss manual v6.12.0, and BusyBox 1_36_1; 9 further sources are pinned to a commit and 9 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-18; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 22 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

Every guide in this repository secures a service; this one secures the machine under them. Apply it once per host before exposing anything.

## 1. SSH: keys only, no root login

Add your public key to a **non-root** admin account's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, and from a fresh connection confirm that key login to that account works and that it can `sudo`, **before** disabling passwords or root login. Keep the current session open while testing changes, so a mistake is recoverable.

Put this in a drop-in that sorts first, `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf`, not only in the main `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`:

```
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

OpenSSH 9.9 documents that, unless noted otherwise, sshd uses the *first* value it reads for each keyword and processes `Include` wildcard matches in lexical order. The fetched Ubuntu focal OpenSSH 1:8.2p1-4 configuration and CentOS Stream 9 packaging place `Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` near the top, before main-file settings; OpenSSH 8.2 added `Include` to `sshd_config`. In cloud-init 26.2, `ssh_pwauth: true` sets `PasswordAuthentication yes` in `50-cloud-init.conf` when the main configuration includes that drop-in directory; cloud-init 20.1 instead updated the main file. Read before a later main-file line or a higher-numbered drop-in, that `yes` value wins and password login stays on. Name the hardening file `00-hardening.conf` so it is read first, and confirm with `sshd -T` (below) that the value took effect; as this guide's reasoning, an upgraded main file may lack the include or an earlier drop-in may already have set it. The fetched packaging does not establish current defaults for every Debian, Ubuntu and RHEL-family release, or how often cloud images contain this drop-in.

```bash
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh    # sshd on RHEL-family systems
sudo sshd -T | grep -iE 'passwordauthentication|permitrootlogin|kbdinteractiveauthentication'
                                             # the EFFECTIVE global values after every include; confirm
                                             # they match what you set, not a drop-in read earlier. If you
                                             # use Match blocks, also check a connection with
                                             # `sudo sshd -T -C user=admin,addr=203.0.113.10`, since Match can override these
```

Add a second factor for SSH per [mfa.md](mfa.md): TOTP via [google-authenticator-libpam](https://github.com/google/google-authenticator-libpam) or push approval via Duo's `pam_duo`.

Both run through PAM's keyboard-interactive path, which the block above turns off. When adding PAM MFA, change the block to:

```
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication yes
UsePAM yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive
PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
```

`AuthenticationMethods` with a comma-separated list requires every method in it, so a key alone is no longer enough. `PasswordAuthentication no` stays: the code prompt is keyboard-interactive, not password. Older sshd_config files spell `KbdInteractiveAuthentication` as `ChallengeResponseAuthentication`; set that one to `yes` where it is the one present.

## 2. Firewall: default deny inbound

```bash
# Debian/Ubuntu (ufw)
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw delete allow OpenSSH                # only if an earlier run of this guide added it: a new rule does not replace an old one
sudo ufw allow proto tcp from REPLACE_WITH_ADMIN_RANGE to any port 22
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable
```

SSH stays closed to the world here for the same reason rule 3 in [cloud-firewalls.md](cloud-firewalls.md) keeps it off the cloud firewall: `ufw allow OpenSSH` opens port 22 to every address on the internet. Restrict it to the range you administer from. AWS SSM Session Manager SSH uses the SSM Agent's outbound TLS connection to Session Manager endpoints and needs no inbound port on the managed node; allow outbound HTTPS 443 to the documented endpoints. A tailnet ordinarily needs no inbound internet firewall port for Tailscale, and Tailscale SSH accepts traffic from the tailnet on port 22 ([tailscale.md](tailscale.md)). GCP IAP TCP forwarding requires a cloud ingress allow from `35.235.240.0/20` (`2600:2d00:1:7::/64` for IPv6 VMs) to SSH's default port 22 or its configured port; where an NSG is applied to the target VM subnet, Azure Bastion requires an inbound SSH rule on default port 22 or a custom port with Standard or Premium SKU. Microsoft's best practice scopes that rule's source to the `AzureBastionSubnet` IP address range. As this guide's advice, check the effective host firewall rules for the broker paths; the fetched IAP, Bastion and Tailscale pages do not specify which UFW or firewalld rules, if any, are needed. See [cloud-firewalls.md](cloud-firewalls.md).

RHEL-family systems use firewalld (`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https` and so on) with the same posture, and that includes SSH: `--add-service=ssh` opens port 22 to every address exactly as `ufw allow OpenSSH` does. Open only the ports the TLS-terminating layer needs; databases and app servers stay unreachable from outside per their guides. With Docker Engine's default Linux bridge firewall rules, published container traffic is diverted before ufw's rules; see [docker.md](docker.md) before relying on the firewall. As this guide's assessment, other modes and paths, including the userland proxy, need separate review in that guide.

```bash
# firewalld, where an earlier run enabled the ssh service: a rich rule does not supersede it.
# Every command below names the zone: without --zone they act on the default zone, which is not
# necessarily the one holding the internet-facing interface.
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones            # find the zone your public interface is in
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=REPLACE_WITH_PUBLIC_ZONE --remove-service=ssh
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=REPLACE_WITH_PUBLIC_ZONE --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="REPLACE_WITH_ADMIN_RANGE" service name="ssh" accept'   # confirm your current address is inside REPLACE_WITH_ADMIN_RANGE first
sudo firewall-cmd --reload                      # --permanent writes the stored config only; nothing changes until this
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=REPLACE_WITH_PUBLIC_ZONE --list-all   # confirm nothing reaches 22 from an unauthorized source: no `ssh` (or other 22/tcp) service, no `22/tcp` or a port range covering 22, no protocol-wide or broad-source rule, the zone target is not ACCEPT, only the admin rich rule matches; check other applicable zones too
```

## 3. Brute-force protection and updates

- fail2ban ([github.com/fail2ban/fail2ban](https://github.com/fail2ban/fail2ban)) or CrowdSec ([crowdsec.net](https://www.crowdsec.net/)) bans repeated authentication failures against SSH and login panels.
- Automate security patches: `unattended-upgrades` on Debian/Ubuntu, `dnf-automatic` on RHEL-family systems. Configure them to install updates: on Ubuntu noble, the unattended-upgrades post-install script writes `20auto-upgrades` when `enable_auto_updates` is true, and `apt-daily-upgrade.timer` runs `apt.systemd.daily install`, which invokes `unattended-upgrade` when its periodic interval permits. Its Ubuntu allowed origins include the release and security pockets; inspect local origins and periodic settings. On CentOS Stream 9, `dnf-automatic` is a packaged subpackage. Upstream DNF 4.14.0 ships the cited `automatic.conf` defaults (`apply_updates = no` and `upgrade_type = default`) and timers; with that configuration the generic timer does not install updates. CentOS Stream 9 applies downstream dnf-automatic patches this guide has not reviewed, so its packaged defaults remain unestablished. Enable `dnf-automatic-install.timer` to install updates, and set `upgrade_type = security` when only advisory-backed security upgrades are intended. Package defaults on other Debian and RHEL-family releases remain unestablished.

## 4. Verify

REASONED: listener, firewall, SSH key-only and PAM MFA checks; no exposed/fixed run is recorded in this guide. Expectations follow the cited SSH, firewall, MFA, iproute2, netcat and BusyBox sources; the authoring environment has no authorized target host or external probe machine.

```bash
sudo ss -4 -tulnp                 # IPv4 TCP and UDP listeners: only intended ones, on intended addresses
sudo ss -6 -tulnp                 # IPv6 TCP and UDP listeners: only intended ones, on intended addresses
sudo ufw status verbose           # default deny incoming; then `sudo ufw show raw` (status verbose omits rules loaded from /etc/ufw): every allowance that can reach 22 (a port-22 rule OR a broader "from <range> to any" allow) is scoped to your admin range, never Anywhere
(                                 # a subshell, so your own script arguments are untouched
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_PUBLIC_IP'   # replace inside the quotes, keeping them
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit; }
  case "$1" in
    *REPLACE_WITH_*|*YOUR_PUBLIC_IP*|"") echo "substitute your own address on the set -- line above; not probing" ;;
    *) nc -vz -w 3 "$1" 22 ;;   # from an address outside the admin range: must fail to connect
    # as this guide's assessment, a refusal or timeout only means THIS connection failed, not that the host firewall denied it (a host with
    # no sshd listening refuses too): confirm SSH works from an allowed source and read `ufw status`/`--list-all`
    # for the effective rule. A local error, an unsupported option (BusyBox small nc lacks -v; its 1.10-compatible applet lists it), or exit 1 with no
    # output at all is inconclusive as this guide's assessment; it does not establish a remote firewall result
  esac
)
# guard-conventions: allow probe of an illustrative user@host; no reader-substituted placeholder in this probe's argv
ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no user@host   # keys-only: require immediate failure with NO password prompt AND a Permission denied (...) method list naming neither password nor keyboard-interactive. As this guide's reasoning, the client prints the server's remaining methods in that list; "Permission denied (publickey)" is expected when only publickey remains; a password prompt or a method list naming either method means that path is still on
# guard-conventions: allow probe of an illustrative user@host; no reader-substituted placeholder in this probe's argv
ssh user@host                     # with PAM MFA: the key is accepted, then a code is required before a shell. Also confirm a wrong or omitted code is REJECTED, that unenrolled users are denied (drop `nullok`), and that Duo fails closed (`failmode=secure`), per mfa.md; otherwise the factor is optional, not mandatory
```

REASONED: preceding block; listener and firewall inventory, disallowed-source SSH reachability, key-only login and PAM MFA comparisons follow the cited SSH, firewall, MFA, iproute2, netcat and BusyBox sources; no authorized target host or external probe machine is available, and no exposed/fixed result is recorded. Run the SSH test from a second terminal before closing your working session. The `nc -vz -w 3` form is sourced for Ubuntu noble netcat-openbsd; CentOS Stream 9 packages Ncat 7.92 as an `nc` alternative, but the fetched Ncat source is a later master commit, so this guide has not established the packaged version's option behaviour. Check the installed `nc` variant before treating this probe as evidence.

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- safe-transition (REASONED; ssh): Confirm non-root key login and sudo in a fresh session before disabling password/root access; retain the working session while testing.
- keys-only (REASONED; ssh): Disable PasswordAuthentication and KbdInteractiveAuthentication; enable PubkeyAuthentication and prohibit root login.
- include-order (REASONED; ssh, openssh81, openssh82, openssh99, ubuntu-focal, rhel-c9s, cloudinit26, cloudinit20): OpenSSH 8.2 added server Include; OpenSSH 9.9 documents that, unless noted otherwise, each keyword uses its first obtained value, and documents lexical wildcard order supporting 00-hardening.conf. The fetched Ubuntu focal OpenSSH 1:8.2p1-4 configuration and CentOS Stream 9 packaging place the drop-in Include near the top, before main-file settings. With ssh_pwauth: true, cloud-init 26.2 writes PasswordAuthentication yes to 50-cloud-init.conf when the main configuration includes that directory; cloud-init 20.1 instead updated the main file. Current distribution defaults and cloud-image prevalence remain unestablished.
- effective-config (REASONED; ssh): Validate with sshd -t before reload; inspect sshd -T global values and -T -C for Match-specific settings. Service names differ by distribution.
- totp (REASONED; ssh, totp): SSH TOTP uses google-authenticator-libpam through PAM keyboard-interactive; keys-only configuration must change before adding this factor.
- duo (REASONED; ssh, duo): Duo pam_duo provides the alternative push factor through PAM keyboard-interactive.
- mfa-methods (REASONED; ssh, duo): UsePAM yes and AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive require both methods; keep password/root login disabled and public keys enabled.
- legacy-name (REASONED; ssh, duo): Older configurations use ChallengeResponseAuthentication for KbdInteractiveAuthentication; enable the spelling present when configuring PAM MFA.
- ufw-default (REASONED; ufw): Set deny incoming and allow outgoing, then enable UFW; permit TCP 80 and 443 for the TLS layer.
- ufw-ssh (REASONED; ufw): Remove any broad OpenSSH allow before adding an admin-source TCP 22 rule; adding a narrower rule does not replace the old allowance.
- brokered-ssh (REASONED; ufw, aws-ssm, gcp-iap, azure-docs, tailscale-docs): SSM SSH uses the agent's outbound TLS connection and needs no inbound port on the managed node; allow outbound HTTPS 443 to the documented Systems Manager endpoints. A tailnet ordinarily needs no inbound internet firewall port, and Tailscale SSH accepts tailnet traffic on port 22. IAP requires cloud ingress from 35.235.240.0/20, or 2600:2d00:1:7::/64 for IPv6 VMs, to SSH's default port 22 or its configured port; where an NSG is applied to the target VM subnet, Bastion requires an inbound SSH rule on default port 22 or a custom port with Standard or Premium SKU. Microsoft's best practice scopes that rule's source to the AzureBastionSubnet IP range. As this guide's advice, check the host firewall for these broker paths; the fetched IAP, Bastion and Tailscale pages do not specify which UFW or firewalld rules, if any, are needed.
- firewalld-zone (REASONED; firewalld): Find the public interface zone explicitly; remove its broad ssh service, add the IPv4 admin rich rule permanently, then reload to activate it.
- firewalld-audit (REASONED; firewalld): Inspect applicable zones for other services, port ranges, protocol/source allowances or ACCEPT targets that reopen 22; the narrow rich rule does not supersede them.
- docker-bypass (REASONED; ufw, docker): With Docker Engine default Linux bridge firewall rules, published container traffic is diverted before UFW settings; consult docker.md before relying on the host firewall. As this guide's assessment, other modes and paths, including the userland proxy, need separate review in that guide.
- fail2ban (REASONED; fail2ban): Use fail2ban to ban repeated authentication failures against SSH/login services.
- crowdsec (REASONED; crowdsec): CrowdSec is the alternative protection for repeated authentication failures.
- updates (REASONED; ssh, ubuntu-uu, ubuntu-apt, c9s-dnf, dnf4): Automate security patches with unattended-upgrades on Debian/Ubuntu or dnf-automatic on RHEL-family systems, configured to install them. Ubuntu noble's postinst conditionally writes 20auto-upgrades, and apt-daily-upgrade invokes unattended-upgrade when its periodic interval permits; its allowed origins include the release and security pockets. CentOS Stream 9 packages dnf-automatic. Upstream DNF 4.14.0 ships the cited automatic.conf defaults apply_updates=no and upgrade_type=default and the cited timers; enable dnf-automatic-install.timer and select upgrade_type=security for security-only installation. CentOS Stream 9 applies downstream dnf-automatic patches this guide has not reviewed, so its packaged defaults remain unestablished. Other Debian and RHEL-family package defaults remain unestablished.
- verify-listeners (REASONED; ufw, iproute2, ubuntu-nc, c9s-nmap, busybox, openssh99): Inventory intended TCP/UDP listeners and addresses in both IP families with explicit ss -4 and -6 runs. Ubuntu noble netcat-openbsd supports -v, -z and -w; CentOS Stream 9 packages Ncat as an nc alternative, but behaviour of packaged 7.92 remains unestablished. BusyBox 1.36.1 small nc lacks -v while its 1.10-compatible applet lists -v. As this guide's assessment, refusal or timeout proves only that this connection failed; local errors, unsupported options and exit 1 without output are inconclusive. The OpenSSH 9.9 client options select password and disable public key; the literal Permission denied (publickey) is this guide's reasoned expectation dependent on server-advertised methods, while immediate failure with NO password prompt and a Permission denied (...) method list naming neither password nor keyboard-interactive are required. As this guide's reasoning, the client prints the server's remaining methods in that list.
- verify-firewall (REASONED; ufw): UFW status should show default-deny ingress and admin-scoped SSH allowances; also inspect show raw because status omits /etc/ufw rules.
- verify-external (REASONED; ufw, firewalld): Disallowed-source TCP 22 must fail while allowed SSH works; correlate effective rules. As this guide's assessment, refusal alone, local errors and unsupported netcat options are inconclusive.
- verify-password (REASONED; ssh, openssh99): A password-only SSH attempt must fail immediately without a password prompt and show a Permission denied (...) method list naming neither password nor keyboard-interactive. As this guide's reasoning, the client prints the server's remaining methods in that list; a prompt or a list naming either method means that path is still on.
- verify-mfa (REASONED; ssh, totp, duo): After key acceptance require a code, reject wrong/omitted codes and unenrolled users without nullok, and use Duo failmode=secure; test before closing the working session.

# Cloud firewalls: security groups and network rules

Cloud firewalls are the network rules AWS, Google Cloud and Azure apply before traffic reaches your servers. This guide helps your AI assistant configure them securely, including only 80 and 443 public, databases reachable from private sources only, SSH limited to your addresses or brokered access, and default deny.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/cloud-firewalls.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against AWS security groups and CLI (no recorded version); 2 further sources are pinned to a commit and 3 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-18; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 14 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

On AWS (security groups), Google Cloud (VPC firewall rules), and Azure (network security groups), the recurring hole is one rule wide open to the world: `0.0.0.0/0` (or `::/0`) on a database, admin, or SSH port, added once to unblock a remote connection and never removed.

## Rules

1. **Public means 80/443 on the TLS layer, nothing else.** Only the load balancer, reverse proxy, or tunnel endpoint accepts traffic from `0.0.0.0/0`, and only on 80 (redirect) and 443.
2. **Databases and internal services accept traffic from private sources only**: the application's security group, subnet, or VPC, never the internet. The per-database guides' TLS and auth still apply on top; the firewall is a layer, not the control.
3. **SSH is not public.** Restrict port 22 to your addresses, or remove the public rule and use brokered access. AWS SSM Session Manager SSH uses the SSM Agent's outbound TLS connection to Session Manager endpoints and needs no inbound port on the managed node; allow outbound HTTPS 443 to the documented endpoints. GCP IAP TCP forwarding requires a cloud ingress allow from `35.235.240.0/20` (`2600:2d00:1:7::/64` for IPv6 VMs) to SSH's default port 22 or its configured port; where an NSG is applied to the target VM subnet, Azure Bastion requires an inbound SSH rule on default port 22 or a custom port with Standard or Premium SKU. Microsoft's best practice scopes that rule's source to the `AzureBastionSubnet` IP address range. Or use a tailnet ([tailscale.md](tailscale.md)): Tailscale ordinarily needs no inbound internet firewall port, and Tailscale SSH accepts traffic from the tailnet on port 22. As this guide's reasoning, these broker paths avoid a public SSH rule. As this guide's advice, check the host firewall separately; the fetched IAP, Bastion and Tailscale pages do not specify which UFW or firewalld rules, if any, are needed. Then harden the host per [host.md](host.md).
4. **Default deny, explicit allow.** Start from no inbound rules and add the minimum; review rules whenever a service is retired. Reference security-group IDs rather than IP ranges where the provider supports it, so app-to-database access survives IP changes without widening.
5. **Both layers matter on VMs running Docker**: as this guide's advice, use both the cloud firewall and the host's rules, remembering that Docker documents published container traffic bypassing host UFW settings ([docker.md](docker.md)).

## Verify

REASONED: rule-enumeration scope and the one allowed public pattern, per the cited AWS security group rules, Google Cloud VPC firewall rules, Google firewall policy, evaluation-order and gcloud references, Azure network security group rule properties, the fetched Session Manager, IAP, Bastion and Tailscale pages, and the Azure security-admin rule and applied-rules pages; no authorized AWS, Google Cloud or Azure account is available in the authoring environment, so no rule inventory was read here, while the fenced commands below passed bash -n and ShellCheck 0.11.0 at marking time with no diagnostics. Enumerate every inbound rule, then, for each one whose source reaches the internet, confirm that the destination port is 80 or 443 on the front layer, nothing else. Rule 3's administrative SSH access is the one other source that may reach 22, and it is a named address or a documented broker source (an IAP `35.235.240.0/20` rule, its IPv6 range for IPv6 VMs, or an Azure Bastion inbound SSH rule on the target VM subnet where an NSG is applied, is expected; Microsoft recommends scoping the Bastion source to `AzureBastionSubnet`), never `0.0.0.0/0`. These commands list rather than select, because no filter catches the exposure class.

REASONED: cloud-rule inventory and external reachability checks; no exposed/fixed run is recorded in this guide. Expectations follow the cited provider rule documentation, Google firewall policy and evaluation-order references, and the Azure security-admin rule and applied-rules pages; the authoring environment has no authorized cloud accounts or allowed/disallowed probe hosts.

```bash
# AWS, once per region. Every rule, not a selection: no filter catches the exposure class, because
# 0.0.0.0/1 together with 128.0.0.0/1 admits every IPv4 address while matching neither literal, and
# a source can be a prefix list or another security group instead of a CIDR.
aws ec2 describe-security-group-rules \
  --query "SecurityGroupRules[].{Group:GroupId,Egress:IsEgress,Proto:IpProtocol,From:FromPort,To:ToPort,V4:CidrIpv4,V6:CidrIpv6,Prefix:PrefixListId,SG:ReferencedGroupInfo.GroupId}" \
  --output table
# read every row whose Egress column reads False. Its source must be a private CIDR, a security
# group, a prefix list you have resolved and trust, or, where the destination port is 80 or 443,
# the internet. A public source on any other port is a finding, except the single administrative
# address rule 3 allows on 22. Rows reading True
# are outbound, a separate question.

# Google Cloud, once per project. Whole records, because a table projection drops the enforcement
# state: an enforced world-open rule and the same rule with "disabled": true project identically.
gcloud compute firewall-rules list --format=json
# for each entry with "direction": "INGRESS", "disabled": false and an "allowed" list, work out what
# its "sourceRanges" actually reach, by the same reasoning as the AWS command above: 0.0.0.0/0 and
# ::/0 are the obvious cases, and so is any set of ranges that together cover the internet. An entry
# with "denied" restricts rather than exposes.
# firewall-rules list displays Compute Engine firewall rules in this project; also enumerate the policy resources:
gcloud compute firewall-policies list --organization=REPLACE_WITH_ORG_ID   # repeat with --folder=REPLACE_WITH_FOLDER_ID for each relevant folder
gcloud compute network-firewall-policies list                              # no scope flag lists global and regional policies in this project
# inspect each hierarchical policy with `gcloud compute firewall-policies describe POLICY_ID --format=json`.
# inspect each global network policy with `gcloud compute network-firewall-policies describe POLICY_NAME --global --format=json`;
# for each regional policy, use `gcloud compute network-firewall-policies describe POLICY_NAME --region=REGION --format=json`.
# Hierarchical policy rules can override or delegate to global network and VPC rules. Read the effective order and matching
# rule: as this guide's reasoning, a policy allow with an internet source can expose the port even when the VPC list
# above is clean, unless an earlier rule denies it. Google documents the VPC network's networkFirewallPolicyEnforcementOrder:
# AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL (default) evaluates hierarchical and regional system policies, VPC rules, then global and
# regional network policies; BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL puts global and regional network policies after hierarchical and
# regional system policies but before VPC rules.
# A matching allow or deny stops evaluation; goto_next continues it. See
# https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order#determine-rule-evaluation
# and https://docs.cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order#default-rule-evaluation

# Azure, once per network security group. JSON, not a table: the table formatter omits array-valued
# columns, so a rule carrying sourceAddressPrefixes rather than sourceAddressPrefix would print an
# empty cell in the exposed state and the safe state alike. --include-default because the platform's
# own rules are inbound rules too, and this step claims to enumerate every one.
az network nsg rule list \
  --resource-group REPLACE_WITH_RESOURCE_GROUP --nsg-name REPLACE_WITH_NSG_NAME \
  --include-default --output json
# for each rule with "direction": "Inbound" and "access": "Allow", work out what its
# "sourceAddressPrefix" and "sourceAddressPrefixes" actually reach: "*", "Internet", "0.0.0.0/0" and
# "::/0" are the obvious cases, and so is any set of ranges that together cover the internet.
# NSG rules are not the whole story: Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules run before NSG rules.
# Allow continues to NSG evaluation; Always Allow bypasses it; Deny stops traffic. For a target VM
# whose virtual network has a Virtual Network Manager configuration applied, use the Azure portal:
# Networking > network interface > Support + troubleshooting > Effective security rules, then select
# the Azure Virtual Network Manager to inspect its applied security admin rules.
# As this guide's advice, when none is applied, the NSG review above alone covers that VM.
# As this guide's reasoning, this check passes when no applied Always Allow from an unauthorized or
# internet source reaches a restricted port, including SSH's default port 22 or its configured port.
# Any such rule is a finding even if the NSG list above looks safe; inspect its source, destination,
# action and port.
# The fetched pages give a portal path for applied rules; this guide has no sourced CLI command to list them.
```

- REASONED: disallowed-source port probes and their failure interpretation, per the guide's cited AWS security group rules and Azure network security group rule properties. No authorized cloud endpoints or allowed/disallowed probe hosts are available. bash -n and ShellCheck 0.11.0 exited 0 without diagnostics; original, missing-assignment, short, empty and embedded-placeholder cases printed refusal messages without reaching nc, while a substituted address reached five nc stubs. Live exposed connections and fixed refusals/timeouts remain unobserved; local errors are inconclusive. From an address outside the range you administer from:

  REASONED: cloud-rule inventory and external reachability checks; no exposed/fixed run is recorded in this guide. Expectations follow the cited provider rule documentation and Google firewall policy and evaluation-order references; the authoring environment has no authorized cloud accounts or allowed/disallowed probe hosts.

  ```bash
  (                                       # a subshell, so your own script arguments are untouched
    set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_PUBLIC_IP'   # replace inside the quotes, keeping them
    [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit; }
    shift
    [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit; }
    case "$1" in
      *REPLACE_WITH_*|*YOUR_PUBLIC_IP*|"") echo "substitute your own address on the set -- line above; not probing" ;;
      *) for p in 22 3306 5432 6379 27017; do nc -vz -w 3 "$1" "$p"; done ;;
    esac
  )
  ```

  Each port must report a refused or timed-out connection; a usage error from `nc` (some netcat variants take one port or a range per invocation) is not a passing result, and neither is exit 1 with no output at all, which is what a denied local socket looks like: in both cases nothing reached the network, so the check is inconclusive rather than passed.
- REASONED: complete address/port coverage and allowed/disallowed controls, per the guide's cited AWS security group rules, Google Cloud VPC firewall rules and Azure network security group rule properties. No authorized cloud endpoints or separate source networks are available. The related shell blocks passed bash -n and ShellCheck 0.11.0 without diagnostics; rejected placeholder cases reached no nc stub and a substituted address reached five. No real scan ran. Exposed services answer disallowed sources; fixed services answer only allowed sources, corroborated by effective rules, with unused or failed services remaining inconclusive. The `nc` list above is a non-exhaustive spot-check (it omits RDP 3389 and application ports such as 8080 or 9200), and a refused or timed-out port only means nothing answered from here, not that the cloud firewall denies it (an allowed port with no listener refuses too). The strongest reachability test is a full-range external scan of every public IPv4 and IPv6 address (for example with nmap, against your own infrastructure only) from a disallowed source: distinguish open, closed, and filtered, since a closed or refused port is not proof the firewall denies it (a port with no listener also reads closed). For each restricted service, confirm it is reachable from its allowed source and unreachable from a disallowed one, and correlate that with the effective firewall rules before crediting the block to the cloud firewall.

## Sources (checked September 2026)

- AWS Session Manager SSH tunnel (rolling) (checked October 2026): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager-getting-started-enable-ssh-connections.html#session-manager-getting-started-enable-ssh-connections

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- public-front (REASONED; aws, gcp, azure): Allow internet sources only to the front TLS layer on 80 for redirects and 443; private sources alone reach databases/internal services, with TLS/authentication still required.
- ssh (REASONED; aws, gcp, azure): Restrict 22 to named administrative addresses or documented broker sources, never unrestricted internet ranges.
- ssm (REASONED; aws): SSM SSH uses the agent's outbound TLS connection and needs no inbound port on the managed node; allow outbound HTTPS 443 to the documented Systems Manager endpoints.
- iap (REASONED; gcp): IAP requires cloud ingress from 35.235.240.0/20, or 2600:2d00:1:7::/64 for IPv6 VMs, to SSH's default port 22 or its configured port.
- bastion (REASONED; azure, azure-docs, tailscale-docs, gcp): Where an NSG is applied to the target VM subnet, Bastion requires an inbound SSH rule on default port 22 or a custom port with Standard or Premium SKU. Microsoft's best practice scopes that rule's source to the AzureBastionSubnet IP range. A tailnet ordinarily needs no inbound internet firewall port, and Tailscale SSH accepts tailnet traffic on port 22. As this guide's advice, check the host firewall for these broker paths; the fetched IAP, Bastion and Tailscale pages do not specify which UFW or firewalld rules, if any, are needed.
- least-access (REASONED; aws, gcp, azure): Start default-deny, add minimum allowances and retire obsolete rules; use security-group references where supported to survive app IP changes.
- docker (REASONED; docker-docs): On VMs running Docker, use both cloud and host firewall layers as this guide's advice; Docker documents that published container traffic bypasses UFW settings, as the linked Docker guide explains.
- verify-aws (REASONED; aws): Per region inspect all inbound rules, protocol/port ranges, IPv4/IPv6 CIDRs, resolved prefix lists and group references; combinations of narrower ranges can still expose the internet.
- verify-gcp (REASONED; gcp): Per project read JSON classic VPC rules, including direction, disabled state, allowed/denied and source ranges; a table can hide whether enforcement is disabled.
- gcp-policies (REASONED; gcp): Also list/describe hierarchical and global/regional network policies and read their effective order. Hierarchical policy rules can override or delegate to global network and VPC rules. The VPC network's networkFirewallPolicyEnforcementOrder defaults to AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL: hierarchical and regional system policies, VPC rules, then global and regional network policies; BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL puts global and regional network policies after hierarchical and regional system policies but before VPC rules. A matching allow or deny stops evaluation; goto_next continues it. As this guide's reasoning, a policy allow with an internet source can expose a port even when the VPC list is clean, unless an earlier rule denies it.
- verify-azure (REASONED; azure): Per NSG include default rules and read JSON direction/access plus singular/plural source prefixes; tables omit arrays and can conceal exposure.
- azure-admin (REASONED; azure, azure-docs): Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules run before NSG rules: Allow continues to NSG evaluation, Always Allow bypasses NSG evaluation, and Deny stops traffic. For a target VM whose virtual network has a Virtual Network Manager configuration applied, review its applied rules in the Azure portal; as this guide's advice, when none is applied, the NSG review alone covers that VM. As this guide's reasoning, this check passes when no applied Always Allow from an unauthorized or internet source reaches a restricted port, including SSH's default port 22 or its configured port; any such rule fails even if the NSG list looks safe. This guide has no sourced CLI command to list applied rules.
- verify-ports (REASONED; aws, gcp, azure): Outside the admin range, spot-check 22, 3306, 5432, 6379 and 27017; refusal/timeout is expected, while netcat usage errors or silent local failure are inconclusive.
- verify-complete (REASONED; aws, gcp, azure): The spot-check omits RDP 3389 and apps such as 8080/9200; scan all public IPv4/IPv6 ports, distinguish open/closed/filtered, and correlate allowed/disallowed controls with effective rules.

# PaaS platforms: what the platform does, what stays yours

Render, Fly.io, Railway, Vercel, Heroku and Hugging Face Spaces host your app and handle parts of running it, such as HTTPS. This guide helps your AI assistant deploy securely, including what each platform's TLS covers, authentication that stays yours, and backend secrets kept server-side, never in a Static Space.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/paas.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against Render documentation (no recorded version), Next.js pinned documentation v16.4.2, Next.js environment variables 15, Express request protocol 5.x, Django proxy security setting 6.1, and MySQL client connection options 8.4; 3 further sources are pinned to a commit and 4 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-22; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 24 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

TLS responsibilities depend on the platform and deployment mode:

- Render: the load balancer terminates HTTPS for web services and forwards HTTP to the app. Render automatically issues and renews certificates for added custom domains, including wildcards. Add the domain, configure DNS, and verify it in the dashboard. Wildcards require the root domain to point to Render and the prescribed wildcard, `_acme-challenge`, and `_cf-custom-hostname` CNAME records; existing CAA records must allow Let's Encrypt and Google Trust Services, with `issuewild` records for wildcards. At the time of writing, included custom-domain quotas depend on the workspace plan and additional domains cost extra.
- Fly.io: Fly Proxy's `tls` handler terminates TLS and forwards plaintext; without handlers, TCP passes through and the app can terminate TLS itself. Add the custom domain and configure DNS for automatic certificate issuance. Issuance and renewal require domain verification through an AAAA record pointing to the app, an `_acme-challenge` CNAME, or a `_fly-ownership` TXT record; wildcard certificates require DNS-01 with the `_acme-challenge` CNAME. This guide's assessment: these passages describe managed certificates and renewal prerequisites but do not explicitly establish automatic renewal. Fly's current custom-domain page says Fly.io needs that verification "To issue or renew a certificate", automatically validates ownership and issues certificates once DNS is configured, and notes that renewals do not count against Let's Encrypt's Certificates per Registered Domain limit. This guide's assessment: that page also does not explicitly state automatic renewal, renewal timing or renewal-failure handling. Fly's pinned Cloudflare page, under custom certificate issues, says: "Unlike Let's Encrypt certificates, which renew automatically, custom certificates must be manually renewed and re-imported before they expire." This guide's reading: the pinned custom-domain page calls Fly-managed certificates Let's Encrypt certificates, so this documents their automatic renewal; it states no renewal timing or renewal-failure handling. Imported certificates require ownership verification and take priority over a coexisting Fly-managed fallback.
- Railway: correctly configured custom domains receive automatically issued Let's Encrypt certificates, renewed with 30 days of their 90-day validity remaining; external certificates are unsupported. Both the supplied CNAME and ownership TXT records are required; wildcards also require the `_acme-challenge` CNAME, unproxied on Cloudflare. Root domains require CNAME flattening or dynamic ALIAS records. At the time of writing, custom-domain limits are one on Trial, two per service on Hobby and twenty per service by default on Pro, with increases available on request; Freenom domains are unsupported. For Cloudflare-proxied domains, issuance can fail and Railway can instead serve its default `*.up.railway.app` certificate; the docs require Full mode and warn that Full (Strict) will not work as intended. Cloudflare proxying below first-level subdomains requires Advanced Certificate Manager or switching those records to DNS Only. Railway's edge proxy (tcp-proxy) terminates TLS; traffic is then forwarded over Railway's internal network to the deployment ([request flow](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/edge-networking.md#L40-L43)).
- Vercel: its CDN terminates TLS. Certificates for deployment URLs are generated and kept updated automatically. Custom-domain issuance requires successful validation after DNS propagation; non-wildcards use HTTP-01 reachable at Vercel, and wildcards require Vercel nameservers for DNS-01. Vercel automatically attempts renewal 14 to 30 days before expiry; correct DNS, proxy, and CAA configuration must still permit validation. At the time of writing, only Enterprise teams can configure custom SSL; uploaded certificates cannot be renewed automatically by Vercel. The `/.well-known` path is reserved and cannot be redirected or rewritten.
- Heroku: the HTTP routing page describes load-balancer SSL termination, with separate Private Spaces routers. At the time of writing, ACM is included free for all applications; enable it for automatic issuance and renewal one month before expiry, using the correct Heroku DNS target. Adding custom domains requires a verified Heroku account. Cedar Private Spaces require a running web dyno for validation and renewal, cannot use ACM with Trusted IPs blocking access, and cannot use ACM for wildcard domains. On wildcards, the page says "You must also upload your own wildcard certificate for Private Space apps." and points to add-ons "If you want to automatically renew a wildcard certificate on a Private Space app"; neither statement names a generation. Its limitations say "Cedar generation Private Space apps using ACM can’t have wildcard domains. For Generation Private Space apps can use ACM with wildcard domains." This guide's assessment: the three statements agree for Cedar Private Spaces; for the other generation, which the page calls "For Generation" and which probably means Fir, the last sentence conflicts with the two unqualified statements, so Fir wildcard eligibility remains unresolved. When checked in October 2026, the Generations page's Feature Parity table, with columns Fir and Cedar, marked "Heroku ACM wildcard domains" with an X in both. This guide's assessment: since that page says "Fir is now generally available with Fir Private Spaces", the Fir mark supports the ACM page's other-generation sentence, but it withdraws neither unqualified statement, so the conflict remains. The same page says "Both the Common Runtime and Private Spaces run on the Cedar generation of the platform." This guide's assessment: the page does not say whether its Cedar wildcard mark covers Cedar Private Spaces, so whether that mark conflicts with the ACM page's Cedar Private Spaces limitation, which this guide keeps, remains unresolved. Uploading a certificate disables ACM. CAA must permit Let's Encrypt, and DNS/CDN configuration must allow validation; ACM must be disabled if the app requires the platform-handled ACME challenge paths.

This guide's advice: where the platform terminates TLS and manages the required certificate, do not bolt certbot or an extra TLS reverse proxy onto the app, and do not apply this repository's server-TLS guides to that managed ingress. What stays yours:

## 1. Authentication: entirely yours

The platform does not authenticate your application's users. Some platforms protect the deployment itself: Vercel Deployment Protection, for example, can require a Vercel login to open preview and deployment URLs on every plan, and production domains too once the All Deployments scope is selected, which Vercel's changelog of 9 September 2026 made free on every plan including Hobby; Password Protection is not available on Hobby, is a paid add-on per protected project on Pro, and is included on Enterprise (at the time of writing). That gate keeps the public out of a preview; it is not your app's login. Every non-public endpoint still needs login or keys per [authentication.md](authentication.md), MFA where viable per [mfa.md](mfa.md), and a hosted provider makes both easy ([identity-providers.md](identity-providers.md)). "It is on Vercel" changes nothing about an open `/api/admin`.

## 2. Secrets: use the platform's store

Each platform provides environment/secret configuration. Set secrets there; never commit `.env` files ([secrets.md](secrets.md)). Rotate anything that ever appeared in the repository, build logs, or client bundles. Public frontend frameworks compile some env vars into the client (for example `NEXT_PUBLIC_`-prefixed values); only put genuinely public values in those.

## 3. Enforce HTTPS and correct proxy awareness

- Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. This guide's advice: use the documented automatic redirect, enable the documented platform setting, or implement the redirect in the app with verified proxy trust:
  - Render's TLS page says all HTTP requests are automatically redirected to HTTPS, and its custom-domains page says the same for custom-domain traffic; neither states the HTTP-to-HTTPS status code. Its static-site redirect rules document 301 for moving a request to a rule's destination. This guide's assessment: that is a separate feature and does not establish the HTTP-to-HTTPS status.
  - Fly.io's pinned configuration reference documents `force_https = true` under `[http_service]` in `fly.toml` for apps managed by Fly Launch. The pinned services page says enabling `force_https` returns 301 for all HTTP requests; the option is only valid on HTTP handlers, and deployment fails if it is set on other handlers.
  - Railway's pinned public-networking specifications describe automatic HTTPS redirects for plain HTTP GET requests with 301, and HTTP POST redirects that convert the request to GET ([GET status and POST conversion](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits.md#L37-L38)). This guide's assessment: these GET/POST statements establish no configurable redirect toggle, POST status code or HEAD response used below. Railway's pinned 405 troubleshooting page explains that a POST request can reach the application as a GET because, when the request is made using HTTP, "Railway will attempt to redirect your insecure request with a 301 Moved Permanently status code", and clients typically change POST to GET when they follow it ([POST redirect status](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/troubleshooting/405-method-not-allowed.md#L8-L18)). This guide's reading: that page documents 301 for an HTTP POST and attributes the change to GET to the client; it establishes no HEAD response or redirect toggle. The pinned specifications page instead says HTTP POST requests to port 80 "are redirected to HTTPS as GET requests" ([request handling](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits.md#L16-L17)) and that plain HTTP POST requests "will be converted to GET requests" ([POST conversion](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/public-networking/specs-and-limits.md#L37-L38)). This guide's assessment: unlike the 405 page, that page does not attribute the change to GET to the client, and this guide does not establish which description is right.
  - Vercel's encryption page says its CDN automatically redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS with 308 and that this redirection cannot be disabled.
  - Heroku's ACM page says that, when ACM is enabled, the platform handles `/.well-known/acme-challenge/*` URLs, redirected away from the app, and requires disabling ACM if the app needs those paths. This guide's assessment: that path handling and the cited HTTP routing page establish none of the following: a general HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect policy, a redirect toggle, an application-only redirect contract, or a status code. This guide's advice: implement application-side redirection unless the deployed ingress is known to enforce HTTPS, and verify the result.

  For application-side handling, this guide's advice is to check the platform's forwarded-protocol header only after verifying the framework's proxy trust requirements. Fly's HTTP handler documents `X-Forwarded-Proto` as the original client protocol, `http` or `https`; Railway's public-networking specifications say it always indicates `https`. Heroku's routing page describes it as the originating protocol but explicitly warns that forwarded headers, including `X-Forwarded-Proto`, are not trusted because the order of pre-existing fields is unknown. These descriptions do not establish header sanitization; the cited Render and Vercel TLS pages do not establish a forwarded-protocol header contract. Keep the Express 5.x `trust proxy` and Django 6.1 `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` trust requirements in view when implementing this guide's advice.
- Behind the platform proxy, configure the framework accordingly (`trust proxy` in Express per [nodejs.md](nodejs.md), `SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER` in Django per [python.md](python.md)) so secure cookies and redirects behave.
- Bind the listener required by the deployment model. Render web services must bind `0.0.0.0`; Render recommends `PORT` (default port 10000, configurable), can usually detect another bound port, and requires the public HTTP server to use `PORT` when multiple ports are bound. Fly Proxy HTTP services must be reachable over IPv4: use `0.0.0.0` and match the service's configured `internal_port` to the app listener; IPv4-mapped IPv6 wildcard behaviour depends on the VM and runtime. Railway domains route to a detected or selected internal target port; its troubleshooting page says web servers should bind `0.0.0.0` and listen on the automatically injected `PORT` ([listener and port](https://github.com/railwayapp/docs/blob/72354493198302677fb6be6c692dd75c64cae2c6/content/docs/networking/troubleshooting/application-failed-to-respond.md#L46-L51)). Heroku assigns web processes a `PORT` environment variable: its runtime-principles page says each web process binds to that port and listens for requests on it, and its Node.js deployment page says the web process command must bind to that port or the dyno does not start. For Fir, the Generations page says Private Spaces networking uses IPv6 by default, that IPv4-only assumptions do not bind properly, and recommends an IPv6 or dual-stack listener (typically `::`); the cited pages do not establish Cedar's listener address. Vercel runtimes transform code into Functions served by its CDN, including Node.js function entrypoints and Python ASGI/WSGI apps; that page establishes neither a universal injected port nor a required listener address. Vercel's Functions overview shows functions as exported `fetch` or HTTP-method handlers and says each incoming request is a new invocation with no servers to manage. This guide's assessment: that overview states no listener address or port either. When checked in October 2026, Vercel's Express page said the Express entry file "must also export the application as a default export of the module or use a port listener", showing the `app.listen` pattern with an example port of 3000, and its Python runtime page described the entrypoint as "the file and top-level variable that Vercel loads as the Vercel Function handler". This guide's assessment: neither page states a required listener address or a port Vercel uses, and the example port is not a requirement. This guide's advice: bind nothing else and do not open extra listeners.

## 4. Databases attached to PaaS apps

Managed databases from these platforms come with TLS endpoints, but check what the specific endpoint supports: require certificate and hostname verification with the client's own setting (`sslmode=verify-full` for PostgreSQL, `--ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY` for MySQL) per the database guides ([postgresql.md](postgresql.md), [mysql.md](mysql.md)) where the endpoint allows it, and note that some managed internal endpoints support encryption but not `verify-full` (Render's internal PostgreSQL connections, where TLS is optional, do not support `verify-ca`/`verify-full`); there, set `sslmode=require` to force encryption and prevent a plaintext fallback, and do not treat that encryption-only connection as identity-verified. Keep the credentials in the platform's secret store, and restrict the network too: many managed databases are reachable from any IP by default (Render's Postgres is), so prefer private connectivity and disable or source-restrict external access with the provider's database network controls, not TLS alone. Databases you run yourself elsewhere follow their own guides plus [cloud-firewalls.md](cloud-firewalls.md).

## 5. Hugging Face Spaces

This guide's advice: explicitly select and verify visibility when you create a Space. The pinned docs describe public, protected, and private visibility; public visibility exposes both the source and the running app, and duplicating a Space defaults to private. At the time of writing, the pinned Advanced Security docs attach repository visibility controls to Team & Enterprise organizations: Public by default creates new repositories with public visibility; Private by default creates new repositories with private visibility, and changing that setting does not affect existing repositories; Private only enforces private visibility for all new repositories, with only organization admins able to change visibility settings. Those lines do not establish a general creation default or a retroactive conversion of existing repositories by Private only. Visibility can be changed to "protected" (the source stays private to the owner and collaborators, but the running app is still public through its embed URL or custom domain) or "private" (both the source and the running app are restricted to the owner and collaborators); protected visibility requires a paid plan, PRO for personal accounts or Team/Enterprise for organizations, at the time of writing. Space secrets belong in the Settings tab's secrets store, never in the repository or its README metadata; anything set as a "variable" instead of a "secret" is still publicly readable. That secrets store is not a safe place for backend or provider credentials on a Static Space: Hugging Face exposes both variables and secrets to client-side JavaScript there, through `window.huggingface.variables`, so anything placed in a Static Space's secrets still reaches the browser. Keep server-side credentials in a server-side service, such as a Docker or Gradio Space or a separate backend, instead.

At the time of writing, the pinned Dev Mode docs require PRO or Team & Enterprise. The Dev Mode Docker image starts the application as a subprocess and starts an SSH server for local editors and terminals and a VS Code server for in-product VS Code Web. Dev Mode exposes the running Space as a standard SSH host; clients use the Space subdomain shown in the Dev Mode controls as the username at ssh.hf.space, and local VS Code uses Remote - SSH to connect to the same host. SSH requires adding the machine's SSH public key to the user's Hugging Face account; these docs do not establish which users or roles may connect, or the access control for in-product VS Code Web. This guide's assessment: access into the running container is materially more access than the app itself, so treat an unattended Dev Mode session the same as any other exposed admin path. For serverless GPU platforms, see [gpu-clouds.md](gpu-clouds.md).

## 6. Verify

REASONED: HTTPS redirect, application-authentication and deployed-secret checks; no PaaS application, tenant credentials or deployed client bundle was supplied for this metadata review, and no run is recorded. The expected readings below follow the cited platform documentation and the guide's application-security reasoning; exact application behaviour remains deployment-specific.

```bash
# 1. This guide checks HTTP->HTTPS redirection. Spot-check on / only: it does not prove HTTPS on every route/method, nor that
#    the app's proxy-awareness (section 3) is set for secure cookies. --noproxy so a client proxy cannot answer.
#    Documented: Vercel 308; Fly HTTP handlers with force_https enabled 301. Render's HTTPS code is unstated; its static-rule 301 differs.
#    Railway documents GET 301 and a 301 for HTTP POST that clients typically follow as GET, not this HEAD response. This guide's assessment:
#    Heroku's ACM challenge-path handling establishes no general HTTPS redirect policy, setting, application-only responsibility or status.
#    This guide's check: require 301/302/307/308 with an https:// Location; HTTP content without that redirect fails.
curl -q -g -sI --noproxy '*' -w 'http=%{http_code}\n' http://app.example.com/          # this guide's redirect check above
# 2. Your APP's own auth must reject an unauthenticated request, NOT the platform deployment-protection gate.
#    Vercel documents that Deployment Protection requires authentication for all requests, and that a valid
#    Protection Bypass for Automation token lets the request access the deployment without authentication,
#    sent as the x-vercel-protection-bypass HTTP header or query parameter carrying the project's generated
#    secret. Disable deployment protection (or use that bypass) so only application auth is in play. That
#    bypass is Vercel's; no Render or Fly equivalent is cited here, so do not assume one exists. If you use
#    the bypass secret, send it as the header, supplied from a file with -H @file per this guide's
#    conventions so it stays out of shell history; the query-parameter form writes it into history and logs.
#    The status codes below are this guide's expected reading; the cited pages state none, including for the
#    platform gate's own challenge (its SSO 401 below):
curl -q -g -s --noproxy '*' -o /dev/null -w 'http=%{http_code}\n' https://app.example.com/REPLACE_WITH_PROTECTED_PATH   # no creds: want the APP's own 401/403, not a platform SSO 401
#    Then repeat with a valid application credential (your app's session cookie or API token, supplied from a file with
#    -b or -H @file so it stays out of shell history) and require a 2xx: that positive control proves the endpoint is
#    reachable and that the app's own auth, not the platform gate, is what gates it.
# 3. Secrets: run secrets.md's history and working-tree scans AND grep the DEPLOYED client bundle (JS, source maps,
#    generated config, runtime-injected values) for every credential type, not just private keys. No matches is evidence, not proof.
#    Why the deployed bundle: as the Next.js case, the pinned v16.4.2 docs say NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into
#    the JavaScript bundle delivered to the client at build time, and production browser source maps are disabled
#    unless productionBrowserSourceMaps opts in. What to grep and which credential types are this guide's procedure,
#    delegated to secrets.md, not taken from the cited pages.
```
