# n8n: binding, TLS, and MFA

n8n is a workflow automation tool with a web editor and webhook endpoints. This guide helps your AI assistant make sure it is configured securely: a private bind, TLS from a proxy or n8n itself, accounts with MFA, webhook authentication, and code-node execution isolated.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/n8n.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against n8n listener source n8n@2.40.6, n8n runtime source n8n@2.40.6, n8n environment policy minimum 2.18.0, n8n SSRF filter minimum 2.12.0, n8n 2.0 default exclusion source n8n@2.0.0, n8n 1.x default exclusion source n8n@1.123.85, and express-openapi-validator v5.5.3, plus 6 more recorded bases; 2 further sources are pinned to a commit and 2 carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-10-21; documentation checked October 2026. The guide records 60 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

n8n includes user management (complete the owner setup on first run), but its network defaults deserve attention: `N8N_LISTEN_ADDRESS` defaults to `::` and `N8N_PORT` to `5678` (both as of n8n 2.40.6), so n8n listens on **all interfaces** over plain HTTP.

## 1. Bind privately

Behind a reverse proxy or tunnel (the recommended layout):

```
N8N_LISTEN_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1
N8N_PORT=5678
N8N_HOST=n8n.example.com
```

`N8N_LISTEN_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1` is right for n8n running directly on the host behind a same-host proxy. INSIDE a bridged Docker container it binds the container's own loopback, so a sibling proxy container or a published port cannot reach it: there, either put n8n and the proxy on a private Compose network with NO published n8n port, or publish to host loopback only (`127.0.0.1:5678:5678`). Keep the Postgres and task-runner broker ports unpublished either way. Publish only the proxy per [caddy.md](caddy.md)/[nginx.md](nginx.md) with a certificate from [free-certificates.md](free-certificates.md), or use [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md)/[tailscale.md](tailscale.md).

Set the public URL fully, not just `N8N_HOST`: `N8N_PROTOCOL=https`, `N8N_WEBHOOK_URL=https://n8n.example.com/` (the external base for generated webhook URLs; it replaces the `WEBHOOK_URL` alias, deprecated from n8n 2.35.0 though the old name still works with a warning), and keep `N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=true` (its default). Behind a proxy also set the trusted proxy-hop count (`N8N_PROXY_HOPS`) so client IPs and rate limiting are read from the right forwarded header. Webhook endpoints are meant to be reachable by external services; that is no reason for the editor UI to be.

## 2. Or terminate TLS in n8n itself

```
N8N_PROTOCOL=https        # default is http
N8N_SSL_KEY=/path/to/privkey.pem
N8N_SSL_CERT=/path/to/fullchain.pem
```

## 3. Accounts and MFA

- Finish the owner-account setup before publication. At n8n 2.40.6, the owner setup handler skips authentication and issues the new owner a session cookie.
- Individual users can enable two-factor authentication on their accounts (verify availability for your version and licence).
- Instance-wide enforcement exists under **Settings > Security** ("Enforce two-factor authentication"), or via `N8N_MFA_ENFORCED_ENABLED=true` with `N8N_SECURITY_POLICY_MANAGED_BY_ENV=true` (the environment-managed policy is available from n8n 2.18.0, so confirm your version and that enforcement actually takes effect); per the n8n docs this enforcement requires a Business or Enterprise licence on self-hosted instances, and it does not apply to SSO logins (enforce MFA at the identity provider for those; [mfa.md](mfa.md)).
- Credentials stored in n8n (API keys for the services your workflows touch) make the instance a secrets vault; treat access to it accordingly ([secrets.md](secrets.md)). Those credentials are encrypted at rest with `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY`: leaving it unset does NOT mean plaintext (n8n generates a random key on first launch and saves it under `~/.n8n`), but losing that key while keeping the database makes every stored credential unrecoverable, and committing it hands the decryption secret to anyone who reads the repo. Set it explicitly, keep the same value across every worker/replica, back it up separately from the database, and keep it out of source control and images ([secrets.md](secrets.md)).

## 4. Webhook authentication

- A Webhook node left on **None** answers anyone who reaches its URL. For a webhook whose caller you control, set the node **Authentication** to **Basic auth**, **Header auth**, or **JWT auth** and attach the matching Webhook credential.
- Webhook authentication is configured per node and is separate from the instance login and the public API key (`X-N8N-API-KEY`). Hardening the editor or `/api/v1` does nothing for webhook endpoints, so audit every Webhook node individually.
- Where a third party must call the webhook and cannot present your credential, **None** is unavoidable at the node, so the workflow itself must authenticate the request: validate the provider's signature (for example an HMAC header) in the first node after the Webhook trigger and reject a missing or wrong signature before any further processing. A **None** webhook with no such check is open.

## 5. Code-node isolation and outbound requests

- Workflow editors can run code: the **Code** node executes JavaScript/Python and the **Execute Command** node runs the command through a shell in a child process of the n8n process executing the node. At n8n 2.40.6, `NODES_EXCLUDE` disables Execute Command by default; the commit-pinned n8n 2.0.0 and 2.43.8 defaults exclude Execute Command and Local File Trigger, while the commit-pinned n8n 1.123.85 default on the 1.x line is empty (excludes none). Commit a4757cf0 ("chore: Initial V2 changes", 2025-12-01) changed this default in `nodes.config.ts` from empty to those two node types; n8n 2.0.0-rc.0, the lowest-version 2.x tag, has that default, while n8n 1.123.0 keeps it empty, and the four later commits to `nodes.config.ts` through ea8417e2 do not change it. This guide's assessment of `nodes.config.ts` at each n8n tag, as of October 2026, is that the default stays empty at every 1.123.x tag and excludes both nodes at every 2.x tag from 2.0.0-rc.0 through 2.45.0, including the commit-pinned 2.45.0 file; releases after 2.45.0 are not covered and no release was run, so confirm the default on your installed version. The rolling 2.0 changes page, which is unversioned, also lists both nodes as disabled by default in n8n 2.0. Leave it off unless a workflow truly needs it. Run code on hardened EXTERNAL task runners rather than the internal mode, which the vendor calls insecure by design, and keep workflow `$env` access blocked (`N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=true`; at n8n 2.40.6 the `$env` proxy is blocked unless the variable is set to `false`). This guide's assessment is that this guard alone does not establish isolation of every node or Code `process.env`. Allow only the modules a workflow needs, narrowly, and set the allowlist where the RUNNER reads it, not just on the main n8n container (whose values the external launcher overrides): for the JavaScript runner, `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN` and `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL` under `env-overrides` in the launcher's `/etc/n8n-task-runners.json`; for the Python runner, `N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW` and `N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW`. At n8n 2.40.6 an unset allowlist allows no modules (both runners' allowlists default to empty), while `*` grants every module of its kind. Because these defaults have shifted across versions and one vendor table is stale, set each value explicitly and confirm it on your installed version.
- At n8n 2.40.6, the JS task runner builds a context with module resolution, console, workflow static data, selected native globals, the data proxy, RPC and additional properties. This guide reasons that no direct `process` binding appears in the explicit native list or context; imported modules and injected properties prevent treating that omission as complete `process.env` isolation.
- At n8n 2.40.6, the JS data proxy receives `envProviderState`; if absent, its fallback is `env: {}`, `isEnvAccessBlocked: false` and `isProcessAvailable: true`. This guide reasons that the fallback avoids using the runner environment for `$env`; the cited consumer does not establish the contents or production of incoming state.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, `createEnvProviderState` sets `env` to `{}` unless `process` exists and `N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE` is `false`, and otherwise to that process's `process.env`. The node context's `startJob` calls it and passes the result through `startRunnerTask` to `TaskRequester.startTask`, which stores it in the task data.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the requester answers a runner's data request with that state, replaced by `env: {}` unless the request's `env` flag is set, and the broker forwards the answer to the runner. The JS runner sets the flag when its parser finds `$env` in the code or cannot parse the code.
- This guide infers from the cited producer, requester and parser sources that, with `N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false`, a JS Code task using `$env` receives the whole environment of the n8n process running the node, including any secrets set there, even on an external runner; with the variable unset or set to anything else it receives `env: {}`. No run observed this.
- At n8n 2.40.6, JS all-items and per-item execution use `runInContext` in secure mode and `runDirectly` in insecure mode. This guide reasons that the latter, using `new Function` with `with(context)`, can resolve ambient `process.env` unless shadowed; this is not a live demonstration or proof of complete isolation in secure mode.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, JS Code's `require` is the runner's resolver, which loads a builtin or external module only if its exact name is in `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN` or `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL`, both empty by default, or the list is `*`. This guide infers that allowing `process`, `child_process` or `*` lets user code reach the runner process's own environment.
- At n8n 2.40.6, Python all-items and per-item execution clear `os.environ` before user code only if `runner_env_deny` is true; the runner sets it from `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS`, read with default `True`, so by default they clear it, and when false, they do not clear the task process environment. This guide did not establish effective module access.
- At n8n 2.40.6, Python `main.py` builds the runner configuration with `TaskRunnerConfig.from_env()`, which reads `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS` with `read_bool_env`; that returns its default when `read_env` returns `None`, otherwise true only when the trimmed, lower-cased value is `true`. This guide reasons that any other set value, such as `1`, disables clearing `os.environ` before user code.
- At n8n 2.40.6, Python `read_env` reads `os.environ` first, otherwise a file named by the corresponding `_FILE` variable, or returns `None`. This guide assesses that this configuration reader does not itself establish which environment values user code can access.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the Python runner reads `N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW` and `N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW` as comma lists that default to empty, so no module is allowed unless set, and `*` must stand alone; checks use the top-level module name. `N8N_RUNNERS_BUILTINS_DENY` defaults to a list including `eval`, `exec`, `open` and `getattr`.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the Python runner checks user code's imports against those allowlists before execution unless both are `*`; the executor limits `sys.modules` to allowed modules, a fixed safe set and their submodules, removes denied builtins and replaces `__import__` and `importlib`'s import entry points with allowlist-checking callables. Effective module access was not observed.
- Launcher 1.5.1 prepares the runner environment from its own `LANG`, `PATH`, `TZ` and `TERM` plus names in `allowed-env`; `env-overrides` sets values directly. This guide advises keeping secrets out of `allowed-env` and keeping that list narrow, because listed values can enter the runner process environment.
- Launcher 1.5.1 sets the task broker URI, health-check enable flag and port, and legacy auto-shutdown and task timeouts. It removes inherited required runtime keys, including the grant token, and ignores their `env-overrides`; other overrides replace prior values, while grant-token insertion is not shown by this preparation function.
- From source reading of launcher 1.5.1, the launch command builds the runner environment with `PrepareRunnerEnv`, fetches a grant token from the task broker, appends `N8N_RUNNERS_GRANT_TOKEN` to that environment and sets the result as the runner command's environment.
- From source reading of the launcher's release tags, `internal/env/env.go` is identical at every tag from 1.3.1 to 1.5.1, `config.go` keeps its `allowed-env` and `env-overrides` fields at each of them, and `launch.go` is identical at 1.5.0 and 1.5.1. Tags before 1.3.1, untagged commits and later releases are not covered.
- From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image Dockerfile defaults `LAUNCHER_VERSION` to 1.5.0, not the 1.5.1 this guide cites, installs that launcher release as the image entrypoint and copies `n8n-task-runners.json` to `/etc/n8n-task-runners.json`. This is image source; a published image's launcher and configuration are not established.
- From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image's `n8n-task-runners.json` lists `PATH` and timeout, concurrency, Sentry and version variables in both runners' `allowed-env`, plus `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `NODE_PATH` and `HOME` for JS and the launcher log level for Python. This is image source, not a published image or a deployed configuration.
- From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image's `n8n-task-runners.json` uses `env-overrides` to set `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN` to `crypto` and `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL` to `moment` for the JS runner and `N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW` and `N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW` to empty for the Python runner. This is image source, not a published image or a deployed configuration.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, `N8N_RUNNERS_MODE` defaults to `internal`, in which the task runner module starts a JS runner and, if the Python requirements check passes, a Python runner as child processes of n8n. Each spawn passes an explicit `env` object of named variables rather than n8n's whole `process.env`.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the internal JS runner's `env` copies `PATH`, `HOME`, `NODE_PATH`, `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, both `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_*` lists, four Sentry names, `N8N_RUNNERS_INSECURE_MODE` and two shutdown settings from n8n, and the Python runner's copies `PATH`, `HOME`, its module settings and `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS`; both add the grant token and runner settings.
- The n8n task runner set-up page, checked October 2026, documents that an internal-mode runner is a child process sharing n8n's uid and gid, that code escaping its sandbox has the same access as n8n, including to stored credentials, and that n8n logs a deprecation warning for internal mode, deprecated from n8n 3.0, including when `N8N_RUNNERS_MODE` isn't set.
- From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, Execute Command spawns its command with `cwd`, `shell: true` and `detached` options and no `env` option. This guide infers from Node.js `child_process` semantics, not cited here, that the shell inherits the environment of the n8n process running the node; no run observed this.
- This guide's `git grep -l` at n8n 2.40.6 for `startJob` or `child_process` under `packages/nodes-base/nodes` and `packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/nodes` matched, outside test files, only the Code node's JS and Python task-runner sandboxes and Execute Command. This bounds those spellings and paths only, not every node that runs code or starts processes.
- This guide's assessment is that the cited n8n 2.40.6 runner and launcher 1.5.1 sources describe specific environment controls, not complete host/container isolation. Internal-mode isolation beyond the spawn environment, nodes beyond the searched spellings and paths, other launcher versions, deployed configuration and complete Code `process.env` isolation remain unestablished.
- Outbound requests are a trust boundary too: a webhook or the **HTTP Request** node can be steered at internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint (SSRF). Enable n8n's own SSRF filter where available (`N8N_SSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED=true`, from n8n 2.12.0) AND restrict the workload's egress so a request cannot reach your internal network or `169.254.169.254` ([egress-metadata.md](egress-metadata.md)); the app-level filter supplements a network control and does not contain arbitrary code- or command-node networking.

## 6. Verify

REASONED: n8n 2.40.6's registry returns the first non-null strategy result, or `false` if all abstain; `ApiKeyAuth`, `BearerAuth` and `CookieAuth` return that result. Its pinned express-openapi-validator 5.5.3 calls `AuthValidator.validate()` before the handler ([lines 165-174](https://github.com/cdimascio/express-openapi-validator/blob/5c204614a5ccb04ddc64f68e8a282e8f661dfb47/src/middlewares/openapi.security.ts#L165-L174)); for a header `apiKey` scheme, a missing header throws an `Error` without a status ([lines 265-271](https://github.com/cdimascio/express-openapi-validator/blob/5c204614a5ccb04ddc64f68e8a282e8f661dfb47/src/middlewares/openapi.security.ts#L265-L271)). This guide's assessment: a false result or a thrown error without a status gets fallback status 401 ([lines 142-185](https://github.com/cdimascio/express-openapi-validator/blob/5c204614a5ccb04ddc64f68e8a282e8f661dfb47/src/middlewares/openapi.security.ts#L142-L185)); when security fails and that failure is selected, the validator forwards an `HttpError` with that status, while exceptions can supply other statuses. The source `openapi.yml` declares `ApiKeyAuth` as a header `apiKey` scheme named `X-N8N-API-KEY`, `BearerAuth` as a bearer JWT scheme and `CookieAuth` as an `apiKey` cookie named `n8n-auth`, each as a separate global security requirement ([lines 167-185](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/024ee46bdc6d57e5c47ef2c26bcac2b3a9efd827/packages/cli/src/public-api/v1/openapi.yml#L167-L185)). n8n serializes `HttpError` as a message object with its status (400 if falsy); `Unauthorized` with a session cookie gets 401 and message `Unauthorized`.

REASONED: source limits and guide advice for the API probes below; no live n8n deployment is available and no API outcome was observed. Compare no `X-N8N-API-KEY` with a valid key at that same URL, keeping proxy credentials constant and feeding the key on stdin; rejection (for example 401) and 200 workflow JSON remain expectations to observe, and a fronting proxy can alter the status.

```bash
# REASONED: listener, TLS, API and webhook comparisons have no recorded n8n run; no live n8n deployment is available in the authoring environment. Expected API status outcomes require a live check; the assessment above traces conditional public-API refusal and the workflows list route's middleware, response body and declared 200 success status; pinned source still establishes the Webhook refusal codes.
# On 2026-10-13 (UTC), against a stub curl, the placeholder was refused with the substitute message and a line feed, carriage return, tab or DEL with the control-character message, before any curl call; a valid dummy key let both curl calls run and reached only the with-key call, on its stdin.
# Owner setup must be COMPLETE before the instance is public: the pinned owner setup handler
# skips authentication and issues an owner session cookie. Confirm the owner exists; do NOT POST
# owner-creation data to a live instance as a "test".
ss -tlnp   # a listener inventory in THIS namespace, not a firewall/NAT check: n8n on 127.0.0.1 (or its
           # private container network), with the Postgres and task-runner ports NOT published. Loopback
           # can be 127.0.0.1 and/or ::1; also probe the real public IPv4/IPv6 path from another host.
# TLS reachability (proves TLS, not authentication):
# guard-conventions: allow probe of an illustrative example host; no reader-substituted placeholder in this probe's argv
curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null \
  -w 'tls=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' https://n8n.example.com/
# Public API auth, matched pair against the same URL: expect rejection without the n8n key
# (for example 401) and 200 workflow JSON with a valid key; verify both outcomes on your instance.
# The key is fed on stdin (-H @-), so it stays out of curl's argv; the one on the set -- line still enters shell history, so use a short-lived key and clear it.
# Stdin closes the argv channel only: it does not hide the key from set -x tracing or your own
# account's view of the process.
(
  trap - DEBUG RETURN ERR  # assumes a clean shell (CONTRIBUTING rule 7): no inherited DEBUG trap, extdebug, function or alias
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_N8N_API_KEY'
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit 1; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit 1; }
  case "$1" in *REPLACE_WITH_*|"") echo "substitute the API key on the set -- line above; not probing"; exit 1 ;; esac
  case "$1" in *[[:cntrl:]]*) echo "the API key must be one line with no control characters; not probing"; exit 1 ;; esac
  u=https://n8n.example.com/api/v1/workflows
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null -w 'no-key=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode}\n' "$u"
  printf 'X-N8N-API-KEY: %s\n' "$1" | curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 -w '\nwith-key=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode}\n' -H @- "$u"
)
# no-key => expect rejection by n8n; check the observed status (a fronting proxy can also 401, so hold its
# credential constant and vary only the n8n key). With-key => expect 200 and workflow JSON.
# The editor login is POST /rest/login with the default REST prefix; confirm editor access separately.
# Webhook auth: the api/v1 check says NOTHING about webhooks. Test each PRODUCTION webhook (prefix
# /webhook/, never /webhook-test/) with the method the node expects and a valid payload, three ways: no
# credential, a WRONG credential, and the valid one. With configured node credentials, missing
# Basic/JWT auth returns 401 and missing Header auth returns 403 in the pinned handler.
# Valid calls must perform the expected action; missing/wrong calls must not. A 200 alone is not proof (a workflow can respond 200 without acting); a 404 means inactive/wrong
# method/wrong path, not protected. For a None webhook that validates a signature in the workflow,
# confirm an unsigned request runs no action. Pick a workflow safe to trigger, and substitute your path.
(
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_WEBHOOK_PATH'
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit 1; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit 1; }
  case "$1" in *REPLACE_WITH_*|"") echo "substitute the webhook path on the set -- line above; not probing"; exit 1 ;; esac
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null -w 'no-cred=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode}\n' -X POST "https://n8n.example.com/webhook/$1"
)
```

Claims (full source mapping in the JSON block below):

- bind-default (REASONED; server): n8n 2.40.6 defaults N8N_LISTEN_ADDRESS to :: and N8N_PORT to 5678, exposing all interfaces.
- protocol-default (REASONED; docs): N8N_PROTOCOL defaults http; private deployment sets listener, port and host explicitly.
- container-bind (REASONED; docs): Host loopback is for a same-host proxy; container loopback blocks sibling/published access, so use a private network without publication or host-loopback 127.0.0.1:5678:5678.
- other-ports (REASONED; docs): Keep Postgres and task-runner broker ports unpublished and publish only the HTTPS proxy.
- public-url (REASONED; docs): Set N8N_PROTOCOL=https and the full N8N_WEBHOOK_URL; WEBHOOK_URL is deprecated from 2.35.0 but still warns and works.
- secure-cookie (REASONED; docs, server): Retain N8N_SECURE_COOKIE=true, its default.
- proxy-hops (REASONED; docs): Set N8N_PROXY_HOPS to the trusted hop count for forwarded client IPs and rate limiting; public webhooks do not require a public editor.
- native-tls (REASONED; docs): N8N_PROTOCOL=https with N8N_SSL_KEY/N8N_SSL_CERT enables native TLS.
- owner (REASONED; runtime): Finish first-run owner setup before publication. The pinned owner setup handler skips authentication and issues an owner session cookie.
- user-mfa (REASONED; docs): Individual users can enable two-factor authentication, subject to version/licence availability.
- mfa-enforcement (REASONED; policy): Enforce MFA through Settings &gt; Security or N8N_MFA_ENFORCED_ENABLED with N8N_SECURITY_POLICY_MANAGED_BY_ENV; env policy requires 2.18.0+ and self-hosted Business/Enterprise.
- sso-mfa (REASONED; docs): Instance MFA enforcement excludes SSO logins; enforce their MFA at the identity provider.
- encryption (REASONED; docs): Stored credentials are encrypted; unset N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY generates a key under ~/.n8n, not plaintext; losing it makes retained credentials unrecoverable.
- key-custody (REASONED; docs): Set the same encryption key across workers/replicas, back it up separately from the database and exclude it from source and images.
- webhook-auth (REASONED; docs): Webhook None is open; controlled callers use per-node Basic, Header or JWT auth with the matching credential.
- auth-boundaries (REASONED; docs): Editor sessions, /api/v1 with X-N8N-API-KEY and per-node webhook auth are separate boundaries.
- signature (REASONED; docs): A None webhook must validate the provider signature before downstream processing when callers cannot supply native webhook credentials.
- code-execution (REASONED; docs, v2-docs, runtime, v2-default, v1-default, v2-later-default): Code runs JavaScript/Python and Execute Command a shell child of n8n; NODES_EXCLUDE turns Execute Command off by default at 2.40.6, and with Local File Trigger at 2.0.0 and 2.43.8, while 1.123.85 (1.x line) excludes none. The unversioned rolling 2.0 changes page also lists both as disabled by default in 2.0.
- code-execution-introduced (REASONED; v2-change, v2-later-commits, v2-first-default, v1-first-default, v1-default): Commit a4757cf0 (2025-12-01) changed the n8n NODES_EXCLUDE default in nodes.config.ts from none to Execute Command and Local File Trigger; 2.0.0-rc.0, the lowest-version 2.x tag, excludes both, 1.123.0 and 1.123.85 exclude none, and four later nodes.config.ts commits through ea8417e2 keep the default.
- code-execution-tags (REASONED; v1-first-default, v1-default, v2-first-default, v2-last-tag-default): This guide's assessment of n8n nodes.config.ts at each tag, as of October 2026: the NODES_EXCLUDE default is empty at every 1.123.x tag and excludes Execute Command and Local File Trigger at every 2.x tag from 2.0.0-rc.0 through 2.45.0. Releases after 2.45.0 are not covered, and no release was run.
- runners (REASONED; docs): Use hardened external task runners; vendor describes internal mode as insecure by design.
- environment (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, keep workflow `$env` access blocked with `N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=true`; the proxy is blocked unless it is `false`. This guide's assessment is that this guard alone does not establish isolation of every node or Code `process.env`.
- environment-js-context (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, the JS task runner builds a context with module resolution, console, workflow static data, selected native globals, the data proxy, RPC and additional properties. This guide reasons that no direct `process` binding appears in the explicit native list or context; imported modules and injected properties prevent treating that omission as complete `process.env` isolation.
- environment-js-state (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, the JS data proxy receives `envProviderState`; if absent, its fallback is `env: {}`, `isEnvAccessBlocked: false` and `isProcessAvailable: true`. This guide reasons that the fallback avoids using the runner environment for `$env`; the cited consumer does not establish the contents or production of incoming state.
- environment-js-state-producer (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, `createEnvProviderState` sets `env` to `{}` unless `process` exists and `N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE` is `false`, and otherwise to that process's `process.env`. The node context's `startJob` calls it and passes the result through `startRunnerTask` to `TaskRequester.startTask`, which stores it in the task data.
- environment-js-state-transport (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the requester answers a runner's data request with that state, replaced by `env: {}` unless the request's `env` flag is set, and the broker forwards the answer to the runner. The JS runner sets the flag when its parser finds `$env` in the code or cannot parse the code.
- environment-js-state-exposure (REASONED; runtime): This guide infers from the cited producer, requester and parser sources that, with `N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE=false`, a JS Code task using `$env` receives the whole environment of the n8n process running the node, including any secrets set there, even on an external runner; with the variable unset or set to anything else it receives `env: {}`. No run observed this.
- environment-js-execution (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, JS all-items and per-item execution use `runInContext` in secure mode and `runDirectly` in insecure mode. This guide reasons that the latter, using `new Function` with `with(context)`, can resolve ambient `process.env` unless shadowed; this is not a live demonstration or proof of complete isolation in secure mode.
- environment-js-require (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, JS Code's `require` is the runner's resolver, which loads a builtin or external module only if its exact name is in `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN` or `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL`, both empty by default, or the list is `*`. This guide infers that allowing `process`, `child_process` or `*` lets user code reach the runner process's own environment.
- environment-python (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, Python all-items and per-item execution clear `os.environ` before user code only if `runner_env_deny` is true; the runner sets it from `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS`, read with default `True`, so by default they clear it, and when false, they do not clear the task process environment. This guide did not establish effective module access.
- environment-python-setting (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, Python `main.py` builds the runner configuration with `TaskRunnerConfig.from_env()`, which reads `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS` with `read_bool_env`; that returns its default when `read_env` returns `None`, otherwise true only when the trimmed, lower-cased value is `true`. This guide reasons that any other set value, such as `1`, disables clearing `os.environ` before user code.
- environment-python-reader (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, Python `read_env` reads `os.environ` first, otherwise a file named by the corresponding `_FILE` variable, or returns `None`. This guide assesses that this configuration reader does not itself establish which environment values user code can access.
- environment-python-allowlists (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the Python runner reads `N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW` and `N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW` as comma lists that default to empty, so no module is allowed unless set, and `*` must stand alone; checks use the top-level module name. `N8N_RUNNERS_BUILTINS_DENY` defaults to a list including `eval`, `exec`, `open` and `getattr`.
- environment-python-enforcement (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the Python runner checks user code's imports against those allowlists before execution unless both are `*`; the executor limits `sys.modules` to allowed modules, a fixed safe set and their submodules, removes denied builtins and replaces `__import__` and `importlib`'s import entry points with allowlist-checking callables. Effective module access was not observed.
- environment-launcher (REASONED; launcher): Launcher 1.5.1 prepares the runner environment from its own `LANG`, `PATH`, `TZ` and `TERM` plus names in `allowed-env`; `env-overrides` sets values directly. This guide advises keeping secrets out of `allowed-env` and keeping that list narrow, because listed values can enter the runner process environment.
- environment-launcher-runtime (REASONED; launcher): Launcher 1.5.1 sets the task broker URI, health-check enable flag and port, and legacy auto-shutdown and task timeouts. It removes inherited required runtime keys, including the grant token, and ignores their `env-overrides`; other overrides replace prior values, while grant-token insertion is not shown by this preparation function.
- environment-launcher-grant (REASONED; launcher): From source reading of launcher 1.5.1, the launch command builds the runner environment with `PrepareRunnerEnv`, fetches a grant token from the task broker, appends `N8N_RUNNERS_GRANT_TOKEN` to that environment and sets the result as the runner command's environment.
- environment-launcher-tags (REASONED; launcher, launcher-150): From source reading of the launcher's release tags, `internal/env/env.go` is identical at every tag from 1.3.1 to 1.5.1, `config.go` keeps its `allowed-env` and `env-overrides` fields at each of them, and `launch.go` is identical at 1.5.0 and 1.5.1. Tags before 1.3.1, untagged commits and later releases are not covered.
- environment-image-launcher (REASONED; runtime, launcher-150): From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image Dockerfile defaults `LAUNCHER_VERSION` to 1.5.0, not the 1.5.1 this guide cites, installs that launcher release as the image entrypoint and copies `n8n-task-runners.json` to `/etc/n8n-task-runners.json`. This is image source; a published image's launcher and configuration are not established.
- environment-image-config (REASONED; runtime): From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image's `n8n-task-runners.json` lists `PATH` and timeout, concurrency, Sentry and version variables in both runners' `allowed-env`, plus `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `NODE_PATH` and `HOME` for JS and the launcher log level for Python. This is image source, not a published image or a deployed configuration.
- environment-image-allowlists (REASONED; runtime): From source reading, the n8n 2.40.6 runners image's `n8n-task-runners.json` uses `env-overrides` to set `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN` to `crypto` and `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL` to `moment` for the JS runner and `N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW` and `N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW` to empty for the Python runner. This is image source, not a published image or a deployed configuration.
- environment-internal-mode (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, `N8N_RUNNERS_MODE` defaults to `internal`, in which the task runner module starts a JS runner and, if the Python requirements check passes, a Python runner as child processes of n8n. Each spawn passes an explicit `env` object of named variables rather than n8n's whole `process.env`.
- environment-internal-env (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, the internal JS runner's `env` copies `PATH`, `HOME`, `NODE_PATH`, `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`, both `NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_*` lists, four Sentry names, `N8N_RUNNERS_INSECURE_MODE` and two shutdown settings from n8n, and the Python runner's copies `PATH`, `HOME`, its module settings and `N8N_BLOCK_RUNNER_ENV_ACCESS`; both add the grant token and runner settings.
- environment-internal-docs (REASONED; docs): The n8n task runner set-up page, checked October 2026, documents that an internal-mode runner is a child process sharing n8n's uid and gid, that code escaping its sandbox has the same access as n8n, including to stored credentials, and that n8n logs a deprecation warning for internal mode, deprecated from n8n 3.0, including when `N8N_RUNNERS_MODE` isn't set.
- environment-exec-command (REASONED; runtime): From source reading at n8n 2.40.6, Execute Command spawns its command with `cwd`, `shell: true` and `detached` options and no `env` option. This guide infers from Node.js `child_process` semantics, not cited here, that the shell inherits the environment of the n8n process running the node; no run observed this.
- environment-nodes-search (REASONED; runtime): This guide's `git grep -l` at n8n 2.40.6 for `startJob` or `child_process` under `packages/nodes-base/nodes` and `packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/nodes` matched, outside test files, only the Code node's JS and Python task-runner sandboxes and Execute Command. This bounds those spellings and paths only, not every node that runs code or starts processes.
- environment-limits (REASONED; runtime, launcher, launcher-150): This guide's assessment is that the cited n8n 2.40.6 runner and launcher 1.5.1 sources describe specific environment controls, not complete host/container isolation. Internal-mode isolation beyond the spawn environment, nodes beyond the searched spellings and paths, other launcher versions, deployed configuration and complete Code `process.env` isolation remain unestablished.
- js-modules (REASONED; docs): Narrow NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN/NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL in external launcher's /etc/n8n-task-runners.json env-overrides; main-container values are overridden.
- python-modules (REASONED; docs): Set N8N_RUNNERS_STDLIB_ALLOW/N8N_RUNNERS_EXTERNAL_ALLOW explicitly; wildcard grants broad module access and version-dependent defaults need confirmation.
- ssrf (REASONED; ssrf): Enable N8N_SSRF_PROTECTION_ENABLED from 2.12.0 and restrict network egress; the app filter does not contain arbitrary code/command networking.
- verify-inventory (REASONED; docs, runtime): Confirm completed owner setup without creating an owner as a probe; the pinned setup handler skips authentication. ss is local inventory, not firewall/NAT proof; check actual public IPv4/IPv6 paths separately.
- verify-tls (REASONED; docs): HTTPS reachability tests TLS, not authentication.
- public-controller-order (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, public controllers precede the lazy validator; every controller route gets auth middleware (401 Unauthorized if the auth registry does not authenticate), and GET /workflows then requires API key scope workflow:list (403 Forbidden if no token grant satisfies it). This guide infers a controller can respond before the validator's security check, not skip authentication.
- public-api-wiring (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, @PublicApiController records a controller's base path and public-API flag and registers it as a service; @Get and @ApiResponse record method, path, success status and response DTO in controller metadata. public-api/index.ts imports the v1 controllers and builds a router per v* folder; the server mounts them under its publicApi.path setting, whose default is not established here.
- public-api-strategies (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, the server registers ApiKeyAuthStrategy then SessionCookieAuthStrategy, and token-exchange init appends ScopedJwtStrategy only after its N8N_ENV_FEAT_TOKEN_EXCHANGE check. Each abstains without its credential (x-n8n-api-key header; n8n-auth cookie; Bearer token or x-n8n-api-key), so the registry returns false; registrations outside the cited files are not established.
- workflows-list-status (REASONED; runtime): At n8n 2.40.6, GET /workflows declares @ApiResponse(200, WorkflowListPublicDto); resolveSuccessStatus returns a route's declared status or throws if none is declared, and, when the handler returns and the DTO parse succeeds, the registry sends 200 with JSON parsed by that DTO (a data array and a nullable nextCursor). This is source reasoning; no response was observed.
- verify-api (REASONED; docs, runtime, validator): At /api/v1/workflows, compare no X-N8N-API-KEY and a valid key (fixed proxy credentials, key on stdin); on success n8n 2.40.6 returns data and nextCursor JSON (spec: 200). This guide assesses 401 if no auth strategy authenticates a keyless call, or a selected express-openapi-validator 5.5.3 security failure lacks a status; rejection and 200 stay unobserved expectations; proxies can alter status.
- verify-editor (REASONED; runtime): Confirm editor session login at /rest/login separately; the pinned login controller registers POST /login under the default rest endpoint, which is configurable. A protected public API does not prove editor protection.
- verify-webhook (REASONED; docs, runtime): Use each production /webhook/ method and valid payload with missing/wrong/valid credentials; the pinned Webhook handler returns 401 for missing Basic/JWT credentials and 403 for missing Header credentials when node credentials are configured. Verify actions, not status alone.
- verify-signature (REASONED; docs): For None plus workflow signature checks, unsigned calls must run no action; 404 from inactive/wrong path/method is not protection.

==> code-server.md

# code-server: browser VS Code without giving away the machine

code-server runs VS Code on a server for use in a browser, and its terminal runs commands on that server. This guide helps your AI assistant configure it securely, including SSH forwarding first, a tailnet or MFA-protected tunnel next, and otherwise a loopback bind behind a TLS proxy adding MFA.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/code-server.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against code-server v4.137.0. Metadata reviewed 2026-09-27; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 18 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

code-server runs a terminal in the browser, so exposure equals remote code execution. Its own documentation is blunt: never expose it directly to the internet without authentication and encryption.

## 1. Prefer no exposure at all

The code-server docs recommend SSH port forwarding first, which needs no additional setup:

```bash
ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L 127.0.0.1:8080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@host   # then open http://127.0.0.1:8080 locally
```

[tailscale.md](tailscale.md) (serve, tailnet-only) and [cloudflare.md](cloudflare.md) (tunnel plus Access with MFA) are the equivalents when SSH is unavailable.

## 2. If it must be reachable: config.yaml

Edit the generated `~/.config/code-server/config.yaml` in place; creating this file yourself before the first start removes the random password code-server would have generated, and password auth with neither `password` nor `hashed-password` fails to start. This is a partial configuration; keep the generated `password` entry (or set another supported credential):

```yaml
bind-addr: 127.0.0.1:8080     # keep loopback behind a proxy or tunnel
auth: password                # default; keep the generated password in this file
cert: false                   # TLS is off by default; terminate it at the proxy (below)
```

Password attempts are rate-limited (2 per minute plus 12 per hour). Replace the generated password with your own long random value, and treat the config file as a secret ([secrets.md](secrets.md)). Know where the effective credential comes from: the `PASSWORD` and `HASHED_PASSWORD` environment variables override the file (the hashed form wins over plaintext), there is no `--password` command-line flag, and any flag passed to code-server overrides the file, so inspect the launcher (including `--bind-addr` and `--config`, and `CODE_SERVER_CONFIG`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` for the config path) rather than assuming the file is authoritative. code-server does not terminate TLS by default (`cert: false`); a bare `--cert` (or `cert: true`) generates a self-signed certificate at `~/.local/share/code-server/self-signed.crt`, while `--cert` with `--cert-key` uses a certificate you supply. For public access, the docs' supported pattern is a reverse proxy with a real certificate: [caddy.md](caddy.md) or [nginx.md](nginx.md) with [free-certificates.md](free-certificates.md), with MFA added at that layer ([mfa.md](mfa.md)) since the built-in login is a single factor. Never disable certificate validation with `-k`.

code-server also proxies other local services through `/proxy/<port>/`, `/absproxy/<port>/` (which does not strip the path prefix), and per-port subdomains under `--proxy-domain`. These routes use code-server's own authentication, so `auth: none` exposes them too, and `--skip-auth-preflight` lets preflight requests through unauthenticated; if you do not need port forwarding, turn it off with `--disable-proxy`, and require your fronting auth and MFA on every enabled path, subdomain, and WebSocket route. Loopback binding only limits inbound reach: the terminal, extensions, and any service code-server proxies can still make outbound requests, so run the process with only the permissions and network it needs and keep it off cloud metadata and internal endpoints ([egress-metadata.md](egress-metadata.md)).

## 3. Verify

```bash
# REASONED: editor, origin and proxy checks follow the cited code-server authentication and proxy
# documentation; no isolated network namespace is available for authorized live listeners.
# Shell syntax and guard checks do not demonstrate authentication or origin isolation.
# ss is a listener inventory in THIS namespace - not a firewall, publication, or authentication check.
ss -tlnp   # expect 8080 on loopback or a private address; then probe the public origin directly (below):
           # ANY HTTP response there (even a 401) means the origin is reachable, which is a finding on its own
# Direct-origin reachability: connect straight to the public IP and published port while keeping the URL
# hostname for TLS. From an untrusted external host, repeat for every public IPv4/IPv6 address and port.
(
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_ORIGIN_URL' 'REPLACE_WITH_PUBLIC_IP' 'REPLACE_WITH_PUBLISHED_PORT'
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo 'paste the whole block; not probing'; exit 2; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 3 ] || { echo 'exactly three values are required; not probing'; exit 2; }
  case "$1|$2|$3" in
    *REPLACE_WITH_*) echo 'substitute all values inside the quotes; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  case "$1" in
    http://*|https://*) ;;
    *) echo 'an HTTP or HTTPS origin URL is required; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  [ -n "$2" ] || { echo 'a public IP is required; not probing'; exit 2; }
  case "$3" in
    ''|*[!0123456789]*) echo 'a numeric published port is required; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  # bracket an IPv6 literal in REPLACE_WITH_PUBLIC_IP. Any HTTP response (incl 401/403) = a finding;
  # http=000 is not a pass (a certificate, timeout, or local error is inconclusive). Never add -k.
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    --connect-to "::$2:$3" -o /dev/null \
    -w 'origin http=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "$1"
)
# Auth discrimination against the SAME editor URL: a proxy 401 proves nothing, so pair an unauthenticated
# request with an authenticated one and confirm the editor in a fresh browser session too.
(
  trap - DEBUG RETURN ERR  # assumes a clean shell (CONTRIBUTING rule 7): no inherited DEBUG trap, extdebug, function or alias
  set +x +a +e
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_HTTPS_EDITOR_URL'
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo 'paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing'; exit 2; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo 'the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing'; exit 2; }
  case "$1" in
    ''|*REPLACE_WITH_*) echo 'substitute the editor URL; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
    https://*) ;;
    *) echo 'an HTTPS URL is required; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  # 1) Unauthenticated: follow redirects and inspect the FINAL body - login or challenge, never the editor.
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    --location --max-redirs 5 --proto-redir '=https' \
    -w '\nunauth http=%{http_code} url=%{url_effective} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "$1"
  # 2) Authenticated positive control: paste a cookie from a valid browser session; it enters via stdin
  #    (curl --header @-), never argv. The authenticated response must contain the editor.
  #    The hidden prompt keeps it out of shell history and set +x keeps it out of set -x tracing. Stdin
  #    closes the argv channel only: the account owner and root can still read it in the subshell and curl.
  { unset -n code_server_cookie && unset -v code_server_cookie; } 2>/dev/null ||
    { echo 'cannot initialize cookie input; not probing'; exit 2; }
  { unset -n IFS; } 2>/dev/null || { echo 'a readonly IFS is set in this shell; not probing'; exit 2; }
  IFS= read -r -s -p 'Cookie value (name=value; name=value), then Enter: ' code_server_cookie < /dev/tty || exit 2
  printf '\n'
  case "$code_server_cookie" in
    ''|*REPLACE_WITH_*|*[[:cntrl:]]*) echo 'a valid session cookie is required; not probing'; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  printf 'Cookie: %s\n' "$code_server_cookie" |
    curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
      --location --max-redirs 5 --proto-redir '=https' --header @- \
      -w '\nauth http=%{http_code} url=%{url_effective} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "$1"
)
# Fixed: unauthenticated lands on login or challenge and authenticated reaches the editor. For MFA, confirm
# password-only access cannot open the editor and completing the second factor can. A transport, certificate,
# or unsuccessful positive control is inconclusive, not a pass.
```

REASONED: preceding block; listener inventory, direct-origin isolation, paired editor access and MFA, per the guide's cited code-server v4.137.0 deployment guide and HTTP controls. No editor, proxy, IdP or external probe host is available; listeners are denied locally. bash -n and ShellCheck 0.11.0 exited 0 without diagnostics and config YAML parsed. Placeholder, missing-assignment, short, empty and embedded-placeholder inputs printed refusal messages without reaching curl stubs; substituted inputs reached the stubs; under a pseudo-terminal, empty, placeholder and control-character cookies exited 2 before the authenticated request, and a fixture cookie exited 0 and reached curl only on stdin as a `Cookie:` header. Live outcomes remain unobserved: exposed access opens the editor anonymously or bypasses MFA; fixed access isolates the origin, challenges anonymous users and requires the second factor while admitting the authenticated control. An unauthenticated editor in a private browser window means whoever finds the URL owns the host. Paste the cookie value alone at the hidden prompt: a multi-line paste leaves every line after the first for your shell to run.

# Self-hosted error trackers: Sentry and GlitchTip

Sentry and GlitchTip are error trackers: apps send them crash reports with stack traces and request details. This guide helps your AI assistant configure an instance securely, including a loopback bind behind a TLS proxy, open sign-up off (GlitchTip ships it on), required MFA, and unpublished backing stores.

<a id="ai-assistant-prompt"></a>

If an AI assistant is helping you secure a deployment, give it the prompt below:

```text
Read the secureconfig guide at
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jposluns/secureconfig/main/self-hosted-error-trackers.md
in full, including the section for AI assistants at the end. Then, for my
deployment: state which of its recommendations apply and the exact changes
to make; compare the versions the guide was written against with the
releases I am running and with the vendor's current releases, and flag any
guidance a newer release may have changed; and run or adapt the guide's
Verify steps where you can. List separately every item you could not
verify instead of reporting it as passed.
```

Written against Sentry and self-hosted distribution 26.8.0 and GlitchTip backend v6.2.6; 3 further sources carry no recorded version. Metadata reviewed 2026-09-26; documentation checked September 2026. The guide records 23 claims, all reasoned from cited sources.

A newer release of any of this software can make version-specific details here outdated. To prioritize an update, open a GitHub issue, send a pull request, add a request under [requests/](requests/README.md), or reach the maintainer as [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes. The machine-readable version basis and claim list are in [the section for AI assistants](#about-the-ai-assistant-section-below) at the end of this guide.

An error tracker exists to collect what your application would otherwise hide: stack traces, the source lines around each frame, request bodies and headers, environment variables, release and server names, and whatever user context the SDK attaches. That makes an exposed tracker one of the richest leaks in a deployment, because it aggregates secrets, tokens, and personal data that were never meant to leave the app, and it does so in a searchable UI. The two common self-hosted choices behave differently at their most important default, so the guide takes them one at a time. [fronting-auth.md](fronting-auth.md) is the reverse-proxy pattern both rely on for TLS, [secrets.md](secrets.md) covers the signing keys, and [mfa.md](mfa.md) is the account layer. Values below are illustrative; replace them.

One thing both share: the DSN a client uses to send events is a public, client-side key by design, not a secret. It authorizes event submission and nothing else, so finding one in shipped JavaScript is expected and is not the exposure this guide is about. The exposure is the tracker's own web and API, and the data they hold.

## Sentry

The `getsentry/self-hosted` Docker Compose distribution fronts the web and API with a bundled nginx. Its published port comes from `SENTRY_BIND` in `.env`, which ships as `SENTRY_BIND=9000` (a bare port), so nginx binds `0.0.0.0:9000` and the instance answers on every interface. Bind it to loopback and let your own proxy terminate TLS in front:

```ini
# .env
SENTRY_BIND=127.0.0.1:9000
```

Everything else in the Compose file (the web and relay processes, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, and the ClickHouse and Snuba services) is an internal service that the distribution does not publish; leave it that way, because those backing stores hold the same event data with no authentication of their own.

Registration is off by default: `auth.allow-registration` defaults to `False`, so an exposed instance does not by itself let a stranger create an account. Do not turn it on for an internet-facing tracker, and create the first administrator with the superuser flag set explicitly (a plain `createuser` prompts for superuser and defaults to no):

```bash
docker compose run --rm web createuser --superuser
```

Set the rest in `sentry/config.yml`, and generate the signing key rather than copying one:

```yaml
system.url-prefix: "https://sentry.example.com"
auth.allow-registration: false
# system.secret-key: generate once with `sentry config generate-secret-key`, keep it out of version control
```

Because your proxy terminates TLS, Sentry has to be told it is behind HTTPS, or its session and CSRF cookies are never marked secure. The bundled `sentry/sentry.conf.example.py` ships the relevant settings commented out; enable them in `sentry/sentry.conf.py`:

```python
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")
USE_X_FORWARDED_HOST = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
```

One catch is specific to the bundled stack: its own nginx sets `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme`, which overwrites whatever an outer proxy sent, so if you add a TLS proxy in front of nginx on `9000` it forwards `http` and Sentry still sees plaintext. Either terminate TLS at the bundled nginx itself, or propagate the real scheme through it, and verify the scheme Sentry actually receives rather than assuming the header setting alone took effect.

Enforce member MFA and data scrubbing at the organization level (an authenticated API call, or the same fields in the org settings UI): `require2FA`, `dataScrubber`, `dataScrubberDefaults`, and `scrubIPAddresses`. Scrubbing matters precisely because the tracker ingests request data, so redacting passwords, tokens, and IPs at intake reduces what a later exposure leaks.

The file setting is authoritative for this option: `auth.allow-registration` is a prioritize-disk option, so the value in `config.yml` wins over any value stored in the database, not the other way around. Unverified until checked in your deployment: any SSO path that provisions accounts around registration, the full list of auxiliary listeners your compose revision publishes, and the effective scrubbing rules.

## GlitchTip

GlitchTip is a single Django application, and its Compose distribution publishes it on port `8000`. Its default is the opposite of Sentry's on the setting that matters most: `ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION` defaults to `True`, which means an exposed instance offers open self-signup to anyone who reaches it. Close it, and remember the value's own nuance:

```ini
# When True (the default), anyone may self-register; when False, self-signup is disabled
# after the first user exists. Set it False once your accounts are provisioned.
ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION=False
```

Bind the app to loopback or a private interface and terminate TLS at a reverse proxy, since GlitchTip serves no TLS of its own. Give it a unique `SECRET_KEY` (Django's session and CSRF signing key) and keep it out of version control. GlitchTip has supported two-factor authentication since v1.8; enable it and require it for your users. PostgreSQL and the optional Valkey or Redis are internal services; do not publish them.

Unverified until checked: the exact host bind in your Compose sample, whether MFA is enforced rather than merely available in your version, and whether any single-sign-on you add carries its own registration path around `ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION`.

## Shared exposures

- **The event data itself.** Both tools store stack traces with source context, request payloads, and user identifiers. An exposed backing store is reachable with the credentials the compose ships and expects on its internal network, so publishing it is a direct disclosure of every event it holds; an exposed web or API discloses to the degree an attacker can authenticate to it, which is why the registration default and the intake scrubbing both matter. Scrub at intake and keep the stores private.
- **Open registration.** GlitchTip ships it on; Sentry ships it off. What a self-registered stranger then reaches differs by tool: Sentry's single-organization mode adds new sign-ups to the default organization, while at GlitchTip backend v6.2.6 [the login signal](https://gitlab.com/glitchtip/glitchtip-backend/-/blob/v6.2.6/apps/users/signals.py#L16-45) adds a user with a linked social provider to an organization linked to that provider on login, with the first member of a memberless organization becoming owner. Confirm your own membership and project permissions rather than assuming a new account has none or all. Confirm the live setting rather than trusting the default.
- **The public DSN misread as a secret.** Rotating a DSN does not protect the tracker; authenticating its web and API does. Do not treat a leaked DSN as the incident.
- **Plaintext.** Neither serves TLS natively, so an instance reachable without a terminating proxy sends session cookies and the event UI in the clear.

## Verify (REASONED: listener and backing-store inventory, Sentry/GlitchTip registration, redirect handling, disposable signup, off-host backing-port reachability and HTTP-to-HTTPS routing comparisons follow the cited tracker sources; no live tracker, backing stores, authorized signup fixture or external host. Bash 5.3.9 bash -n accepted both Verify fences. With curl replaced by printf LOCAL_CURL in the complete registration subshell, https://fixture.internal/api/chat reached one marker and exit 0; empty input, original placeholders, set -- without arguments and bad value printed guard diagnostics with exit 2 and no marker. This tests those guards only, not registration, protocol reachability, redirects or TLS)

Every probe below is reasoned, not demonstrated: the authoring environment has no container runtime, so the outcomes are derived from the cited vendor sources rather than observed. A redirect to a login page, a 404, or a TLS error is inconclusive, never the fixed state.

```bash
# REASONED: listener expectations follow the cited vendor sources; no container runtime is available.
sudo ss -tlnp    # the tracker's own port only, on a private address: 9000 for Sentry, 8000 for
                 # GlitchTip; and no PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, or ClickHouse port published beside it
```

REASONED: following block; registration and backing-port checks follow the cited Sentry and GlitchTip sources; no container runtime is available.

```bash
# Registration discriminator against the plaintext listener. Substitute the URL inside the single
# quotes on the set -- line and paste the whole block so the guard runs; read the body, since an
# open form and a closed one can both return 200.
(
  set -- PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK 'REPLACE_WITH_REGISTER_URL'
  [ "${1-}" = PASTE_WHOLE_BLOCK ] || { echo "paste the whole block, including its set -- line; not probing"; exit 2; }
  shift
  [ "$#" -eq 1 ] || { echo "the set -- line needs exactly 1 value; not probing"; exit 2; }
  case "$1" in
    *REPLACE_WITH_*|"") echo "substitute a full URL on the set -- line above; not probing"; exit 2 ;;
    http://*|https://*) : ;;
    *) echo "expected an http:// or https:// URL; not probing"; exit 2 ;;
  esac
  curl -q -g -sS --noproxy '*' --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
    -w '\nhttp=%{http_code} exit=%{exitcode} err=%{errormsg}\n' "$1"
)
```

Point that block at Sentry's `http://tracker.example.com:9000/`: because the bundled config sets `SENTRY_SINGLE_ORGANIZATION`, `/auth/register/` redirects to the organization login, so follow the redirect (add `-L`) to the served login page, where an instance with registration on presents a create-account path and a closed one (the default) does not. For GlitchTip's `http://tracker.example.com:8000/`, an instance with `ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION=True` accepts a new account through its signup, and one set `False` refuses after the first user exists; confirm by attempting a throwaway registration in an operator-controlled test, never against a shared instance. For each backing store, run the same guarded block against its port from off-host: those ports speak their own protocols, not HTTP, so read the connection outcome in the `exit` and `err` fields (a refused connection is the closed, fixed state; an accepted one is reachable) rather than any HTTP status. The `ss` inventory shows what Docker has published on the host, but a container port can be reachable through Docker's forwarding without a matching host socket, so the off-host probe is what proves it closed. Distinguish the public HTTPS proxy from the direct backend ports, and confirm plain HTTP to the web redirects to that proxy rather than serving the app. A reachable login page alone proves only that the port is open, not that registration or the backing stores are closed.

## Common mistakes

- Publishing Sentry with the shipped `SENTRY_BIND=9000`, which binds every interface, instead of a loopback address behind a proxy.
- Leaving GlitchTip's `ENABLE_USER_REGISTRATION` at its default `True` on an internet-facing instance, so anyone can self-register.
- Treating a leaked client DSN as the exposure while the tracker's own web and API stay unauthenticated.
- Publishing a backing service (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, ClickHouse) beside the tracker, which holds the same event data with no auth of its own.
- Skipping data scrubbing, so secrets and personal data captured in events sit in the tracker in the clear.

## Sources (checked September 2026)
